texts.text: Counting boards and abaci let people calculate by moving pebbles or beads in columns, without written figures. A marble board from Salamis, Greece, of about 300 BCE, is the oldest surviving one, although some think it served for games. The Chinese bead abacus, the suanpan, grew from counting-rod practice and is pictured in Ming-dynasty books.

Around 1800 BCE, or perhaps somewhat later, Semitic-speaking people in contact with Egypt adapted a few dozen signs to stand for single consonants. Inscriptions from Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and Wadi el-Hol in Egypt are early examples. By about 1050 BCE the Phoenician form, with 22 letters and no vowel signs, was standardised and spread through Mediterranean trade.

Abolition is the legal ending of slavery or hereditary bondage, freeing those held and forbidding re-enslavement. Solon cancelled debt bondage at Athens around 594 BCE; Britain's Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended slavery in most of its colonies, and Russia emancipated its serfs in 1861. Freed people often faced apprenticeship, redemption debts or land shortages; some former owners received compensation.

Absolute monarchy is rule by a monarch claiming authority that no estate, parliament or assembly can call to account, often justified by divine right. Louis XIV of France is the standard example, and Peter I of Russia is often grouped with him. Rulers centralised taxation, armies and administration, yet still bargained with nobles, churches, courts and local privileges.

Alternating current can be raised by a transformer to high voltage, sent far with small losses, and lowered again for use. Engineers at the Ganz works in Budapest built practical closed-core transformers in 1884-85. In 1891 a three-phase line carried power about 175 km from Lauffen to Frankfurt, and from 1896 Niagara's generators supplied Buffalo.

Academic exchange programmes fund students and scholars to study and teach in other countries. The Fulbright Program, established by the United States in 1946, used proceeds from sales of surplus war property to pay for exchanges. The European Union's Erasmus Programme, begun in 1987, has allowed millions of students to spend part of their studies at a university abroad.

Additive manufacturing builds an object layer by layer from a digital design instead of cutting it from a block or casting it in a mould. Charles Hull filed a patent on stereolithography, which hardens liquid resin with ultraviolet light, in 1984; it was granted in 1986. Hideo Kodama in Japan had described similar layering in 1981, and other methods followed.

Before compound glues, toolmakers used single substances such as bitumen, found on Levallois flints at Umm el Tlel, Syria, about 71,000 years ago. At Sibudu Cave, South Africa, around 70,000 years ago, people mixed plant gum with red ochre, or gum with fat, to fix stone points into handles; experiments show ochre strengthens such glues.

Administrative courts let citizens challenge the acts of government officials before specialist judges. France's Council of State, created under Napoleon in 1799, advised on disputes between citizens and the administration. A law of 1872 gave it independent judicial power, and its rulings came to annul acts by which officials exceeded their legal authority.

Administrative procedure law sets rules for how government agencies make decisions. The United States Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 required agencies to publish proposed rules, invite public comment and allow courts to review their actions. West Germany adopted a federal Administrative Procedure Act in 1976, requiring authorities to hear affected parties and to give reasons for their decisions.

Under adoptive succession a ruler adopts a capable adult as heir instead of relying on birth alone. Rome's emperors from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius, 96 to 180 CE, largely followed this pattern: Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus each came to power by adoption. The period is often remembered as the era of the five good emperors.

Advertising agencies buy space in newspapers and magazines for clients and write notices telling readers what is for sale. Volney B. Palmer, often called the first American advertising agent, opened an agency in Philadelphia around 1841, selling space in country newspapers. Later agencies, such as N. W. Ayer & Son, founded in 1869, also designed advertisements and planned campaigns.

Aerial reconnaissance observes and photographs territory from the air. Observers in tethered balloons watched battles from the 1790s, but the first reconnaissance flight by aeroplane is generally credited to an Italian pilot over Libya in 1911, during the Italo-Turkish War. In the First World War both sides photographed the Western Front daily, mapping enemy trenches in fine detail.

In an age-set system, boys initiated in the same years form a named set that stays together for life. The set serves first as warriors guarding herds and camps, then advances as a body to the grades of married men and ruling elders. Ethnographers recorded such systems among the Maasai and Nuer and in the Oromo gada system.

Agricultural chemistry asks what plants take from the soil and why fields lose fertility. Humphry Davy's lectures, published in 1813, were an early textbook. In 1840 Justus von Liebig argued that plants need mineral nutrients, notably nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and that the scarcest limits growth. From 1843 Rothamsted field trials tested such claims, partly refuting Liebig on nitrogen.

Agricultural colleges applied chemistry, botany and field trials to farming and trained estate managers and farmers' sons. In Württemberg, an agricultural institute opened at Hohenheim in 1818, and many German states followed with their own academies. In the United States, the Morrill Act of 1862 granted federal land to fund state colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts.

Agricultural extension carries research from colleges and experiment stations to working farmers. In the United States, the Smith-Lever Act of 1914 created the Cooperative Extension Service, funding county agents linked to land-grant colleges. Agents ran demonstration plots, visited farms and organized clubs, teaching improved seed, fertilizer use and methods. Many countries later built similar services, notably during the Green Revolution.

Agronomic treatises are practical manuals on farming, covering crops, soils, manuring, livestock and estate management. In Rome, Cato the Elder wrote On Agriculture about 160 BCE, the oldest surviving complete work of Latin prose, advising owners of slave-worked estates. In Han China, Fan Shengzhi wrote a farming manual in the first century BCE, now known only from quotations.

Civil aviation agreements set the rules by which aircraft cross and land in other states' territory. The Paris Convention of 1919 affirmed each state's sovereignty over the airspace above it. The Chicago Convention of 1944 created the International Civil Aviation Organization, which sets common safety and navigation standards, while separate bilateral agreements granted airlines their landing and traffic rights.

Powered heavier-than-air flight combines lifting wings, a light engine, propellers and three-axis control. Building on their 1900-1902 gliders, the Wright brothers made the first sustained, controlled powered flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903, the longest lasting 59 seconds. Within a decade aircraft flew military reconnaissance; in the First World War they also bombed and fought.

The all-metal monoplane replaced wood, wire and fabric with a metal structure whose skin carries load. Hugo Junkers flew the J 1, built of sheet steel, in 1915, and aluminium alloys later made the approach light enough for wide use. By the mid-1930s airliners such as the Douglas DC-3 set the pattern for strong, streamlined, long-range aircraft.

Alchemy sought to transform substances, perfecting metals or preparing elixirs, and joined craft knowledge with philosophy and religion. In China it was tied to Daoist pursuits of longevity. In Roman Egypt, Greek-writing practitioners drew on goldsmiths' techniques; Zosimos of Panopolis, active around 300 CE, is the earliest whose writings survive. Whether these traditions share an origin is an open question.

Algebra finds unknown quantities by general rules. In Baghdad around 820, al-Khwarizmi gave the first systematic treatment of linear and quadratic equations, justifying steps geometrically, and his title gave the subject its name. In India Brahmagupta had already given rules for zero and negatives; in China, Qin Jiushao (1247) and Zhu Shijie (1303) solved high-degree equations.

The alimenta were Roman imperial foundations that paid monthly allowances to support poor freeborn children in Italian towns. Begun under Nerva around 97 CE and greatly expanded by Trajan, they were funded by interest on loans made to local landowners against their estates. Bronze tablets from Veleia and the territory of the Ligures Baebiani record the scheme in detail.

Greeks adapted Phoenician letters, probably during the eighth century BCE, and reassigned some signs for consonants Greek lacked to write vowels. The result recorded consonants and vowels alike, so a reader could sound out unfamiliar words. Early examples are short inscriptions on pottery, and the Greek alphabet became the source, directly or through Etruscan, of Latin and Cyrillic.

Aluminium is abundant in rocks but bound tightly to oxygen, so the metal was long a costly rarity. In 1886 Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France independently found that alumina dissolved in molten cryolite could be split by electric current. With Karl Josef Bayer's cheaper alumina from bauxite (1888-89), prices fell steeply.

Surgical anaesthesia makes a patient insensible to pain during an operation. In Boston in 1846, William Morton publicly demonstrated ether at Massachusetts General Hospital, though Crawford Long had used ether in Georgia from 1842 and priority remains contested. James Simpson introduced chloroform in Scotland in 1847. In Japan, Hanaoka Seishū had operated under his own anaesthetic formula in 1804.

Systematic anatomy describes the body's structures from repeated human dissection rather than inherited authority. Andreas Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica, printed in Basel in 1543, corrected errors that Galen had drawn partly from animal dissection and set its text beside detailed woodcut plates. Human dissection had been taught in Italian universities since the early fourteenth century.

As people settled in villages, many kept their dead close. Between roughly 9000 and 7000 BCE, villagers at Jericho removed skulls and modelled faces on them in plaster, perhaps to honour ancestors. At Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, from about 7000 BCE, the dead were buried beneath house floors. Honouring lineage ancestors helped tie a household's claim on house and land to descent.

Harnessing cattle to pull loads multiplied the work one farmer could do. Deformed foot bones of cattle from Neolithic sites in the western Balkans, about 6100 to 4500 BCE, suggest occasional light pulling. Regular traction is clearer from the fourth millennium BCE, when ploughs and wheeled vehicles appear in Europe and Mesopotamia, part of wider use of living animals.

An anti-corruption commission is an independent agency empowered to investigate, and often arrest, officials who take bribes. Singapore's Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau was founded in 1952 under British colonial rule. Hong Kong created its Independent Commission Against Corruption in 1974, after scandals involving police officers, and it became a widely studied model combining investigation, prevention and public education.

Later antibiotics widened the range of bacteria that drugs could treat. Streptomycin, isolated from a soil microbe by Albert Schatz in Selman Waksman's laboratory in 1943, soon proved effective against tuberculosis; credit for it was later contested. Chloramphenicol (1947) and the first tetracycline, chlortetracycline (1948), followed, both found by screening soil organisms.

Penicillin was the first antibiotic to be produced industrially. Alexander Fleming noticed in London in 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria around it. Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and colleagues at Oxford purified it and showed its effect in patients in 1940-41. Wartime deep-tank fermentation in the United States made mass production possible by 1943-44.

Antibiotic resistance arises because drugs select for bacteria that survive them. A penicillin-destroying enzyme was described in 1940, and resistant staphylococci spread through hospitals in the 1950s. Britain's 1948 streptomycin trial showed tuberculosis becoming resistant under single-drug treatment, which led to combination therapy. Managing resistance relies on surveillance, prudent prescribing and new drugs.

Antiscorbutics are foods that prevent or cure scurvy, a disease now known to be caused by lack of vitamin C. In 1747 the naval surgeon James Lind compared remedies aboard HMS Salisbury and found that oranges and lemons brought rapid recovery. Lemon juice became a regular Royal Navy issue in 1795, and scurvy sharply declined on its ships.

Antiseptic surgery applied germ theory to wounds. In Glasgow from 1867, Joseph Lister treated dressings, instruments and incisions with carbolic acid and reported fewer infections after compound fractures. Aseptic practice later aimed to keep germs out entirely, with sterilised instruments, gowns and gloves. Together with anaesthesia, it made abdominal and other long operations survivable far more often.

Antitrust or competition law forbids firms to fix prices or carve up markets, and lets courts break up monopolies. The United States passed the Sherman Act in 1890 in response to giant trusts in oil, railways and other industries; Canada had enacted a similar law a year earlier. Standard Oil was ordered broken up under the Sherman Act in 1911.

Antiviral drugs interfere with a virus's own replication while sparing the patient's cells. Acyclovir, developed at Burroughs Wellcome from 1974 with Gertrude Elion's team, is activated mainly inside herpes-infected cells. Zidovudine became the first approved HIV drug in 1987, and from 1996 combinations of drugs with different targets made HIV a manageable chronic infection where treatment was available.

Courts of appeal let a higher authority review local judgments and hear complaints against officials. In the Abbasid caliphate, mazalim courts, held by the caliph or his deputies, heard grievances about abuses by governors and tax collectors. In thirteenth-century France the Parlement of Paris took shape as the royal court that heard appeals from lordly and provincial courts.

Rulers who govern through appointed officials rely on agents they choose, pay and can dismiss, who act on written instructions and report in writing, holding office by commission, not birth. Old Kingdom Egypt, in the third millennium BCE, had ranked royal officials headed by a vizier, and the Third Dynasty of Ur (about 2100-2000 BCE) placed governors over its provinces.

Apprenticeship binds a young person to a master for years of training, usually in return for board and lodging. Around 1268 the provost of Paris, Étienne Boileau, compiled the Livre des métiers, recording the statutes of about a hundred city crafts, including the length and terms of apprenticeship. Completing training allowed the apprentice to work as a journeyman.

An arcaded aqueduct keeps a water channel on its gentle gradient across valleys by raising it on tiers of arches. Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia of 312 BCE, ran almost entirely underground; the Aqua Marcia, begun in 144 BCE, carried water on long arcades. By the early third century CE, eleven aqueducts supplied the city's fountains, baths and houses.

An aqueduct channel is a built conduit that carries water by gravity over long distances, which requires surveying a slight, steady downward slope. To supply Nineveh, the Assyrian king Sennacherib built canals around 700 BCE, including a stone aqueduct bridge at Jerwan. A long canal attributed to the Urartian king Menua, of about 800 BCE, reflects another, earlier tradition.

A rock-cut water tunnel carries a spring or stream through a hill to a city, supplying it even when enemies hold the land outside. Jerusalem's Siloam tunnel, about 700 BCE, was cut from both ends; an inscription records the crews meeting. On Samos, the kilometre-long Tunnel of Eupalinos was also dug from two ends in the sixth century BCE.

A true arch is built from wedge-shaped bricks or stones, voussoirs, that press against one another and turn the load above into thrust on the supports, spanning gaps wider than a single lintel. Mesopotamian builders made mudbrick arches at Ur by about 2,000 BCE; stone voussoir arches appear in Etruscan city gates by about the fourth century BCE.

Old Babylonian scribal schools, around 1900-1600 BCE, taught calculation through standard tables learned by copying: multiplication tables, and reciprocal tables that replaced division, since dividing by a number meant multiplying by its reciprocal. A school tablet from Nippur preserves a teacher's and a pupil's copy of the 45-times table, both containing errors. Such training served land measurement, rations and accounts.

Arms control treaties cap or limit weapons and provide ways to verify that states comply. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, opened for signature in 1968, sought to stop the spread of nuclear arms beyond existing nuclear powers. In 1972 the United States and the Soviet Union signed the SALT I agreements, limiting strategic launchers and missile defences.

Army magazines are state grain stores along a frontier that feed troops without foraging. Under Louis XIV, the war minister Louvois built up a system of magazines from about the 1670s that let French armies campaign early in the season. Frederick the Great opened Prussia's stores to relieve hunger in the famine of the early 1770s.

Copper containing a few percent arsenic, often from smelting arsenic-rich ores, is harder than pure copper and casts well, without any tin. Arsenical copper was widely used in Anatolia, the Caucasus and the Iranian plateau in the fourth and third millennia BCE; elaborate Nahal Mishmar castings contain 4-12 percent arsenic. Its fumes endangered metalworkers.

Military treatises set down doctrine on scouting, spies, supply and terrain so that officers could study war, not only learn it by experience. In China, the Art of War attributed to Sunzi reached its present form around the fifth or fourth century BCE. In Greece, Aeneas Tacticus wrote a surviving manual on defending besieged cities in the fourth century BCE.

Arts academies are chartered bodies that train artists, set standards of taste and hold exhibitions. In Florence, the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno was founded in 1563 under Cosimo I de' Medici, with Giorgio Vasari among its promoters. In 1648 the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was founded in Paris, later holding exhibitions known as the Salon.

Arts councils are public bodies that distribute government money to theatres, orchestras, galleries and individual artists, usually at arm's length from ministers so that experts choose recipients. The Arts Council of Great Britain was established in 1946, growing from a wartime council chaired by John Maynard Keynes. The United States created the National Endowment for the Arts in 1965.

Ashlar masonry uses stone blocks dressed to flat faces and square edges, so they sit with thin, regular joints. Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara, Egypt, of about 2,670 BCE, is among the earliest large buildings in dressed stone. Greek temple builders refined it, and Inca masons in the Andes independently developed tightly fitted stonework in the fifteenth century CE.

In assembly democracy the citizens govern directly. At Athens after the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BCE, an assembly open to every citizen decided almost all political questions, while a Council of 500 was chosen by lot for one-year terms, as were some magistrates. Citizenship was limited to adult men, excluding women, enslaved people and resident foreigners.

Assisted emigration used public money to pay the passage of chosen settlers to distant colonies. From 1831 Britain funded passages to New South Wales from the sale of colonial land, following ideas promoted by Edward Gibbon Wakefield. In 1840 a Colonial Land and Emigration Commission was set up in London to select emigrants, favouring young labourers and servants.

Asteroid mining is the proposed extraction of water, metals or other materials from asteroids, for use in space or on Earth. It has not yet been done. Robotic missions have returned only small samples, such as Japan's Hayabusa2 from asteroid Ryugu in 2020. Two firms founded to pursue it, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were sold in 2018-19.

The planispheric astrolabe flattens the sky onto a plate by stereographic projection, so an observer who sights a star or the Sun can read off the hour and latitude. The projection goes back to Hipparchus and Ptolemy; the oldest dated instrument, signed by Nastulus, was made in the Islamic world in 927/928 CE, where astrolabes also timed prayers.

Geometric astronomy models the motions of the Sun, Moon and planets with circles so that their positions can be calculated. Hipparchus, in the second century BCE, combined Greek geometry with older Greek and Babylonian observations to estimate precession and compile a catalogue of about 850 stars. Ptolemy's Almagest, written at Alexandria in the second century CE, systematised such models.

From at least 652 BCE until about 60 BCE, Babylonian scholars kept regular diaries of the Moon, planets and other phenomena, alongside notes of events; most surviving tablets are in the British Museum. Separate eclipse reports reach back to 747 BCE. Records kept over such long spans let them anticipate eclipses with an 18-year cycle now called the Saros.

A spear-thrower is a short board or shaft with a hook that engages the butt of a light spear, or dart, lengthening the arm's lever so the dart flies farther. Carved examples survive from Upper Palaeolithic France, roughly 20,000 to 15,000 years ago. Aboriginal Australians and peoples of the Americas also used it; Aztec warriors still did.

An atomic clock keeps time from the radiation that atoms absorb or emit when changing energy state. The US National Bureau of Standards announced an ammonia-based atomic clock in 1949. Louis Essen and Jack Parry built the first caesium clock at Britain's National Physical Laboratory in 1955. In 1967 the second was redefined using caesium.

Automatic switching connects telephone calls without a human operator. Almon Strowger patented a stepping switch in 1891, and the first Strowger exchange opened in La Porte, Indiana, in 1892, with pulses from the caller's telephone driving the switch. Crossbar systems, patented from 1919, later challenged stepping mechanisms. Telephone-style relays also went into early computers such as Konrad Zuse's Z3.

Mass production turned the motor car from a costly handmade machine into a common one. Ford's Model T, introduced in 1908, was standardised for low cost; in 1913 Ford installed a moving assembly line at Highland Park, Michigan, cutting chassis assembly from about twelve hours to about an hour and a half. Falling prices spread cars and trucks.

Balloon flight lifts people by buoyancy: an envelope of gas lighter than the surrounding air, either heated air or hydrogen. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers' hot-air balloon and Jacques Charles's hydrogen balloon made the first free flights with people aboard, in Paris, ten days apart. French forces used a tethered observation balloon at the Battle of Fleurus in 1794.

Balloon framing builds a house from light, machine-sawn studs and joists held together with mass-produced nails instead of heavy timbers joined by mortise and tenon. It is usually traced to Chicago in the early 1830s, credited to George W. Snow or to the carpenter Augustine Taylor, who built St Mary's Church there in 1833. It helped western towns grow fast.

Forager bands usually occupy a known home range, but its boundaries are permeable. Among the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari, ethnographers recorded that each group holds rights around waterholes, and others may forage there by asking leave through kin. Distinct regional styles of personal ornaments in Aurignacian Europe, roughly 40,000 to 30,000 years ago, may mark such group areas.

Private banking houses were family firms that took deposits, paid on written orders, lent money and managed property. In Babylonia the Egibi family was active across much of the sixth century BCE, and the Murashu house of Nippur, later in the fifth century, leased land and lent to holders of Persian royal land grants. Both left large clay archives.

Bankruptcy law gathers a failed trader's assets and divides them among creditors by fixed rules instead of a scramble. England's first bankruptcy statute, passed in 1542 under Henry VIII, treated bankrupts as offenders against creditors. An act of 1705 allowed honest bankrupts who cooperated to receive a discharge from remaining debts and start trading again.

In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli, following a suggestion by Galileo, inverted a mercury-filled glass tube in a dish: the column dropped and left an apparently empty space above it, and its height varied with the air's pressure. Otto von Guericke's air pump of about 1650 and the pump Robert Hooke built for Robert Boyle made vacuum experiments repeatable.

Barter is the direct swap of goods at agreed equivalents, settled at once rather than through a later return gift. In the farming villages of Neolithic Anatolia and the Levant, obsidian, sea shells and other materials moved between settlements by about 7000 BCE. Anthropologists doubt that barter was ever the main form of exchange before money, as older economists assumed.

Acid-lined converters could not remove phosphorus, which made steel brittle. Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and his cousin Percy Gilchrist, experimenting at Blaenavon in Wales, lined the converter with basic material such as lime, which drew phosphorus into the slag. Announced in 1878, the method opened phosphoric ores in Lorraine and elsewhere, and its slag was sold as fertiliser.

Basketry interlaces stiff plant materials by twining, coiling or plaiting into containers, mats, sieves and fish traps. Fibres rarely survive, so early evidence is often indirect: twined impressions on fired clay at Pavlov and Dolní Věstonice, Czech Republic, about 27,000 years old. Dry Guitarrero Cave in Peru preserved twined plant artefacts roughly 12,000 to 10,000 years old.

Beekeeping houses honeybee colonies in hives so honey and wax can be taken repeatedly without destroying the nest. A relief in King Nyuserre's sun temple in Egypt, about 2400 BCE, shows horizontal hives and honey sealed in jars. At Tel Rehov in Israel, an apiary of clay cylinder hives of the tenth to ninth century BCE housed Anatolian honeybees.

Bellows force air into a fire, raising its temperature beyond what natural draught allows. Leather bags or skins stretched over clay pots were pumped by hand or foot to feed furnaces. Egyptian tomb paintings of about 1500 BCE show workers treading such bellows; earlier Near Eastern pot-bellows and possible Chalcolithic examples are debated. Medieval blast furnaces later used water-driven bellows.

The Bessemer process made steel by blowing air through molten pig iron in a tilting vessel; burning out carbon and silicon released enough heat to keep the charge liquid without added fuel. Henry Bessemer described it at Cheltenham in August 1856, while William Kelly reached a similar idea independently in the United States. It made bulk steel far cheaper.

The safety bicycle of 1885, John Kemp Starley's Rover, had two wheels of similar size and a chain drive to the rear wheel, replacing the precarious high-wheeler. Pneumatic tyres followed by 1888. Its ball bearings, steel tubing and roller chains demanded precise standardised parts, and several early car and aircraft makers began as bicycle builders.

A big-man polity has leaders whose standing comes from personal achievement rather than inherited office. Ethnographers in Melanesia, especially in highland New Guinea, described big men who gathered followers by sponsoring feasts and pig exchanges, and lost them when generosity failed. Archaeologists infer similar competitive feasting from food debris at some early Neolithic villages, though the reading is debated.

A bill of exchange is a written order directing someone elsewhere to pay a sum, often in another currency, at a later date. Italian merchants and notaries developed it between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries, letting payment and credit pass between fairs and cities without shipping coin. Comparable instruments, such as the suftaja, existed earlier in the Islamic world.

A bill of rights is a law binding the ruler that guarantees specified rights of subjects or citizens, such as due process, petition, and freedom from arbitrary arrest and from taxation without consent. Magna Carta (1215) is often cited as a precursor; the English Bill of Rights (1689) and the United States Bill of Rights (1791) are landmark examples.

Birch-bark tar is produced by heating bark with restricted air until a sticky pitch forms, a manufactured rather than gathered adhesive. Flint flakes bearing birch tar at Campitello quarry, Italy, more than 191,000 years old, are the earliest European evidence. A tar-coated Neanderthal flint recovered from the Zandmotor off the Dutch coast is about 50,000 years old.

A blast furnace is a tall shaft furnace in which a strong, steady air blast drives the charge hot enough for iron to absorb carbon and run out as liquid cast iron. In Europe water-wheels powered the bellows; at Lapphyttan, Sweden, such a furnace worked from around the late twelfth century, apparently a local development long after China's furnaces.

Bleaching linen and cotton once took weeks of soaking and exposure to sunlight. In 1785 Claude-Louis Berthollet showed that chlorine bleaches fabric, and by 1791 the method was in commercial use in England. Charles Tennant's bleaching powder of 1799, chlorine absorbed in slaked lime at Glasgow, could be stored and shipped; the same hypochlorite chemistry later disinfected water.

Compensation for injury replaces revenge with payment: the offender's kin pay the victim's kin a set price for a killing or wound. Many societies recorded by ethnographers settled feuds with livestock or valuables. The laws of Ur-Nammu, from about 2100 BCE, already fixed silver payments for injuries, and early medieval Germanic law codes listed a wergild for each person.

Blood transfusion replaces lost blood from a donor. Richard Lower transfused blood between dogs in 1665 and early human attempts followed, but many ended in harm. Karl Landsteiner's discovery of the ABO blood groups in Vienna in 1901 explained the dangerous reactions. Cross-matching, citrate anticoagulant from 1914 and cold storage made blood banks possible, including Chicago's in 1937.

A plebiscitary empire combines authoritarian rule with periodic popular votes that confirm the ruler's power. Napoleon Bonaparte became Emperor of the French in 1804 after a plebiscite, governing through appointed prefects, a mass army and public works. His nephew Louis-Napoleon repeated the pattern, founding the Second Empire in 1852 after a coup and plebiscite.

Bone, antler and ivory can be cut, grooved, scraped and polished into points, awls, needles and harpoons. At Katanda on the Semliki River, Democratic Republic of the Congo, barbed bone points with rings carved at the base for fastening to shafts are dated to roughly 90,000 years ago, alongside catfish remains, though the experimental dating methods drew scepticism.

A simple bow is a single wooden stave bent by a string; drawing it stores energy that is released into a light arrow. Stone points from Sibudu Cave, South Africa, about 64,000 years old, have been read as arrow tips from wear and residues. Wooden arrows from Stellmoor, northern Germany, date to the end of the last Ice Age.

Brahmi appears as a fully developed script in the third century BCE, notably in the Mauryan emperor Ashoka's edicts, though sherds from Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, have been dated earlier. Each consonant carries an inherent vowel that attached marks modify. Whether it derived from Aramaic or developed locally is debated. Brahmi is ancestral to many South and Southeast Asian scripts.

Zinc boils at a temperature below copper's melting point, so early brass was made indirectly: copper was heated with zinc ore and charcoal and absorbed zinc vapour. After Augustus's coinage reform of 23 BCE, Rome struck coins in this brass, orichalcum, with up to about 30 percent zinc. Cementation brass later supplied European instrument and wire makers.

Breech-loading rifles take the cartridge at the rear of the barrel, so soldiers can reload faster, even lying down. Prussia began buying Dreyse's needle gun, whose long firing pin pierced a paper cartridge, in 1841, and its success in 1866 drew wide attention. Bolt-action rifles such as Mauser's followed, using metallic cartridges, and smokeless powder later allowed smaller bullets.

Bridewealth is a payment from the groom's kin to the bride's kin, often in livestock, that seals a marriage and places the children in the father's lineage, which must then support them. Ethnographers recorded it widely in Africa, as in Nuer cattle payments and Zulu lobola. The Laws of Eshnunna, about 1800 BCE, already name a marriage payment called terhatum.

A stone arch bridge carries a road on masonry arches whose thrust rests on piers and on abutments in the banks. Rome's Pons Fabricius, built in 62 BCE, still carries pedestrians across the Tiber. China's Zhaozhou Bridge, finished around 605 CE, uses a flat segmental limestone arch with small open arches in its shoulders that lighten it and pass floodwater.

In medieval Europe, religious brotherhoods and endowed trusts raised alms, rents and bequests to build stone bridges and repair them over centuries. A bridge brotherhood built the Pont Saint-Bénézet at Avignon from about 1177. London Bridge's estate was run by wardens from the thirteenth century, and the Rochester Bridge Trust, founded about 1399, still maintains bridges today.

Building regulation sets legal limits on how city buildings are made. In Rome, Augustus restricted the height of buildings, reportedly to about 70 Roman feet, and after the great fire of 64 CE Nero ordered wider streets, lower heights and fire-resistant stone in rebuilt districts, according to Tacitus. Later cities from London to Edo adopted comparable fire rules.

A bureaucratic empire governs a large realm of many peoples from a capital through salaried, ranked officials, appointed provincial governors, registers, standard taxes and a standing army; the dynasty heads the system but rules through it. Achaemenid Persia from about 520 BCE, China after the Qin unification of 221 BCE, and imperial Rome are often cited examples.

Calculus is the mathematics of continuous change: rates of change (derivatives) and accumulated quantities (integrals). Isaac Newton worked out his method of fluxions by about 1671 but left it unpublished for decades, while Gottfried Leibniz published his differential calculus in 1684. A bitter priority dispute followed; a Royal Society report of 1712, shaped largely by Newton, went against Leibniz.

Ancient Egypt's civil calendar had twelve 30-day months plus five extra days. With no leap day until the Roman period, its new year slipped through the seasons by about one day every four years, realigning with the dawn rising of Sirius only after some 1,460 years. Its origin is disputed; proposals cluster near 2800 BCE.

Counting the Moon's phases gives a way to track time through the year. At Warren Field, Aberdeenshire, Scotland, hunter-gatherers dug a line of pits around 8000 BCE that its excavators read as mirroring lunar phases and months, aligned on midwinter sunrise so the count could be reset annually to the solar year. This remains the excavators' hypothesis.

Twelve lunar months fall about eleven days short of a solar year, so lunisolar calendars periodically insert an extra month. From about 499 BCE Babylon regulated these with a 19-year cycle of 235 months, seven of them added, applied without exception by about 380 BCE. Meton proposed the same cycle at Athens in 432 BCE, possibly learning it from Babylon.

The caliphate was the office of successor to the Prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community in war, law and taxation. The first four caliphs, known as the Rashidun, ruled from Medina after 632 CE. The Abbasid dynasty, which took power in 750, governed from Baghdad through provincial governors and central revenue registers known as diwans.

Two camel species were domesticated separately. Two-humped Bactrian camels were domesticated in Central Asia and were present in southern Turkmenistan by the third millennium BCE. One-humped dromedaries, descended from wild herds of south-east Arabia, appear as domestic animals much later; a Babylonian school text of about 1300 BCE calls one the "donkey of the Sealand". The timing remains debated.

Desert caravans used strings of camels, with guides, wells and halting places, to carry goods across country no cart could cross. Domesticated dromedaries carried incense from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean world from around 1000 BCE. Camels became common in North Africa in the early centuries CE, opening regular caravan trade across the Sahara.

Campaign supply depots let an army march far from home without stripping the land it crosses. Before his campaigns in the Levant in the fifteenth century BCE, the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III had harbours on the Phoenician coast stocked with grain and provisions, as his annals record. The Assyrian empire later kept stores at stations along its royal roads.

A pound lock is a chamber between two gates in which boats are raised or lowered by filling or emptying it. Chinese records credit the official Qiao Weiyue with building one on the Grand Canal system in 984 CE, replacing dangerous double slipways. In Europe, pound locks appear in the Low Countries and Italy from the late fourteenth century.

A navigation canal is a built waterway for freight boats, often crossing a watershed with locks and with reservoirs that feed water to its summit level. France's Canal du Midi, opened in 1681, joined the Atlantic and Mediterranean by way of the Garonne. England's Bridgewater Canal of 1761 carried coal to Manchester. China's Grand Canal had crossed summits centuries earlier.

Canning preserves food by heating it in a sealed container. In 1810 Nicolas Appert, working with glass bottles, published his method after a French government award. The same year Peter Durand patented tin cans in Britain, and Bryan Donkin and John Hall soon set up a cannery supplying the army and navy. Why heating worked was understood only later.

Gun founders adopted the methods of bell founders, casting large bronze barrels in one piece in loam moulds. During the fifteenth century cast bronze became a preferred material for European and Ottoman artillery, as it was less prone than early wrought-iron pieces to burst violently. Ottoman bronze bombards helped breach the walls of Constantinople in 1453, prompting new fortification designs.

Cast-iron guns were cheaper than bronze because iron is far more plentiful than copper and tin, though they were heavier and more likely to burst. Founders in the Weald of Sussex, England, cast serviceable iron muzzle-loaders from 1543, using water-powered blast furnaces. Cheap iron ordnance later armed merchant ships and warships in large numbers, notably from English and Swedish foundries.

Early cannon drive a projectile from a closed metal tube with the gas of burning gunpowder, which reached Europe from China in the thirteenth century. The oldest known guns are Chinese: a bronze gun found at Xanadu bears a date corresponding to 1298. An English manuscript depicts a gun in 1326. Many early European guns were hooped wrought-iron staves.

Canon law is the body of rules by which the Christian church governed clergy, marriage, oaths and church property through its own courts. Around 1140 the teacher Gratian, working at Bologna, compiled the Decretum, which organised centuries of conflicting rulings into one work. It became the standard textbook for university study of church law across medieval Europe.

The caravel was a small, light Portuguese ship, usually lateen-rigged, with a sternpost rudder, able to sail close to the wind and return against prevailing winds. From about the 1430s it carried exploration along the West African coast and among the Atlantic islands. Later caravels mixed square and lateen sails for longer ocean passages.

Carbon capture separates carbon dioxide from gas streams for use or storage. In amine scrubbing, used since about 1930 to remove carbon dioxide from natural gas and hydrogen, an amine solution binds the gas chemically. At Norway's Sleipner field, amines strip carbon dioxide from produced gas for storage, a process its operator found costly to develop.

The carrack joined northern and Mediterranean shipbuilding. Genoese builders of the early 14th century placed the cog's square rig and sternpost rudder on a frame-first hull and added a lateen mizzen. By the mid-15th century the type had become three-masted and full-rigged, large enough to carry heavy cargo and stores on long oceanic voyages.

An ox cart couples wheels and an axle to a draught animal, so that one driver can move far more grain, timber or stone than porters could carry. Carts and wagons spread with the solid wheel from the later 4th millennium BCE, as cattle were used more widely for traction. Their range depended on fodder, firm tracks and gentle slopes.

Mathematical cartography places features on a grid of measured coordinates instead of sketching them by eye. Ptolemy's Geography, about 150 CE, listed thousands of places by latitude and longitude, derived from astronomy and travellers' distances. In 3rd-century China, Pei Xiu set out principles for scaled grid maps. Such maps recorded what was already known.

Iron with several percent carbon melts at a much lower temperature than pure iron and can be poured into moulds like bronze. In China, where bloomery iron came first, casting seems to have developed independently, and blast furnaces producing liquid iron may date from the fifth century BCE. By the Han dynasty cast iron from large furnaces was normal.

Two-piece moulds clamp together around a cavity, sometimes with a clay core inserted, so both faces of an object are shaped and hollow sockets can be cast. Socketed axes and spearheads cast this way became common in later Bronze Age Europe; soapstone moulds for socketed axes survive from Scotland and Norway. Stone moulds could be reused many times.

The simplest casting pours molten metal into a hollow carved in stone or shaped in clay and left open at the top, so only one face takes the mould's shape while the upper face cools flat. Flat axes and blades were made this way in many early metalworking regions; some surviving stone moulds carry matrices on several faces.

A catalytic converter passes engine exhaust over a platinum-bearing catalyst that speeds reactions cleaning it. Under the 1970 Clean Air Act, new United States cars carried converters from the 1975 model year; these early units oxidised carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons. Lead coats the catalyst, so unleaded petrol spread alongside. Three-way converters, which also reduce nitrogen oxides, followed from 1977.

Between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, endowed schools attached to cathedrals in Latin Europe and to mosques in the Islamic world taught grammar, law and theology to future clergy, judges and officials. The Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya madrasa in Baghdad, opened about 1067, and papal rulings from 1079 onward required bishops to keep schools at their cathedrals.

Cattle descend from the aurochs, a large and formidable wild ox. They were domesticated in Southwest Asia roughly 10,000 years ago, and humped zebu cattle separately in South Asia, most likely the Indus region. Ancient DNA shows that early herds repeatedly mixed with wild aurochs and later with zebu. Cattle supplied meat, milk, hides, dung fuel and pulling power.

Cavalry means fighting from horseback rather than from chariots. Riding is older than mounted warfare, but organised mounted units are clearest from the ninth century BCE, when Assyrian reliefs show riders in pairs, one holding both horses' reins while the other shoots. On the steppe, mounted archery underpinned the power of peoples such as the Scythians and Xiongnu.

Celestial navigation with instruments measured the altitude of the Sun or the Pole Star with a mariner's astrolabe or quadrant, then corrected the reading with tables of solar declination. Portuguese pilots developed the practice in the late 15th century, as voyages south of the equator lost sight of the Pole Star. It gave latitude reliably, but not longitude.

Cell theory holds that living things are built of cells. The botanist Matthias Schleiden argued this for plants in 1838 and the zoologist Theodor Schwann extended it to animals in 1839. Rudolf Virchow added that every cell arises from a pre-existing cell, rejecting Schwann's idea of cells forming from fluid, and in 1858 located disease in cells themselves.

Second-generation cellular networks carried speech as digital data. The European GSM standard entered commercial service in 1991, with an early call made in Finland. Digital coding allowed encryption, text messages and more users per channel. Later generations, including 4G LTE first launched commercially in 2009, were designed mainly around data.

A census counts a state's people, households and property at intervals, through registration by officials, to assess taxes, labour and military duties. Early Egyptian kings recorded regular counts of cattle and other wealth; Rome's censors registered citizens and their property, in principle every five years; and China's Han dynasty recorded about 57 million people in 2 CE.

A central bank is a public bank that holds the government's accounts, issues notes and settles payments between other banks, and later became lender of last resort in crises. Sweden's Riksbank, founded by decision of the Riksdag in 1668, and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, are usually counted the oldest, though their central functions developed gradually.

Central planning is the direction of an economy's output, investment and allocation by state plans rather than mainly by market prices. The Soviet state created Gosplan, its planning commission, in 1921 and launched the first Five-Year Plan in 1928. Planning drove rapid heavy industrialisation but struggled with information, incentives and quality, and accompanied forced collectivisation and famine.

Before domestication, people sowed, tended and reaped wild cereal stands. In the Levant's Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, about 11,600 to 10,700 years ago, wild emmer, einkorn and barley were cultivated, judged from arable weeds and larger grains, though whether those grains reflect selection or wetter conditions is debated. Similar cultivation began independently with millet, rice and maize in China and Mexico.

Domestication changed the plants themselves. In the Fertile Crescent, einkorn, emmer and barley gradually acquired ears that hold their grain until harvest instead of shattering, so they came to depend on human sowing. Domestic-type wheat ears appear at the start of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B. With lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax, they form Southwest Asia's founder crops.

Chancery enrolment means copying outgoing charters, letters and writs onto long parchment rolls before they leave the royal writing office. In England the practice began around 1199, early in King John's reign, under Chancellor Hubert Walter, and charter, patent and close rolls followed. Kept for centuries, the rolls let the crown check what it had already granted or ordered.

Charcoal is wood heated with little air, so water and volatile substances are driven off and nearly pure carbon remains. Burned in earth-covered piles, it gives hotter, cleaner fires than wood, and early metal smelting relied on it. Demand for it consumed woodlands; as charcoal grew costly in Britain, Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke at Coalbrookdale in 1709.

A war chariot is a light two-wheeled vehicle with spoked wheels, drawn by horses and carrying a driver and a fighter. The oldest known spoke-wheeled chariots come from Sintashta culture burials in the southern Urals, about 2000 BCE. Within centuries chariots were used from Egypt and Anatolia to China, where Shang tombs at Anyang of about 1200 BCE contain them.

Universities began as self-governing guilds of masters and students that won legal privileges and granted degrees recognized widely. Bologna, famous for law, traditionally dates its origin to 1088. In Paris, masters teaching around the cathedral school formed a guild by the later twelfth century and received royal and papal privileges from about 1200.

Mineral fertilizers return plant nutrients to soil in concentrated form. In 1842 John Bennet Lawes patented a process treating phosphate rock with sulphuric acid to make superphosphate and opened a factory to produce it. From the 1840s Peru exported seabird guano, a natural fertilizer, almost as a world monopoly, and mined nitrates later competed with it.

Antoine Lavoisier made chemistry a science of measured weights. Weighing every input and product, gases included, he showed that metals gain weight when burned because they combine with oxygen, undermining the phlogiston theory. His Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789) stated that matter is conserved through a chemical operation and listed simple substances he treated as provisional elements.

Cancer chemotherapy treats tumours with drugs that kill dividing cells. Paul Ehrlich had coined the word for synthetic drugs against microbes. In the 1940s nitrogen mustards were tested against lymphoma, and in 1948 Sidney Farber reported temporary remissions in children with leukaemia using aminopterin, an antifolate. Combination regimens later cured many childhood leukaemias and Hodgkin lymphoma.

A chiefdom, in anthropologists' usage, is a regional society of several villages under the lasting authority of a paramount chief. Classic models have the chief collect tribute and redistribute it, though studies of Hawaii and the Mississippian southeast suggest tribute and prestige goods mattered more than redistribution. Tonga, under its paramount Tu'i Tonga, is a classic Polynesian case.

A warrior retinue is a band of armed followers fed in their chief's hall who fight at his call and gather his tribute. Archaeologists infer such followings from weapon-rich male graves, as at Varna in Bulgaria in the fifth millennium BCE and in Corded Ware battle-axe burials after about 2800 BCE. Roman writers later described the Germanic comitatus.

Child nutrition programmes weigh young children regularly and give extra food to those falling behind, and to pregnant and nursing mothers. India launched its Integrated Child Development Services in 1975, running village courtyard centres called anganwadis. In 1982 UNICEF began promoting growth monitoring on weight charts, together with oral rehydration, breastfeeding and immunization.

The oldest substantial body of Chinese writing is inscribed on turtle shells and cattle shoulder blades from the late Shang capital near Anyang, dated to about 1250-1050 BCE. Diviners recorded questions about harvests, warfare, weather and other matters, then read cracks from heating. The script was already fully developed, implying earlier development, and is ancestral to modern Chinese characters.

A popular assembly gathers all free adult members of a community, historically almost always men, to decide on war and peace, approve laws and choose leaders by acclamation or vote. Sparta's assembly voted by shouting on proposals brought by its council or officials, and the Roman historian Tacitus described assemblies of armed free men among Germanic peoples.

In a citizen militia, men who own enough property arm themselves at their own expense and serve as heavy infantry for their city. The hoplite phalanx of the Greek city-states, which took shape around the seventh century BCE, is the classic example: ranks of citizens with large round shields and spears fought shoulder to shoulder.

Rome extended citizenship to outsiders on a scale no ancient city had matched. After the Latin War ended in 338 BCE, several Latin towns received full or partial Roman rights, and freed slaves of citizens became citizens themselves. In 212 CE the emperor Caracalla's Constitutio Antoniniana granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.

In an oligarchic city-state a city and its countryside are governed by a council of leading families, which chooses magistrates and controls law and finance. Many Greek poleis were run this way; in the Ganges valley the Licchavis of Vaishali were ruled by an assembly of heads of leading families; north Italian communes under elected consuls spread from about 1100 CE.

Mass democracies came to depend on citizens active between elections. Trade unions, cooperatives, women's associations and parent bodies trained members to debate, keep minutes and run meetings. Public libraries, adult schools and civic education spread the habits of participation, and town meetings and consultations gave ordinary people a recognised voice in public affairs.

Civic ritual gives a nation its own shared ceremonies, symbols and sacred days. Revolutionary France staged the Festival of the Federation in Paris on 14 July 1790, adopted La Marseillaise as its national anthem in 1795, and made 14 July a national holiday in 1880. Flags, anthems, war memorials and annual festivals spread to nearly every modern state.

A civil code replaces scattered local customs with one systematic statute governing persons, family, property and contracts. The French Civil Code of 1804, often called the Napoleonic Code, unified the law of a country that had been divided among hundreds of local customs. It spread with French conquest and inspired codes across Europe, Latin America and beyond.

Nonviolent resistance means breaking unjust laws openly and accepting punishment, using boycotts, strikes and marches to win over public opinion. Mohandas Gandhi led satyagraha campaigns in India against the Rowlatt Acts in 1919 and against the salt tax with the Salt March of 1930. In 1955-1956 the Montgomery bus boycott in Alabama challenged racial segregation on city buses.

A professional police force is a salaried civil body under public authority that patrols, prevents crime and keeps public order, distinct from both the army and private or volunteer watchmen. Paris gained a lieutenant-general of police in 1667, and London's Metropolitan Police, established in 1829 under Robert Peel, became a widely copied model of uniformed patrol policing.

Civil registration is the recording of births, marriages and deaths by public officials rather than by parish clergy. Revolutionary France transferred these registers from the church to municipal authorities in 1792, and England and Wales opened a General Register Office in 1837. Such records gave each person a legal identity and let officials measure infant and child mortality.

Civil rights law forbids discrimination by race, religion, sex or national origin in public life and employment. In the United States, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, passed after years of protest by the civil rights movement, outlawed segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment. The Voting Rights Act followed in 1965.

Civil service examinations recruit officials through competitive written tests on a fixed curriculum, open in principle beyond the hereditary elite, with graded degrees qualifying holders for office. China's imperial examinations took shape under the Sui dynasty around 600 CE and lasted until 1905; Korea adopted them in 958, and in Britain the Northcote-Trevelyan Report of 1854 recommended competitive examinations.

Liberalism joins individual rights, the rule of law, free markets and limited government into a single political programme. Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, argued that open markets and the division of labour enrich nations. John Stuart Mill's On Liberty, in 1859, defended freedom of thought and conduct against both the state and the pressure of public opinion.

A mixed-constitution republic has no monarch. Annually elected magistrates, such as paired consuls, hold executive power; a senate deliberates and advises on policy; and citizen assemblies elect officials and pass laws, so that power is shared among the three. Rome, whose republic traditionally began in 509 BCE, is the case the historian Polybius analysed this way.

Under rights of clearance, the person who clears a plot from forest or bush holds it while cropping it, but it returns to the lineage or community when left fallow. Ethnographers record such rules among shifting cultivators in Africa, Southeast Asia and Amazonia. Similar rules are inferred for early farmers opening the European forest from about 5500 BCE.

A clerical republic combines elected institutions with supervision by senior clergy. The Islamic Republic of Iran, established in 1979 after the revolution against the Shah, has an elected president and parliament, but a Supreme Leader holds ultimate authority, and a Guardian Council of clerics and jurists can veto laws and disqualify candidates for office.

Climate accords are agreements among states to limit greenhouse gas emissions and cope with climate change. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was adopted in 1992 and opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit. It was followed by the Kyoto Protocol in 1997, with binding targets for richer nations, and the Paris Agreement of 2015.

Cloud computing rents processing power and storage from large networked data centres on demand, instead of each organisation running its own servers. Amazon Web Services launched rented storage and computing in 2006, and other firms followed. Users pay for what they use and can expand quickly, while the physical machines are concentrated in a few very large facilities.

Very-large-scale integration put tens of thousands and then millions of transistors on a single chip. It relied on CMOS logic, invented in 1963 by Frank Wanlass and Chih-Tang Sah, which draws little power except when switching, and on structured design methods popularised by Carver Mead and Lynn Conway around 1980. The cost of each transistor fell steadily.

Coal became a major fuel where forests had been cut back. In Northern Song China, from around 1000 CE, coal heated homes in the capital Kaifeng and fuelled iron furnaces in the north. In thirteenth-century England, sea-coal shipped from Newcastle to London was burned by lime-burners and smiths, and complaints about its smoke were already being made.

Steamships burned coal quickly and needed frequent refuelling, so naval powers secured chains of ports stocked with coal. Britain seized Aden in 1839, and it became a key coaling stop on the route to India, especially after the Suez Canal opened in 1869. In 1898 the United States annexed Hawaii and acquired Guam, partly to gain Pacific coaling bases.

The codex is a book of folded sheets bound along one edge, unlike a scroll. Parchment, prepared animal skin, is traditionally linked with Pergamon in the second century BCE. The Roman poet Martial, around 85 CE, mentions his poems in small parchment codices. By about 400 CE the codex had largely replaced the scroll, helped by early Christian preference for it.

The cog was a broad, flat-bottomed cargo ship with high clinker-built sides, a single square sail and, later, a sternpost rudder. It developed along the Frisian coast around 1000 CE and by 1200 carried grain, timber, fish and cloth across the North Sea and Baltic, serving Hanseatic towns. The Bremen cog, built around 1380, survives.

Coins, metal pieces of guaranteed weight stamped with an issuer's mark, appeared in western Anatolia in the late seventh century BCE, first struck in electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, in Lydia and neighbouring Greek cities. Cast bronze spade and knife money in China and punch-marked silver coins in India developed separately, with their dates still debated.

Wage labour in coin pays workers in money rather than in rations, land or goods, so work and its reward are measured in a common unit. Coinage began in Lydia and Ionia in the late seventh or sixth century BCE. In classical Athens, workers on public buildings such as the Erechtheion received daily wages in coin, recorded in inscribed accounts.

Coke is coal baked with little air to drive off its volatile matter, leaving a strong, porous carbon fuel. In 1709 Abraham Darby fired his Coalbrookdale blast furnace in Shropshire with coke as charcoal grew costly. Earlier trials had faltered; his was Europe's first lasting success, permitting larger furnaces and much cheaper cast iron.

The breast-strap harness passes a broad band across a horse's chest, moving the pull from the neck to the breastbone. A Chu lacquer box of the fourth century BCE shows a horse pulling against a chest yoke; breast straps then appear widely in Han-dynasty tomb reliefs. They preceded the padded collar, attested in China by about the fifth century CE.

Collective bargaining law requires employers to recognise a union chosen by their workers and to negotiate with it in good faith. In the United States, the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, often called the Wagner Act, protected the right to organise, created a board to hold union elections, and made refusal to bargain an unfair labour practice.

Collective security is a pledge by member states to act together against any aggressor among them. The Covenant of the League of Nations, adopted in 1919, embodied the idea, but the League failed to stop aggression in the 1930s. The United Nations Charter of 1945 gave the Security Council power to authorise sanctions and military action to restore peace.

Colonial administration governed distant territories through institutions in the home country and officials sent abroad. Spain created the Council of the Indies in 1524 to oversee its American possessions, issuing laws, hearing appeals and nominating officials. In the Americas, viceroys ruled New Spain from 1535 and Peru from the 1540s, assisted by high courts called audiencias.

Colonial regiments were raised from local recruits, usually under European officers, to garrison and police colonial territories. The British East India Company formed regular battalions of Indian sepoys in the 1750s, which soon formed most of its armies. France raised the Tirailleurs sénégalais in West Africa in 1857; they later fought in both world wars.

Remotely piloted aircraft are flown by crews on the ground through radio and satellite links. Reconnaissance drones are decades older, but long-endurance surveillance became practical with satellite navigation and compact electronics. The American Predator flew unarmed reconnaissance from 1995, and armed versions carrying missiles were used from 2001. Many states, and some non-state groups, now use them.

In a commenda one partner supplied capital and another travelled with the goods; if the venture prospered they divided the profit in agreed shares, while losses fell on the capital. The Islamic world knew the arrangement as qirad or mudaraba by the early Middle Ages, and Venetian contracts of the same kind, called colleganza, survive from about 1072.

International commercial arbitration lets traders from different countries submit disputes to private arbitrators instead of foreign courts. The International Chamber of Commerce set up its Court of Arbitration in Paris in 1923. The New York Convention of 1958 obliged signatory states to recognize and enforce foreign arbitral awards, and most trading nations have since joined it.

Merchant law is the body of rules and specialized courts that enforce contracts, partnerships, bills and sales between traders who may be strangers, quickly and across jurisdictions. Islamic jurists elaborated partnership and credit law from about the eighth century CE, and in medieval Europe fair and town courts applied customary merchant law to disputes between travelling traders.

A commodity exchange is a market where graded staples such as grain and cotton are traded, either for immediate delivery or through futures contracts for later delivery. The Chicago Board of Trade was founded in 1848 as railways and grain elevators made the city a hub, and by 1865 it had adopted standardized futures contracts. Grading made lots interchangeable.

Common law is law shared across a whole realm, built by judges from decided cases rather than from a single code. It grew in England under Henry II, whose reforms of the 1160s and 1170s sent royal justices on circuit. The treatise known as Glanvill, written around 1188, described the writs and procedures of the king's courts.

The Commonwealth grew from the British Empire into a voluntary association of independent states. The Statute of Westminster of 1931 gave dominions such as Canada full legislative independence. The London Declaration of 1949 allowed India to remain a member as a republic, accepting the British monarch as Head of the Commonwealth. Members cooperate as equals.

Communal feasts gathered many households to eat and celebrate together, binding allies, displaying the hosts' standing and marking seasons. At Hilazon Tachtit cave in Israel, a Natufian burial of about 12,000 years ago held remains of many tortoises and wild cattle, read as a funeral feast. Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, built from about 9500 BCE, also shows feasting debris.

Communal storehouses keep a village's grain under agreed rules, so households with a poor crop can draw on the shared stock. At Dhra' near the Dead Sea in Jordan, archaeologists found free-standing granaries with raised floors built about 9300 BCE, before plants were fully domesticated. They are among the earliest known purpose-built food stores.

Communications satellites relay radio signals between distant ground stations. Arthur C. Clarke developed the idea of geostationary relays in a 1945 article. Telstar 1 and Relay 1, launched in 1962, worked from lower, non-geostationary orbits. Syncom 3 became the first geostationary communications satellite in 1964, and Intelsat I, nicknamed Early Bird, began commercial service in 1965.

Community forestry hands state-owned or degraded forests to local user groups, which set harvesting rules, guard the woods and share timber, fodder and firewood among members. Nepal began transferring forests to local councils in the late 1970s, and its 1993 Forest Act created community forest user groups. India's Joint Forest Management programme, from 1990, shared management with villages.

A magnetic compass uses a magnetised iron needle that aligns roughly north-south. In 1088 Shen Kuo described such needles and noted they point slightly away from true south, and Zhu Yu, writing in 1111-1117, recorded ships steering by compass under cloud. European texts mention mariners' compasses around 1190; whether this was transmission or reinvention is debated.

A composite bow laminates a wooden core, horn on the belly and sinew on the back, bonded with animal glue; horn and sinew store more energy than wood, so the bow can be short yet powerful. Horn composite bows are well attested in the Near East and Egypt by the later second millennium BCE; Tutankhamun's tomb held several.

Composite materials embed strong fibres in a resin so that each covers the other's weakness. A US patent for making glass fibres with air jets was sought in 1933, and glass fibre was paired with new plastic resins from 1936. In 1963 Britain's Royal Aircraft Establishment developed strong carbon fibre, later used in airframes and turbine blades.

Compulsory education is a legal duty on parents or guardians to have children schooled. Prussian decrees of 1717 and the General School Regulation of 1763 required attendance, though enforcement long lagged behind the law. Massachusetts passed an attendance law in 1852. Such laws aimed at literacy, religious instruction and civic loyalty, but depended on teachers, buildings and funding.

Compulsory vaccination laws required infants to be vaccinated against smallpox, using the cowpox method Edward Jenner published in 1798. Bavaria made vaccination compulsory in 1807, among the first states to do so. In England the Vaccination Act of 1853 required infants to be vaccinated within months of birth, and later acts added fines for parents who refused.

A stored-program computer keeps its instructions in the same fast memory as its data, so a new program can be loaded instead of rewiring the machine. The Manchester Baby ran the first such program in June 1948, using a cathode-ray-tube store developed from wartime radar work. Cambridge's EDSAC, with mercury delay-line memory, began regular service in 1949.

Roman builders found that lime mixed with volcanic ash from around the Bay of Naples, plus rubble aggregate, set hard even under seawater. The ash reacts with lime and water to form durable binding minerals; in 2,000-year-old harbour concrete from Pozzuoli Bay, rare aluminous tobermorite crystals formed within the mortar. The material served for harbour structures, vaults and domes.

Conditional cash transfers pay poor families, usually through mothers, a regular sum on condition that children attend school and health checks. Mexico launched Progresa in 1997, later renamed Oportunidades, and evaluated it with randomized trials. Brazil combined earlier schemes into Bolsa Família in 2003, which grew to reach tens of millions of people.

Confessionalization describes how early modern European states bound religion and government together. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each prince of the Holy Roman Empire choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory. After the Council of Trent, which closed in 1563, Catholic parishes were required to register baptisms and marriages, and churches of every confession disciplined their members.

Congregations are groups of lay believers who meet regularly to hear scripture, pray and look after their own members. Jewish synagogues are attested in inscriptions from Ptolemaic Egypt in the third century BCE. Early Christian assemblies of the first century CE shared meals and collected funds for widows and the poor. Buddhist lay followers kept regular observance days at monasteries.

Conservatism defends inherited institutions, customs and gradual reform against plans to rebuild society from abstract principles. Its classic statement is Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, which warned that tearing down established order would end in violence. Through the nineteenth century, parties of crown, church and landed property across Europe drew on such arguments.

A constitutional court is a specialised tribunal that decides whether laws and government acts conform to the constitution and settles conflicts between institutions. The jurist Hans Kelsen shaped the first such court, in the Austrian constitution of 1920. After the Second World War the model spread widely, and West Germany's Federal Constitutional Court began work at Karlsruhe in 1951.

A constitutional monarchy keeps a hereditary monarch but binds the crown by law and by the consent of a legislature. In England, the settlement of 1689, including the Bill of Rights, required parliamentary consent for taxation and for a standing army in peacetime. British monarchs later kept formal powers but became largely ceremonial, as cabinets answerable to the Commons governed.

Consuls are officials posted to foreign ports to protect their nationals and report on commerce. Merchant consuls are old, but in the nineteenth century states turned consulates into salaried public services. Britain reorganised its consular service by an act of 1825, and the United States reformed its service in 1856. Consular reports on markets, prices and shipping informed governments and traders.

Consumer protection law requires that goods be honestly labelled, safe and of the stated quantity, and gives authorities power to act against dangerous products. In the United States the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938 required new drugs to be shown safe before sale. Britain's Fair Trading Act of 1973 created a director general to oversee trading practices.

Container shipping moves cargo in standard steel boxes that pass between ship, train and truck without unpacking. Malcom McLean's converted tanker Ideal X carried 58 containers from Newark to Houston in 1956. International size standards agreed in the late 1960s let cranes, ships and ports worldwide handle the same boxes, sharply cutting handling time and cost.

A cooperative is a business owned and controlled by its members, who share its surplus according to how much they use it rather than how much capital they hold. The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers, founded in 1844 by weavers and other workers in Lancashire, opened a shop whose rules became a model. Credit cooperatives soon followed in Germany.

Some copper occurs naturally as metal. Hammering it cold makes it harder but brittle, and heating (annealing) restores workability, so beads, pins and awls could be made without smelting. Annealed native copper appears at Cayonu in southeastern Anatolia around the end of the ninth millennium BCE, and independently near North America's Great Lakes from about 8,500 years ago.

Smelting reduces copper minerals, such as green malachite, to metal by heating them with charcoal in a hot, oxygen-poor fire. Slag from Belovode, Serbia, about 5000 BCE, is among the earliest securely dated evidence, though comparable Near Eastern finds may prove as old. Smelting freed metalworkers from scarce native copper and made metal a regular trade good.

Copyright gives authors a time-limited exclusive right to print and sell their works. Before it, printing privileges went to printers and guilds, such as the Stationers' Company in London. The Statute of Anne, passed in Britain in 1710, vested the right in authors for fourteen years, renewable once, after which works passed into free use.

Cordage is made by twisting plant or animal fibres into strands, then plying strands in the opposite direction. The oldest direct find is a tiny three-ply cord, probably of inner-bark fibre, on a Neanderthal stone tool at Abri du Maras, France, roughly 41,000 to 52,000 years old. Lashing, nets, snares and carrying depend on it.

Early gunpowder was a loose meal whose ingredients could separate in transport and burned unevenly. Corning, attested in Europe in the fifteenth century, mixed the ingredients wet and broke the dried cake into grains of chosen size. The air spaces between grains made burning faster and more consistent, and grained powder later proved more resistant to damp.

Corvée is labour owed to the state rather than produce: households supply workers for a set period to dig canals, build walls and roads, or raise monuments, organized in rotating gangs under officials. Old Kingdom Egypt used rotating crews on royal building projects, and comparable labour duties existed in Mesopotamia, imperial China and the Inca empire (the mit'a).

Cotton seeds carry long fibres that can be spun into soft, washable cloth. Remarkably, four cotton species were domesticated independently, two in Africa and Asia and two in the Americas. Cotton fibres preserved inside copper beads at Mehrgarh, Pakistan, date to the sixth millennium BCE, and indigo-dyed cotton fabric from Huaca Prieta, Peru, is about 6,000 years old.

A roller gin separates cotton fibre from seed by drawing lint through a narrow gap, first between a roller and a flat stone, later between two counter-rotating rollers, while the seeds are held back. It was in use in India by around the middle of the first millennium CE. Sticky-seeded short-staple cottons resisted it until the saw gin of 1793.

A saw gin separates cotton fibre from its sticky seeds: toothed discs on a turning cylinder pull lint through slots too narrow for seeds. Eli Whitney patented a wire-toothed gin in 1793; Hodgen Holmes's 1796 patent used circular saws. Cheap ginning made short-staple upland cotton profitable across the American South, where the resulting boom greatly expanded plantation slavery.

Counter-insurgency doctrine holds that an insurgency is defeated by protecting and winning over the population, not only by killing fighters. In British Malaya, the Briggs Plan of 1950 moved rural squatters into guarded new villages to cut guerrillas off from food and recruits. David Galula's book Counterinsurgency Warfare, published in 1964, drew on French experience in Algeria.

In early China, numbers were laid out with rods on a counting board, one column per decimal place, an empty column standing for zero. Bamboo slips carbon-dated to about 305 BCE hold the oldest known decimal multiplication table. The Nine Chapters, compiled by Han times, used red and black rods for positive and negative quantities in solving linear equations.

Court patronage is the support of artists and craftsmen by rulers and temples, which fed and housed them in return for monuments, statues, jewellery and other works of prestige. In Old Kingdom Egypt, from about 2600 BCE, royal workshops supplied sculptors, painters and stoneworkers for pyramid complexes and tombs. The patron's taste and needs shaped what was made.

Powerful kings sometimes raised the sons of subject rulers at their own court. The princes were educated alongside royal children, absorbed the court's language and loyalties, and served as hostages for their fathers' good conduct. Egyptian records of Thutmose III, about 1450 BCE, describe sons of Levantine rulers brought to Egypt and later sent home to rule.

Craft guilds are associations of masters in a trade that control admission, apprenticeship, quality and often prices, and represent their members before town or state authorities. Roman craft associations, the collegia, were well established by the late republic, and chartered guilds spread through European towns from the eleventh and twelfth centuries CE. Comparable bodies, such as India's srenis, existed elsewhere.

Craft specialization arises when some people spend part of their working time making goods for others, such as pots, beads or metal ornaments, and receive food in return. Finely painted Halaf pottery of northern Mesopotamia, around 6000 BCE, suggests skilled potters, and the worked gold of the Varna cemetery in Bulgaria, about 4500 BCE, points to accomplished early goldsmiths.

A crank and connecting rod convert rotation into back-and-forth motion, or the reverse.
