A relief on a third-century-CE tomb at Hierapolis, in western Turkey, shows a waterwheel driving two stone-cutting saws in this way, and remains of similar Roman saws survive at Gerasa and Ephesus. Medieval European millwrights used it widely from about 1400, later in pumps, bellows and engines.

Crewed spaceflight means sending people beyond the atmosphere and bringing them back alive, which demands life support, a heat shield for re-entry and reliable guidance. On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin made one orbit of Earth in Vostok 1. The United States flew suborbital missions that year and its first orbital flight, John Glenn's, in February 1962.

Gene editing changes a chosen DNA sequence inside living cells. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's teams showed that Cas9, an enzyme from a bacterial defence system against viruses, could be guided by designed RNA to cut DNA at a chosen site, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Rules for edited crops differ between countries.

Crop insurance compensates farmers when weather or pests cut yields below an insured level, in return for premiums paid each season. The United States created a federal crop insurance programme by an act of 1938, starting with wheat. India introduced a Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme in 1985, linked to farm credit, and many governments now subsidise similar cover.

The four-course rotation grew wheat, then turnips, then barley undersown with clover and ryegrass, then the clover itself, removing the fallow year. Turnips and clover fed livestock through winter, extra manure enriched the fields, and clover added nitrogen. It was practised in Flanders before spreading in eighteenth-century Britain, where landowners such as Charles Townshend promoted it.

A crossbow mounts a short, stiff bow crosswise on a stock and holds the drawn string with a trigger, so it can be loaded in advance and aimed steadily. Bronze trigger mechanisms survive in China from the Warring States period, when armies issued crossbows in large numbers. A magazine-fed repeating version from Chu remained in use until the late Qing.

Crucible cast steel is made by melting blister steel in sealed clay crucibles and casting it into ingots, producing uniform steel free of slag. Benjamin Huntsman, a clockmaker near Sheffield, developed the process around 1740, firing his crucibles with coke. Sheffield became famous for its files, razors and cutlery. Older crucible steels had also been made in South Asia.

Cultural institutes are state-funded bodies that teach a country's language abroad and present its arts, books and ideas to foreign publics. The British Council was founded in 1934, and West Germany's Goethe-Institut in 1951. France's older Alliance française began in 1883 as a private association, and China opened Confucius Institutes from 2004. Such work is often called cultural diplomacy.

During the early third millennium BCE, Mesopotamian scribes extended accounting signs to record sounds, using syllable signs alongside word signs. Wedge-shaped impressions made with a cut reed stylus gave the script its modern name, cuneiform. It wrote Sumerian, then Akkadian, Hittite and other languages, carrying laws, letters, literature and scholarship for about three thousand years.

Much ancient silver came not from native metal but from silver-bearing lead ores. In cupellation, smelted lead is heated to about 800 C in an oxidising blast: the lead turns to litharge and is absorbed or skimmed, leaving silver and gold. Litharge from Habuba Kabira, Syria, and Fatmali-Kalecik, Anatolia, attests the process in the fourth millennium BCE.

In small societies without police or courts, order is kept by shared norms and informal penalties. Ethnographers of foragers, including the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari, describe ridicule of boasters, gossip, shunning of shirkers and, in serious cases, expulsion or collective action against a persistent bully. Such sanctions are inferred to be very ancient, though they leave no direct archaeological trace.

Modern customs services replaced paper declarations and blanket inspections with electronic filing and checks targeted by risk. The ASYCUDA software, developed by UNCTAD from the early 1980s, was adopted by many developing countries. The Harmonized System, a shared six-digit product nomenclature, came into force in 1988, letting goods be classified the same way by most of the world's customs services.

Customs and tolls are duties charged on goods as they cross a frontier, ford a river or pass through a city gate. Some of the earliest detailed evidence comes from Old Assyrian trade of about 1900 BCE, when merchant letters found at Kanesh in Anatolia record tolls paid to local rulers along the donkey-caravan route from Assur.

A customs union removes tariffs among its members and sets a single tariff toward outsiders. The German Zollverein, led by Prussia, came into force at the start of 1834 and gradually drew in most German states, binding their economies together decades before political unification in 1871. The European Economic Community completed a customs union among its six founders in 1968.

Cyber operations use computer networks to spy on, disrupt or damage an opponent's systems, while defenders rely on encryption, authentication, monitoring and prompt repair of software flaws. Stuxnet, malicious code publicly identified in 2010, sabotaged uranium-enrichment centrifuges at Iran's Natanz plant. It is often called the first known code built to cause physical destruction; no government has officially acknowledged responsibility.

Precision boring cuts a true, smooth cylinder inside a casting. In 1774 the English ironmaster John Wilkinson patented a cannon-boring machine whose cutting head travelled on a rigid bar supported at both ends. Adapted to engine cylinders, it supplied Boulton and Watt from 1776, and the closer piston fit helped make Watt's steam engine practical on a commercial scale.

Data protection law limits how governments and companies collect, store and use records about individuals. The German state of Hesse passed what is often called the first data protection act in 1970, as computers made large personal databases possible. Sweden adopted a national data law in 1973, and the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation took effect in 2018.

A daughter colony was a new city founded overseas by settlers from a mother city, governing itself but tied to its founder by cult, kinship and custom. Phoenician Tyre is traditionally said to have founded Carthage in 814 BCE. From about 750 BCE Greek cities sent settlers to found apoikiai around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, such as Syracuse.

Debt remission edicts cancelled debts and freed people held in bondage for debt, usually when a king took the throne or in a crisis. Urukagina of Lagash, about 2400 BCE, recorded reforms easing burdens on the poor. Old Babylonian kings, including Hammurabi and later Ammi-saduqa, proclaimed misharum edicts, and part of Ammi-saduqa's edict survives.

Decolonization was the passing of colonies to independent statehood, mostly between the 1940s and 1970s. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947 amid partition and mass migration. In 1960 the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 1514, declaring that all peoples have the right to self-determination. That same year seventeen African states gained independence, and dozens more followed.

Deep learning trains neural networks with many layers on large datasets, each layer learning features from the one below. The methods had accumulated for decades, but in 2012 a network trained on graphics processors by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton sharply cut errors in the ImageNet image-recognition contest. Similar methods soon advanced speech recognition and translation.

Demand management is the use of government spending, taxation and interest rates to steady the economy, spending more in slumps and restraining demand in booms. John Maynard Keynes gave it a theoretical basis in his General Theory of 1936, written during the Great Depression. The United States Employment Act of 1946 committed federal policy to promoting maximum employment.

Elected village councils give each village its own funds and duties for public works and relief. In India, panchayati raj was inaugurated in Rajasthan in 1959, following a committee's recommendation of elected local bodies. The 73rd Amendment to the Indian constitution, passed in 1992, made elected village, block and district councils mandatory throughout the country.

Deposit insurance guarantees bank deposits up to a set limit, so savers are repaid even if their bank collapses and have less reason to start a run. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created by the United States Banking Act of 1933, after thousands of banks had failed in the early Depression. Many other countries later adopted similar schemes.

Desalination removes dissolved salt from seawater or brackish water. Ships and chemists distilled small amounts for centuries, but large plants came after the Second World War. Multi-stage flash plants, boiling heated brine in chambers of falling pressure, spread from about 1960, often beside Gulf power stations. Reverse osmosis forces water through a membrane; practical membranes emerged at UCLA around 1960.

Development lending channels international capital to governments for roads, dams, power plants and other public works. At the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, Allied governments agreed to create the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the core of the World Bank. Its first loans, from 1947, financed European reconstruction, and lending soon shifted toward poorer countries.

A developmental state steers private industry toward national catch-up, using cheap credit, output targets, import protection and export promotion. Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry, created in 1949, became the model case. Latin American economists at the UN Economic Commission for Latin America argued for import substitution, and South Korea set up an Economic Planning Board in 1961.

Rudolf Diesel began from heat-engine theory. In an 1893 treatise he proposed an engine approaching the ideal efficiency described by Sadi Carnot, igniting fuel by the heat of strongly compressed air rather than by a spark. After years of trials a working engine was tested in 1897. Diesel engines later powered ships, submarines, locomotives, lorries and generators.

A hoe sets a stone or wooden blade on a handle to break, turn and weed soil with chopping strokes. In early farming villages of northern China, such as those of the Peiligang culture about 8,000 years ago, ground-stone spades with wooden handles accompanied millet cultivation. Hafted blades allowed heavier soils to be worked than a pointed stick.

Digital identity systems give each resident a unique identity that can be checked electronically. Estonia began issuing a national electronic ID card with a chip for digital signatures in 2002. India's Aadhaar programme, launched in 2009, assigns a twelve-digit number linked to fingerprints and iris scans, covers over a billion people and is used for welfare payments and subsidized rations.

Disaster management agencies plan for floods, droughts, earthquakes and other emergencies, stockpile relief, issue warnings and coordinate rescue. In the United States, the Federal Civil Defense Administration was created in 1950, and FEMA was formed in 1979 by merging several agencies. India established its National Disaster Management Authority in 2005, after the Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004.

Distance education lets adults study for qualifications at home rather than on a campus. Correspondence courses by post spread in the nineteenth century, and the University of London allowed external degrees from 1858. Britain's Open University, chartered in 1969, combined printed course units, lectures broadcast on BBC television and radio, and local tutors; online study later followed.

Distillation separates liquids by boiling them and condensing the vapour. Greek alchemical writings from Roman Egypt describe stills, and Zosimos credits an earlier woman alchemist, Maria, with apparatus including a three-armed still. Arabic works attributed to al-Kindi in the ninth century describe distilling wine, and Latin recipes for "burning water", alcohol from wine, appeared in the twelfth century.

The divine right of kings holds that a monarch receives authority directly from God, answers to God alone and may not lawfully be resisted by subjects. James VI of Scotland, later also James I of England, set out the doctrine in The Trew Law of Free Monarchies in 1598. Robert Filmer and Bishop Bossuet later elaborated it.

Among foragers recorded by ethnographers, work is commonly divided by sex and age: men more often hunt large game far from camp, while women, children and elders gather plants, trap small animals and process food. Archaeologists Steven Kuhn and Mary Stiner have argued that this pattern arose with modern humans in the Upper Palaeolithic, though the question remains open.

DNA sequencing reads the order of the four bases along a DNA strand. Two methods were reported in 1977: Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert's chemical cleavage, and Frederick Sanger's chain termination, which used modified nucleotides that halt DNA copying. That year Sanger's group also published the first complete DNA genome, of the virus phiX174, over 5,000 bases long.

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick proposed that DNA is a double helix of two strands joined by paired bases, suggesting how genes are copied. It drew on X-ray data, including Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's Photo 51, published alongside it in Nature. Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize; Franklin died in 1958.

Dogs descend from wolves and were domesticated by hunter-gatherers long before farming. Genetic estimates of when the lineages separated range from about 15,000 to over 30,000 years ago, and single versus multiple origins are debated. A puppy buried with two people at Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, about 14,200 years ago had survived repeated distemper, apparently through human care.

In a dominant-party system, one party wins every national election for decades while opposition parties remain legal and compete. Mexico's National Revolutionary Party, founded in 1929 and later renamed the Institutional Revolutionary Party, held the presidency until 2000. Japan's Liberal Democratic Party, formed in 1955, governed almost without interruption for decades, with real contests fought among its factions.

Donkeys descend from African wild asses. Genomes of over two hundred modern and thirty-one ancient animals point to a single domestication in Africa around 5000 BCE, followed by spread into Eurasia. At Abydos in Egypt, ten donkeys buried in an early royal funerary complex, about 3000 BCE, show joint damage from carrying loads, although their bones still look partly wild.

Double-entry bookkeeping records every transaction twice, as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another, so the books can be checked by balancing them. Surviving early examples include a Florentine firm's ledger of 1299-1300 and Genoa's treasury accounts of 1340. Luca Pacioli's printed account of 1494 codified Venetian practice for a wide readership.

A pattern loom stores a woven design in its harness: warp threads are tied to cords grouped so each pattern row can be lifted in turn. Han-dynasty loom models from Laoguanshan, of the later second century BCE, are China's earliest evidence of pattern looms. Drawlooms later wove figured silks in Persia, Byzantium and Italy, until French inventors automated them.

Drip irrigation releases water slowly at the roots through plastic emitters, wasting less than flooding or sprinklers. Perforated-pipe trials predate it, but Israeli engineer Simcha Blass found that long, narrow passages inside an emitter slowed flow without the clogging of tiny holes. Tested at Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev, the design was commercialised by Netafim, founded in 1965.

Drug regulation requires new medicines to be tested before sale. In the United States, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, passed after a toxic sulfanilamide elixir killed over a hundred people, required proof of safety. The Kefauver-Harris amendments of 1962, prompted by the thalidomide disaster, added proof of effectiveness through controlled trials.

A dugout is a boat carved from a single large log, hollowed with stone adzes and sometimes with fire to char the wood for easier removal. The oldest preserved example, from Pesse in the Netherlands, dates to roughly 8,000 BCE. Sturdier than bark or reed craft, dugouts carried freight and fishers on lakes, rivers and estuaries.

Dyeing fixes colour to fibre, yarn or cloth. Indigo must be chemically reduced in a vat and then oxidises in the air; madder red binds best with a mordant such as alum. The oldest known indigo-dyed fabric, cotton from Huaca Prieta in Peru, is about 6,000 years old. Colour signalled status and made dyestuffs valuable trade goods.

Nitroglycerin is powerful but dangerously shock-sensitive; an 1864 explosion at the Nobel works killed Alfred Nobel's younger brother Emil. Nobel found that soaking it into kieselguhr, a porous siliceous earth, gave a dry granular solid that could still be detonated deliberately. Patented in 1867, dynamite made blasting rock in mines, quarries and tunnels far safer.

A dynamo turns mechanical work into electric current by spinning coils through a magnetic field, using the induction Michael Faraday discovered in 1831. In 1866-67 Henry Wilde, Werner Siemens, Charles Wheatstone and others made machines that fed part of their output to their own electromagnets, and Zénobe Gramme's ring dynamo of about 1870 gave steady current.

Dynastic marriage uses royal weddings to seal alliances and claims between ruling houses. The Amarna letters, diplomatic correspondence of the mid-fourteenth century BCE, show Egyptian pharaohs negotiating for daughters of the kings of Mitanni and Babylon, with large dowries and gifts exchanged. The practice remained central to European diplomacy into the early modern era, notably for the Habsburgs.

Digital government moves public services online, letting citizens file taxes, register businesses and claim benefits without visiting an office. Many tax authorities offered online filing by around 2000. Estonia introduced X-Road in 2001, a secure data-exchange layer letting separate public and private databases share information, and became a widely cited example of a state run largely through networks.

Earth observation uses satellite instruments to image land, oceans and atmosphere repeatedly. Weather and military reconnaissance satellites returned images from 1960, but systematic civilian land monitoring began when NASA launched the first Landsat satellite in July 1972, recording multispectral images. Repeated coverage lets analysts track crops, forest loss, floods and mineral prospects, though cloud and resolution limit visibility.

The ecumenical movement sought cooperation rather than rivalry among Christian churches, and later dialogue with other faiths. The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 is often treated as its starting point. The World Council of Churches was founded in Amsterdam in 1948, and in 1965 the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra aetate urged respect for non-Christian religions.

Elected magistracies fill executive offices by vote for a fixed, usually one-year term, often shared between colleagues, and holders answer for their conduct when the term ends. Athens listed annual archons from about 683 BCE, though early archons were not chosen by popular vote; Rome's paired consuls, by tradition first elected in 509 BCE, are the classic example.

In an elective monarchy the ruler is chosen by a body of electors rather than by birth alone, and often must accept conditions before crowning. The Golden Bull of 1356 fixed seven prince-electors for the Holy Roman Empire. From 1573 the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth elected its kings in assemblies of nobles, who bound each one with the Henrician Articles.

Under elective succession a ruler is chosen by a body of leading men rather than inheriting the throne automatically. After the East Frankish Carolingian line died out in 911, the great nobles elected Conrad of Franconia king. In the Holy Roman Empire, Emperor Charles IV's Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the choice in seven prince-electors and set majority voting rules.

Independent electoral administration puts the running of elections in the hands of an impartial body rather than ministers seeking re-election. Canada created the office of Chief Electoral Officer in 1920, answerable to Parliament, and India established its Election Commission in 1950, which has since organised the world's largest elections. Trust in the count helps losing parties accept defeat.

An incandescent lamp makes light by heating a thin filament until it glows inside a glass bulb emptied of air, so the filament does not burn. Many inventors tried the idea; around 1878-80 Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in the United States produced durable carbon-filament lamps. Unlike arc lamps, they were small, safe indoors and individually switched.

An electric motor reverses the dynamo, turning current into rotation, a possibility opened when Hans Christian Oersted saw a current deflect a compass needle in 1820. Battery-driven motors of the 1830s were too costly for real work. Once stations supplied current in the 1880s, practical direct-current motors and polyphase alternating-current motors spread to trams, lifts and factory machines.

Electric traction drives trains and trams with motors fed from overhead wires or a live rail instead of onboard steam. Werner von Siemens demonstrated an electric railway in Berlin in 1879; Frank Sprague's tram system in Richmond, Virginia, opened in 1888; London's first deep electric tube line followed in 1890. Frequent, smoke-free service made underground metros practical.

Electric cars are not new: battery vehicles were common in some cities around 1900 before petrol cars overtook them. The modern electric vehicle pairs a mass-produced car body with rechargeable lithium-ion battery packs and efficient electric motors. Tesla's Roadster, delivered from 2008, showed lithium cells could give useful range; falling battery costs since then have enabled wider, though uneven, adoption.

A central power station generates electricity in one place and sells it to many customers over wires. In 1882 Edison's companies opened stations at Holborn Viaduct in London and Pearl Street in New York, where steam engines drove dynamos supplying direct current to nearby lamps. Low-voltage direct current could not travel far, so each station served only its surrounding district.

James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 paper 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' joined electricity and magnetism in equations that predicted waves travelling at the speed of light, and he concluded that light is such a wave. Around 1887-88 Heinrich Hertz generated and detected these waves with spark gaps, showing that they reflect and travel at light's speed.

Alessandro Volta's pile of 1800, a stack of metal discs separated by moist card, gave the first continuous electric current. In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted saw a compass needle swing beside a current-carrying wire, and André-Marie Ampère soon showed that parallel currents attract. In 1831 Michael Faraday produced current from changing magnetism, the principle of generators.

Eighteenth-century experimenters studied static electricity with friction machines. In 1745 and 1746, Ewald Georg von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek independently found that a glass jar could store charge, the Leyden jar. Benjamin Franklin proposed that lightning was electrical, and from around 1752 his grounded lightning rods began protecting buildings, church steeples and gunpowder stores.

A council of notables is a standing body limited to leading families, office-holders or the wealthy, which deliberates on war, law and finance and may advise or restrain a single ruler. Sparta's gerousia, twenty-eight men over sixty who served for life alongside its two kings, and the senate of the Roman Republic are well-known examples.

An employment guarantee obliges the state to provide paid work to anyone who asks. The Indian state of Maharashtra began an Employment Guarantee Scheme in the early 1970s, during a severe drought. India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Act of 2005 promised each rural household up to 100 days of unskilled work a year, with an allowance if none was offered.

Endocrinology studies hormones, chemical messengers that glands release into the blood. In London in 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling identified secretin, often called the first hormone; Starling introduced the word hormone in 1905. In 1922 a diabetic patient, Leonard Thompson, received insulin purified by James Collip, after work by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in John Macleod's laboratory.

The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century European movement that applied reason and criticism to religion, law and government. It drew on the scientific achievements of the previous century, notably Isaac Newton's Principia of 1687. Writers corresponded and published in a public republic of letters; Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie, begun in 1751, aimed to gather and spread useful knowledge.

Environmental regulation uses permits, emission standards and inspections to limit pollution of air, water and soil. Many countries passed such laws in the 1960s and 1970s, after smog episodes and polluted rivers drew public attention. The United States created its Environmental Protection Agency in 1970, the same year as major amendments to its Clean Air Act.

Epic literature arose when long heroic tales, once sung or recited, were fixed in writing and copied by scribes. The earliest Gilgamesh material is a set of separate Sumerian poems, probably composed around 2100 BCE; an Old Babylonian version wove them into one epic by about 1800 BCE. Greek and Indian epics later followed similar paths from performance to text.

Epidemiology studies how disease is distributed across populations and why. In 1662 John Graunt analysed London's bills of mortality, counting deaths by cause. In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths and water pumps in London and compared two water companies' customers, arguing that cholera spread through water. Randomised trials, such as Britain's 1948 streptomycin trial, extended its comparative method.

Equal pay laws require employers to pay women and men the same for the same work, or for work of equal value. The International Labour Organization adopted its Equal Remuneration Convention in 1951. The United States passed the Equal Pay Act in 1963, and Britain its Equal Pay Act in 1970, which came into force in 1975.

An escapement lets a weight-driven gear train advance in small, regular steps. In the verge-and-foliot, a crown wheel pushes alternately against two pallets on a rod carrying a swinging weighted bar. It appeared in European tower clocks in the late thirteenth century, inventor unknown, making equal hours practical. Su Song's 1092 clock tower in China used a water-driven escapement.

In the first millennium BCE, several traditions taught that the divine demanded justice and right conduct, not offerings alone. The Hebrew prophet Amos, active around 750 BCE, condemned the rich for oppressing the poor and judged rulers by that standard. Zoroastrian teaching on the struggle between truth and falsehood is also often placed in this period, though its dating is debated.

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the theory of evolution by natural selection independently; their papers were read together at the Linnean Society in London on 1 July 1858. Darwin's On the Origin of Species followed in November 1859. Variation, inheritance and unequal survival explained how species change, drawing on breeders' experience and naturalists' classifications.

The Exchequer was the English royal accounting office, named after the chequered cloth on which counters were moved to reckon sums. It appears under Henry I around 1110. Twice a year sheriffs answered for the revenues of their shires, and the results were written on pipe rolls; the oldest surviving roll covers the year 1129 to 1130.

An executive budget gathers every department's spending requests into a single plan prepared under the head of government and presented to the legislature. In the United States the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 created the Bureau of the Budget to draft it and the General Accounting Office to audit spending afterwards. Before then, agencies largely bargained with Congress separately.

Mass immunization programmes vaccinate every child against major diseases on a fixed schedule. After Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe in 1955, the United States vaccinated millions of schoolchildren. In 1974 the World Health Organization launched its Expanded Programme on Immunization to bring vaccines against measles, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and tuberculosis to children worldwide.

In an extended-family household, parents, married children and grandchildren live under one roof and share hearths, stores and labour under a senior couple. In central Europe, farmers of the Linear Pottery culture built timber longhouses up to about 40 metres long around 5500 to 5000 BCE. Among the Iroquois, related women and their families shared longhouses in later centuries.

Factory inspection uses state officials to enforce limits on child labour and working hours. Britain's Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from textile mills, limited the hours of older children, and, unlike earlier acts, appointed paid inspectors with power to enter mills. Later acts extended inspection to other industries and to adult women.

Family law fixes rules for marriage, divorce, adoption and inheritance, deciding who belongs to a household and how its property passes on. Mesopotamian codes wrote such rules down early: the laws of Ur-Nammu, about 2100 BCE, set payments on divorce, and the Code of Hammurabi, about 1754 BCE, regulated dowries, adoption and the division of estates among sons.

Famine early warning systems combine satellite monitoring of rainfall and crops with reports on market prices and household conditions to forecast food crises months in advance. The United States set up the Famine Early Warning Systems Network in 1985 after the Ethiopian and Sahelian famines, and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization runs its own global warning system.

Before engines reached farms, horse-drawn machines began replacing hand labour. Andrew Meikle's threshing machine, first used in Scotland in 1786, separated grain from straw. Patrick Bell's 1828 reaper was pushed by two horses; in the United States Cyrus McCormick (1831) and Obed Hussey (1833) built rival reapers, with priority disputed. John Deere made his first steel plough in 1837.

Fascism is an ultranationalist mass movement that rejects liberal democracy and socialism, glorifies violence and seeks national rebirth under a single party and leader. Benito Mussolini founded the Fasci di Combattimento in Milan in 1919, drawing many members from war veterans. Its squads attacked socialists and unions, and similar movements soon spread across interwar Europe.

A fascist state is a single-party dictatorship of an ultranationalist movement under a leader, mobilizing society through propaganda, mass organizations and state-controlled corporations of employers and workers. Mussolini became Italian prime minister in 1922 and built a dictatorship over the following years. In Germany, Hitler took power in 1933 and quickly abolished rival parties and independent trade unions.

A fast breeder reactor uses unmoderated fast neutrons, usually with liquid-sodium cooling, and surrounds its core with uranium-238 that becomes plutonium, so it can make more fissile fuel than it burns. Idaho's EBR-I, which first generated usable nuclear electricity in December 1951, was a breeder. France closed Superphénix in 1998; Russia's BN-600 has fed its grid since 1980.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing is a goal rather than an achieved technology: machines correcting their own errors faster than errors arise, keeping long calculations reliable. Quantum error-correcting codes, first proposed by Peter Shor in 1995, spread one robust logical qubit across many fragile physical ones. If built at scale, such machines could simulate molecules and materials beyond practical classical reach.

A federation divides sovereignty between a central government and member states or cantons, each holding powers protected by a constitution. The United States Constitution of 1787 created a durable federal model, and Switzerland adopted a federal constitution in 1848 after a brief civil war. Federations can accommodate regional diversity but must keep settling disputes over which level holds which powers.

Crushed fruit ferments readily in a sealed vessel. Pottery from Jiahu in China, about 7000 BCE, holds residues of a mixed drink of rice, honey and fruit. Grape wine is attested chemically in jars from Georgia of about 6000 BCE, and at Areni-1 cave in Armenia a pressing basin and fermentation vat date to about 4100 BCE.

Brewing turns grain starch into sugar, by malting or cooking, then lets yeasts ferment it into alcohol. Residues in stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel, about 13,000 years old, have been read as a weak cereal beer, a contested claim. Later brewers used barley in Mesopotamia, rice in China, maize in the Andes and sorghum in Africa.

In a feudal monarchy the king grants land as fiefs to vassals for loyalty and military service; vassals grant parts of their fiefs to vassals of their own, dividing authority along a hierarchy of increasingly hereditary holdings. It took shape in France as Carolingian royal power weakened in the tenth century; historians compare medieval Japan and debate the label itself.

Optical fibres guide light along thin glass strands by total internal reflection. In 1966 Charles Kao and George Hockham argued that purified glass could carry signals over long distances; Kao later shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1970 Corning researchers made fibre below 20 decibels loss per kilometre, and fibre began carrying telephone traffic in the late 1970s.

The film industry grew from short films into studios making feature films for thousands of cinemas. The first Hollywood studio opened in 1911, and southern California soon became the centre of American production, drawn by sunshine. The Jazz Singer of 1927 popularized synchronized sound, and by the 1930s tens of millions of Americans went to the cinema weekly.

Organised fire-fighting gave towns trained crews and standing equipment instead of improvised bucket chains. In Amsterdam, Jan van der Heyden's improved fire engine with flexible hoses, introduced around 1672, was used by municipal fire companies. After the Great Fire of 1666, London's private fire insurance offices, from about 1680, kept their own fire brigades.

Controlled fire became a technology when people learned to hold hearths at chosen temperatures. At Pinnacle Point, South Africa, silcrete was deliberately heated by about 164,000 years ago, making the stone easier to flake into fine points. Managed fire also cooked food in earth ovens and burned landscapes to renew plants. When hominins first used fire remains debated.

Firing moulded clay bricks in a kiln makes them hard and water-resistant, unlike sun-dried mudbrick, so they suit foundations, drains and baths. Fired brick was used in early Indus Valley towns such as Kalibangan by about 3000 BCE, and in the mid-third millennium BCE the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro used bricks of standard 1:2:4 proportions.

First-comer precedence gives descendants of a place's founders lasting authority over its land and spirits. In many West African societies an earth priest from the founding lineage performs the land's rituals and grants fields to later arrivals, even when political power lies elsewhere. Some archaeologists see similar claims at Neolithic Çatalhöyük, where houses were rebuilt on one spot for generations.

Fiscal equalization moves revenue from a central treasury to poorer regions by formula, so every province can offer similar public services at similar tax rates. Australia set up its Commonwealth Grants Commission in 1933 to advise on payments to weaker states, and Canada introduced a formal equalization programme in 1957. Germany and other federations run comparable schemes.

Fisheries management sets catch limits, seasons and gear rules so that fish stocks can recover and remain productive. In the 1970s, coastal states extended control over fishing in their offshore waters; the United States' Magnuson Fishery Act of 1976 set up regional management councils, and the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea recognized 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zones.

At Jerimalai rock shelter in East Timor, layers about 42,000 years old hold thousands of fish bones, many from tuna and other open-sea species. Catching them implies planning and seagoing skill. How they were caught, by hook, trolled line or net, is unresolved: the site's oldest shell hook is younger, about 23,000 to 16,000 years old.

Among many fishing peoples, a kin group owned a particular weir or fishing place, kept it in repair and controlled who else could fish there. Peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast held such inherited rights to fishing stations. In Ireland, wooden fish traps of Mesolithic age, about 6000 BCE, found in Dublin's docklands, suggest weirs rebuilt at one spot.

A fission weapon assembles highly enriched uranium or plutonium so fast that a chain reaction runs out of control. The wartime Manhattan Project tested a plutonium implosion device in New Mexico on 16 July 1945; atomic bombs were then used against Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August. Four more states had tested such weapons by 1964.

Flax yields linen fibre from its stems and oil from its seeds. Wild flax fibres, some spun, dyed and knotted, occur in Dzudzuana Cave, Georgia, in layers about 36,000 to 31,000 years old. Domesticated flax is one of Southwest Asia's founder crops: larger cultivated seeds at Tell Ramad in Syria date to the seventh millennium BCE.

The flintlock produced sparks by striking a flint, held in the cock, against a hinged steel, the frizzen, which also covered the priming pan. It is usually credited to the French gunmaker Marin le Bourgeoys in the early 1600s, refining earlier snaphance locks. Simpler and cheaper than the wheellock, it armed most European infantry from the late 1600s.

John Kay's flying shuttle, patented in England in 1733, ran on small wheels and was knocked across the loom by pickers jerked with a cord, rather than passed from hand to hand. One weaver could then weave broad cloth alone and faster. Widely adopted from the mid-eighteenth century, it raised demand for yarn and so put pressure on spinning.

Among recorded foragers, a hunter who brings in large game is expected to share it across the camp, and others may ask for a portion as of right, which anthropologists call demand sharing. It evens out the luck of the hunt. Butchered bones around ancient hearths suggest food sharing is very old.

Medieval forest law reserved woods, and especially deer and other game, for the king, and licensed other people's use of timber, pasture and hunting. William the Conqueror created the New Forest in England around 1079. Resentment of harsh forest courts led to the Charter of the Forest of 1217, which restored some common rights to free men.

Free trade is a policy of low or no tariffs, letting goods cross borders on equal terms. Britain made the decisive turn in 1846, when Robert Peel's government repealed the Corn Laws that had protected domestic grain growers. The Cobden-Chevalier Treaty with France in 1860 cut duties further and set off a wave of tariff-reducing treaties across Europe.

Freedom of information laws give anyone the right to request government documents, which must be released unless a stated exemption applies. Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 is often called the first. Finland passed its Act on the Publicity of Official Documents in 1951, and the United States adopted its Freedom of Information Act in 1966.

Friendly societies were clubs of wage-earners who paid small weekly sums into a common fund that paid benefits in sickness, old age and at death. They spread widely in eighteenth-century Britain, and Rose's Act of 1793 gave registered societies legal protection. By the nineteenth century millions belonged to societies such as the Oddfellows and Foresters.

Climate engineering means deliberate, large-scale intervention in the climate system. A 2009 Royal Society report split proposals into two families: removing carbon dioxide from the air, and reflecting some sunlight back to space. It judged removal preferable; reflection could cool quickly but would not lower carbon dioxide, and no method had been shown affordable with acceptable environmental effects.

Computation research seeks more calculation per unit of energy, material and labour. For decades transistor counts on chips doubled roughly every two years, a trend Gordon Moore described in 1965 and revised in 1975; the pace has since slowed. Rolf Landauer argued in 1961 that erasing one bit must release a minimum of heat, a floor far below present chips.

Crop genomics reads and edits the DNA of food plants to guide breeding. The rice genome, published in 2005 by a project begun in 1997, mapped about 37,500 genes and became a reference for related cereals. Breeders pair such maps with editing tools like CRISPR, which alters chosen sites without leaving foreign DNA; rules for it vary by country.

Cyber research is the contest between attackers and defenders of networked systems. Any advantage is relative and temporary: new software brings new flaws, discovered weaknesses are patched, and techniques spread to rivals. The field spans cryptography, secure software design, intrusion detection and human error, such as staff tricked into revealing passwords. Governments, companies and criminal groups all invest in it.

Energy-conversion research seeks more useful work per unit of fuel or sunlight. Physics sets ceilings: Sadi Carnot's 1824 analysis bounds any heat engine's efficiency by its operating temperatures, and William Shockley and Hans-Joachim Queisser calculated in 1961 that a single-junction solar cell cannot convert much more than about a third of sunlight. Combined-cycle plants and multi-junction cells show continuing gains.

Frontier fortresses were chains of garrisoned forts that held a border, controlled river crossings and reported movements to the capital. Middle Kingdom Egypt built massive mudbrick forts at the Second Cataract of the Nile in Nubia, many under Senusret III in the nineteenth century BCE. Papyrus copies called the Semna Despatches preserve fort reports on Nubians arriving to trade.

Reaching low orbit means accelerating a payload to about 7.8 kilometres per second, roughly 30 megajoules per kilogram plus the climb. That energy is cheap; launch prices were historically dominated by hardware discarded after each flight, propellant handling and small production runs. Reuse, larger vehicles and higher flight rates have cut prices per kilogram; further gains are uncertain.

Materials science studies how a material's structure, from atoms to grains, governs its properties, and how processing changes that structure. It took shape as a discipline in the 1950s, when Northwestern University broadened metallurgy into a department renamed materials science in 1958-59. Recent programmes, such as the US Materials Genome Initiative (2011), pair computation with experiment.

Biomedical research is the continuing, organised effort to understand disease at the level of genes, cells and populations and to turn that understanding into treatment. Since the late twentieth century it has drawn on genome sequencing, large clinical trials and computing. Its results arrive unevenly: some conditions became treatable or preventable, while others, including many dementias, still resist.

Since the Second World War, many states have funded permanent military research through government laboratories, defence agencies and contracts with industry and universities; the United States created ARPA in 1958 after Sputnik. Such programmes seek advantage over rivals rather than one decisive invention, and each side's gains often prompt countermeasures. Some results, such as computer networking, found civilian use.

The rocket equation governs space travel: a craft's final speed depends on how fast it expels propellant and how much of its starting mass is fuel. Chemical rockets expel gas at a few kilometres per second; ion thrusters, flown on probes such as Deep Space 1 (1998) and Dawn, reach far higher exhaust speeds at very low thrust.

Fulling cleans and thickens woven wool by pounding it wet, often with fuller's earth, so the fibres felt together. Once done by trampling, it was mechanised with water-driven hammers lifted by cams on a wheel shaft; such mills are recorded in Europe by about the eleventh century. They drew some cloth-making toward fast streams, though how much is debated.

Fusion power is the still-unrealised goal of generating electricity from controlled fusion. A plant would need a plasma yielding far more energy than the whole facility consumes, wall materials that survive intense neutron bombardment, and tritium fuel bred from lithium. ITER in France does not aim to generate electricity; it aims to sustain burning plasmas, leaving power to later plants.

Fusion propulsion is a proposed way to drive spacecraft by expelling the products of nuclear fusion, which release vastly more energy per kilogram than chemical fuels. None has been built. Design studies such as the British Interplanetary Society's Project Daedalus in the 1970s sketched an uncrewed probe reaching a nearby star in about fifty years, assuming undemonstrated technology.

Galvanized corrugated iron is iron sheet coated with zinc against rust and pressed into ridges that make it stiff. Henry Palmer patented corrugated iron in London in 1829, and the French engineer Stanislas Sorel patented hot-dip galvanizing in 1837. Light, cheap and shipped flat, it roofed warehouses, settlers' houses and mining camps across the British Empire and beyond.

The stationary gas engine burned its fuel inside the cylinder instead of under a boiler. Étienne Lenoir's engine of 1860, the first practical one, burned gas without compressing it first. In 1876 Nikolaus Otto's Cologne firm built an engine that compressed the gas-air mixture before igniting it in a four-stroke cycle, making small boiler-less workshop engines economical.

A power-station gas turbine burns gas or oil to spin a turbine coupled to a generator, adapting jet-engine principles to continuous duty. In the combined cycle, widely adopted from the 1970s, hot exhaust also raises steam for a second turbine, recovering otherwise wasted heat. Its blades run hotter than ordinary steels tolerate, relying on nickel superalloys such as Nimonic 80.

Gear trains pass rotation between toothed wheels, changing speed, force or direction. The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze device recovered from a shipwreck off a Greek island, used dozens of small gears to calculate positions of the sun and moon and to predict eclipses; it was built around the second or first century BCE. Right-angled gears drove Roman watermills.

General machine intelligence means hypothetical computer systems able to learn and perform most intellectual tasks people can, not one narrow job. The idea runs from Alan Turing's 1950 paper on machine thinking and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop to recent large language models. Whether current methods can reach it, when, and how it should be governed remain open, strongly disputed questions.

A general staff is a permanent body of trained officers who plan mobilisation, gather intelligence and prepare operations in peacetime. Prussia built one in reforms led by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau after Napoleon defeated it at Jena and Auerstedt, and founded a war academy in Berlin in 1810. It later became the envy of other armies, though planning never removed uncertainty.

Recombinant DNA joins genetic material from different sources and copies it in living cells. In 1973 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer inserted foreign DNA into a bacterial plasmid that Escherichia coli then copied as it multiplied. The 1975 Asilomar conference set safety guidelines for such research, and engineered bacteria were later used to make human insulin for diabetes treatment.

Gregor Mendel crossed garden peas in Brno and, by counting offspring, found that traits pass on as separate units in predictable ratios. Presented in 1865 and published in 1866, his results were rarely cited. In 1900 Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak rediscovered them, and from 1902 Sutton and Boveri linked inheritance to chromosomes.

Genome sequencing reads an organism's entire genetic material. In 1995 a whole-genome shotgun method, which needed no prior physical map, gave the first complete genome of a free-living organism, the bacterium Haemophilus influenzae. The Human Genome Project declared completion in April 2003, though about 8 percent, mostly repetitive DNA, stayed unread until 2022. A finished rice genome followed in 2005.

Geographic compendia gathered reports from travellers, merchants and envoys into descriptions of the known world. In Sicily, the geographer al-Idrisi completed a world map and accompanying book for King Roger II in 1154, known as the Tabula Rogeriana. In Song China, the trade official Zhao Rugua compiled Records of Foreign Peoples around 1225 from merchants' accounts of distant lands.

Geographical societies were learned associations that sponsored expeditions, published journals and maps, and trained travellers in survey methods. The Société de Géographie, founded in Paris in 1821, is often called the oldest. London's Royal Geographical Society followed in 1830 and supported travellers such as David Livingstone in Africa. Their medals and lectures made explorers public figures.

Geological disposal isolates long-lived radioactive waste hundreds of metres underground, relying on stable rock and engineered barriers rather than continued human care. In 1957 an American scientific panel favoured salt formations. New Mexico's WIPP began receiving defence transuranic waste in 1999, about 650 metres deep in salt. At Oklo, Gabon, natural reactor wastes stayed largely put for two billion years.

Axiomatic geometry derives every result by proof from a few stated starting points. Greek thinkers sought proofs from at least the sixth century BCE, and Euclid's Elements, compiled at Alexandria around 300 BCE, organised earlier work into thirteen books deducing hundreds of propositions from definitions, postulates and common notions. Doubts about its fifth, parallel, postulate eventually produced non-Euclidean geometries.

Scribes in Egypt and Mesopotamia calculated areas and volumes with tested rules rather than proofs. Egypt's Moscow papyrus, of about 1850-1700 BCE, finds the volume of a truncated pyramid, and the Rhind papyrus, copied around 1650-1550 BCE, treats a round field nine units across as a square of side eight. Old Babylonian tablets of about 1800 BCE solve comparable problems.

Geophysical prospecting measures physical contrasts underground to find deposits with no surface trace. Swedish miners traced iron ore with magnetic compasses; later magnetometers mapped magnetite bodies. Roland Eötvös's torsion balance sensed density differences, locating an oil structure at Egbell in 1915 and Texas salt domes from 1924. Reflection-seismic tests began in Oklahoma in 1921; electrical methods targeted sulphide ores.

Germ theory holds that specific microorganisms cause specific infectious diseases. Leeuwenhoek had first seen bacteria through his microscopes nearly two centuries earlier, but evidence for disease causation came between the 1860s and the 1880s. Louis Pasteur linked microbes to fermentation and spoilage, and Robert Koch tied anthrax (1876) and then tuberculosis (1882) to identified bacteria using culture and staining.

A slave-soldier corps is raised by buying or levying boys from outside the realm, training them as soldiers loyal only to the ruler, and promoting the able. The Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim, ruling from 833 CE, built a guard of Turkic ghulams. The Ottoman Janissaries, formed in the fourteenth century, came to be filled through the devshirme levy of Christian boys.

Gift exchange binds people through obligation: a gift creates a debt to be repaid later, often between partners in distant groups. Sea shells carried far inland in the Upper Palaeolithic, about 40,000 years ago, and obsidian traded hundreds of kilometres from Anatolian sources by about 10,000 years ago are often read as traces of such networks.

Glassblowing inflates a gather of molten glass on the end of a tube into a bubble that can be shaped quickly and thinly. It emerged on the Syro-Palestinian coast around the mid-first century BCE; waste from a workshop in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter includes glass tubes and tiny blown bottles. Blowing made glass cheap enough for everyday use.

Before blowing, glassworkers cast glass in moulds or fused pieces of coloured glass into mosaic patterns, then ground and polished the results like stone. A green glass jar inscribed for the Assyrian king Sargon II, 721-705 BCE, was probably cast and then cut. From about 220 BCE Hellenistic workshops sagged mosaic glass over moulds to make vivid bowls.

The first glass vessels were built around a removable core of clay-based material: molten glass was trailed or wound over it and the core scraped out after cooling. Such small, colourful bottles were made in western Asia and, from the reign of Thutmose III (about 1479-1425 BCE), in Egypt, where glass had arrived shortly before 1500 BCE.

Faience is a non-clay ceramic of crushed quartz or sand that forms a glassy surface when fired with alkaline salts. In Egypt, glazed steatite beads appear in the Badarian culture, about 4400-4000 BCE, and quartz-paste faience by about 3500 BCE. Glaze could be brushed on, or form from a glazing powder in which an object was buried.

Lead crystal is glass made heavy and brilliant with lead oxide. In 1674 George Ravenscroft patented a clear English glass meant to rival rock crystal; when early pieces clouded, a defect called crizzling, he added lead, a change dated between 1674 and 1676. The denser, more refractive glass suited cut tableware and, later, the flint elements of achromatic lenses.

Gliding flight depends on wings that generate lift and on controls that keep the craft balanced. George Cayley analysed lift, drag and thrust and flew a crewed glider at Brompton Dale in 1853. Otto Lilienthal made about 2,000 glides in 1891-1896 and published lift data. The Wright brothers' gliders of 1900-1902 developed control around three axes.

Gold, which does not tarnish, and more rarely silver occur as soft native metal that can be worked without smelting. The cemetery at Varna, Bulgaria, used around 4600-4200 BCE, held more than 3,000 gold objects weighing about six kilograms, the oldest large assemblage of worked gold known. How far that wealth reflects a ranked society is debated.

Satellite navigation fixes position by timing radio signals from several satellites that carry atomic clocks. The United States Global Positioning System, developed from 1973, reached full operational capability in 1995. Its clocks are corrected for special and general relativity, about 38 microseconds a day; uncorrected, fixes would drift by kilometres daily. Civil receivers spread widely during the 1990s.

Graphics processors were built to compute colours for millions of screen pixels at once, using many simple cores working in parallel. Chips marketed as GPUs appeared in 1999, and from 2006-07 programming tools such as NVIDIA's CUDA let scientists use them for general calculations. They suited simulation and matrix arithmetic, later the core workload of machine learning.

Purpose-built granaries keep stored grain dry and safe from pests, so a harvest can last until the next one and beyond. At Dhra' in the Jordan Valley, raised-floor storehouses of about 9300 BCE predate the full domestication of cereals. By about 7000 BCE, sealed pits, silos and plastered bins were common across the Near East.

Graphite-moderated reactors use very pure carbon to slow neutrons, letting unenriched uranium sustain a chain reaction. Oak Ridge's X-10 (1943) pioneered plutonium production that Hanford's B reactor (1944) took to full scale. Britain's Magnox stations, from Calder Hall in 1956, cooled such cores with carbon dioxide for power. Flaws in the Soviet RBMK variant contributed to Chernobyl in 1986.

A concert of powers is a system in which the strongest states meet to settle disputes and keep a balance among themselves. The Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815 redrew Europe after Napoleon's defeat. Afterwards the Concert of Europe used periodic congresses and conferences, which many historians credit with helping to avoid a general European war for decades.

Greek fire was a liquid incendiary used by the Byzantine navy, projected from pressurised siphons in the bows of ships. Byzantine tradition credits a refugee architect from Syria named Kallinikos, with its first use during the Arab sieges of Constantinople around 672–678. The composition was a closely guarded state secret, probably petroleum-based, and its formula was later lost.

From the 1940s Norman Borlaug, working in Mexico, bred short-stemmed wheat that could take heavy fertilizer without toppling; in 1966 the International Rice Research Institute released IR8, a semi-dwarf rice. With irrigation, fertilizer and pesticides, these varieties sharply raised yields in India, Pakistan and elsewhere. Critics note uneven gains favouring irrigated, better-off farmers, and environmental costs.

Grid-scale storage holds surplus electricity and returns it when demand peaks or wind and sunlight fall away. The oldest method is pumped storage: water is pumped uphill and later released through turbines, used in Switzerland and Italy from the late nineteenth century. It still holds most installed storage capacity, while large battery installations multiplied in the 2010s.

Grinding wild seeds and roots between two stones turns tough plant tissue into flour or paste that cooks quickly. Starch grains on grinding tools from Bilancino in Italy, Kostenki in Russia and Pavlov in Czechia show mobile hunter-gatherers processing plants this way about 30,000 years ago. Later, Natufian foragers of the Levant pounded wild cereals in stone mortars.

Grinding a stone blade against an abrasive rock produces a smooth, strong edge that can be resharpened by further grinding, suited to felling and heavy woodworking. A ground-edge axe fragment from Carpenter's Gap 1 in Western Australia's Kimberley is dated to 44,000-49,000 years ago; Japan has ground-edge axes about 35,000-38,000 years old, long before farming.

Guest right is the custom of feeding and protecting peaceful strangers for a time. Ethnographers have recorded it among many foraging and herding peoples, and it allowed travel across other groups' lands for trade, marriage and resettlement. Its prehistoric origin is only inferred: shell beads carried far from the coast suggest exchange networks linked distant bands more than 40,000 years ago.

Guest-worker programmes recruit foreign workers on fixed contracts to fill labour shortages. The Bracero Program, begun in 1942, brought Mexican workers to American farms and railways until 1964. West Germany signed recruitment agreements with several countries, including Turkey in 1961. Many workers expected to return home instead stayed, and their families settled in the host country.

Guided missiles combine propulsion with a guidance system that corrects their course in flight. Germany's Henschel Hs 293, a rocket-boosted glide bomb steered by radio, was first used in August 1943 and soon sank Allied ships, including HMS Egret. In the 1950s homing missiles entered service, such as the American infrared-guided Sidewinder, adopted by the US Navy in 1956.

Precision-guided munitions steer onto a marked or located target. American laser-guided bombs, homing on laser light reflected from the target, destroyed the Thanh Hoa bridge in North Vietnam in 1972 after years of failed raids with unguided bombs. From the 1990s, bombs guided by satellite navigation could strike set coordinates in any weather. Misidentified targets still cause civilian deaths.

Gunpowder mixes saltpetre (potassium nitrate), sulphur and charcoal; the saltpetre supplies oxygen, so the mixture burns fiercely without air. Chinese alchemists searching for elixirs came upon such mixtures by the ninth century. The Wujing Zongyao, compiled about 1040-1044, holds the earliest surviving military formulas, which were low in saltpetre and made incendiaries rather than explosives.

Plants need fixed nitrogen, yet the nitrogen in air is unreactive. By 1908 Fritz Haber showed that high pressure and a catalyst could make ammonia directly from nitrogen and hydrogen. Carl Bosch's team at BASF, running thousands of catalyst trials, scaled it up, and the Oppau plant began production in 1913. Its ammonia supplied fertiliser and, in wartime, explosives.

Before coins, silver served as money by weight. Mesopotamian texts state prices and debts in shekels, a weight unit of about 8.4 grams. Payers cut rings, coils and ingots into pieces, now called hacksilver, and weighed them on balances. The silver itself was refined from lead-bearing ores by cupellation, attested from the fourth millennium BCE.

Composite hafting joins a stone tip or blade to a shaft or handle with a shaped tang or socket, binding and glue, to survive repeated impact. Damage on points from Kathu Pan 1, South Africa, about 500,000 years old, has been read as hafted spear tips, a contested claim; glued hafts are secure by about 70,000 years ago.

Controlled heating of silcrete or chert alters the stone so that it fractures more smoothly; heated pieces leave glossy rather than dull flake scars. Evidence from Pinnacle Point, South Africa, points to the practice by about 164,000 years ago, and experiments showed unheated Blombos silcrete could hardly be pressure-flaked. It is an early case of fire altering a material.

The heavy plough combined a coulter, an iron share and a mouldboard, and might need up to eight oxen. It turned the wet clay soils of northern Europe that resisted the ard. Linguistic evidence suggests Slavic peoples used it by the sixth century CE, and it is recorded in Italy's Po valley by 643; how fast it spread is debated.

Heavy water, whose hydrogen carries an extra neutron, absorbs so few neutrons that a reactor moderated by it can run on natural uranium. Canada's ZEEP at Chalk River, critical in September 1945, was the first reactor outside the United States. The CANDU design, from a 1962 prototype, holds fuel in pressure tubes and refuels while running. India also uses it.

In a hegemonic league, allied states swear loyalty to an alliance led by its strongest member. The Delian League, formed in 478 BCE against Persia, pooled contributions from Greek cities to pay for a fleet under Athenian command. In 338 to 337 BCE, Philip II of Macedon organised the League of Corinth to bind Greek states to him.

A helicopter lifts and steers itself with powered rotating wings, so it can hover, take off vertically and land without runways. Rotor torque and uneven blade forces defeated many early attempts. In 1935 and 1936 France's Breguet-Dorand Gyroplane Laboratoire and Germany's Focke-Wulf Fw 61 made controlled flights; Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 (1939) then established the single main rotor with tail rotor.

Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Revolutions (1543) placed the Sun at the centre and treated Earth as one of the planets, though he kept circular orbits. Using Tycho Brahe's careful observations, Johannes Kepler showed in Astronomia nova (1609) that Mars moves on an ellipse and sweeps equal areas in equal times. The Sun-centred system remained contested for decades.

Herbal medicine uses plants and fungi to ease pain, expel worms and treat wounds. Chemical traces in the dental calculus of Neanderthals at El Sidrón in Spain, about 49,000 years ago, have been read as signs of eating chamomile and poplar, though this is debated. Ötzi the Iceman, about 3300 BCE, carried birch polypore, a medicinal fungus.

Herding contracts entrusted the flocks of temples and palaces to herdsmen who owed a fixed return. Under the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2050 BCE, accounts set quotas of lambs and wool for each flock and allowed for losses. The Laws of Hammurabi, about 1754 BCE, also regulate hired herdsmen, including their liability for animals lost through negligence.

Hereditary rank exists when status and leadership pass by descent within particular families, so control of land, herds and surplus is inherited rather than won anew each generation. Archaeologists infer it from burials: at Varna in Bulgaria, graves of about 4600-4200 BCE range from plain pits to a few rich in gold. Whether such wealth was inherited is debated.

Heritage preservation is the listing and legal protection of historic buildings and sites. France created the post of Inspector General of Historic Monuments in 1830, held from 1834 by Prosper Mérimée, who toured the country and listed buildings for repair. In 1972 UNESCO adopted the World Heritage Convention, under which states nominate sites of outstanding value to an international list.

The herring buss was a decked fishing vessel from the Low Countries that stayed at sea for weeks using drift nets. Its crew gutted and salted the herring aboard and packed it in barrels, a method developed in the fourteenth century and often credited to the Fleming Willem Beukelszoon. Dutch busses dominated the North Sea herring fishery for centuries.

Hide working turns raw skins into durable leather or fur by scraping away flesh and fat, then drying, stretching and softening them, sometimes with fat or smoke. Stone scrapers with hide-use wear, and specialised bone tools in Africa and Europe, show the practice by at least 100,000 years ago. Hides gave clothing, containers and tent covers.

Egyptian hieroglyphic writing combined signs for words with signs for consonant sounds. Inscribed labels from tomb U-j at Abydos, dated to around 3250 BCE, are among its earliest known examples. Whether Egypt invented writing independently or after contact with Mesopotamia is debated. Hieroglyphs served monuments and ritual for over three millennia, while cursive hieratic handled daily administration.

High-speed rail runs passenger trains at sustained speeds above roughly 200 kilometres per hour on dedicated, carefully engineered track. Japan opened the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka in October 1964, using electric multiple-unit trains, gentle curves, tunnels and viaducts. France followed with the TGV in 1981. Over medium distances, such lines often rival air travel on door-to-door journey time.

National highway programmes plan and finance networks of limited-access motor roads linking a country's regions. Germany began building its Reichsautobahn network in the 1930s, drawing on plans from the Weimar years, and the United States' Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded the Interstate system, paid for largely through federal fuel taxes.

Indian mathematicians developed decimal place-value numerals with a sign for zero by the mid-first millennium CE, and in 628 Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers. Al-Khwarizmi's treatise on Indian reckoning, written in Baghdad around 820, spread the system westward, and Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 promoted it in a Europe still using Roman numerals.

Wage and hire tariffs set by law what labour and equipment earn for a period of work. The Laws of Eshnunna, from Mesopotamia around 1800 BCE, fix the wage of a harvester and the hire of a wagon with its oxen and of a boat. The Laws of Hammurabi contain similar schedules, sparing employers from bargaining over every price.

Holy war doctrine declares fighting against unbelievers a religious duty that earns spiritual reward. Early Islamic jurists developed rules of jihad during the eighth century CE. In 1095 Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade at Clermont, offering remission of penance to those who went. In Iberia and the Baltic, conquered frontier land was settled by colonists of the victorious faith.

The horizontal treadle loom lets the weaver's feet raise and lower sets of warp threads through cords and levers, freeing both hands to pass the shuttle and beat in the weft. Loom models from a Han-dynasty tomb at Laoguanshan, Chengdu, date to about 150 BCE. In Europe, eleventh-century loom parts mark its arrival as the professional weaver's tool.

The oral contraceptive uses synthetic hormones resembling progesterone to stop ovulation. It joined reproductive endocrinology to steroid chemistry: Russell Marker's route from Mexican wild yams made steroids cheap, and norethindrone was synthesised in Mexico City in 1951. Gregory Pincus, John Rock and colleagues ran clinical trials, and a pill was first approved for contraception in the United States in 1960.

A padded collar rests on a horse's shoulders, letting it pull heavy loads with its full strength instead of against straps across its chest or neck. Collar harness is attested in China by about the fifth century CE and became widespread in Europe around the tenth to twelfth centuries. Horses could then plough and haul faster than oxen.

Horse husbandry began on the Eurasian steppes. At Botai, Kazakhstan, people depended heavily on horses by about 3500 BCE, though whether those animals were domestic is disputed; genomes show they were not ancestors of today's horses. The modern domestic lineage emerged near the lower Don and Volga and spread across much of western Eurasia from about 2200 BCE.

A nailed horseshoe is an iron rim fixed to the hoof wall with nails, protecting hooves worn by hard roads, stony ground or wet conditions. Romans used strap-on hipposandals; nailed shoes were common in Europe by about the 10th century CE, though the date of the first ones is contested. Shod horses could keep working on paved and muddy surfaces.

Hot blast means preheating the air blown into a blast furnace. James Beaumont Neilson, manager of the Glasgow gas works, patented the idea in 1828. Heating the air to about 300 degrees Fahrenheit cut coal per ton of iron by over a third in one reported case, allowed raw coal instead of coke, and made Scotland's blackband ironstone worth smelting.

Household fields are plots worked by one family within marked boundaries and passed to its heirs, with neighbours recognizing the holding. At the Céide Fields in County Mayo, Ireland, Neolithic farmers of about 3700 to 3500 BCE built long stone walls dividing the land into regular fields, now preserved under blanket bog. Who owned them is debated.

Household registers list every household and its members so the state can levy taxes, labour and soldiers. In the Chinese state of Qin, households were registered and grouped in fives from about the 370s BCE, a system of mutual responsibility later tightened under Shang Yang. The Han census of 2 CE counted close to 58 million people.

Nineteenth-century housing laws in Britain gave local councils power to condemn unfit slums and set standards for new dwellings. The Artisans' and Labourers' Dwellings Improvement Act of 1875, passed under Disraeli, allowed slum clearance schemes, and the Housing of the Working Classes Act of 1890 extended councils' powers to clear and build. Other industrial countries followed.

Human rights law holds that certain rights belong to every person by virtue of being human, not by grant of a particular state. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris in 1948, set out civil, political, economic and social rights. Later treaties created committees and courts to monitor how states comply.

Renaissance humanism was a scholarly movement that recovered and studied classical Latin and Greek texts and taught grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry and moral philosophy. Petrarch, active in the mid-fourteenth century, is often called its founder. In fifteenth-century Florence, humanists such as Leonardo Bruni served as chancellors, and humanist education became a mark of lay elites.

Humanist colleges of the sixteenth century taught boys in graded classes, moving them year by year through Latin and Greek grammar, rhetoric, history and classical authors, often from printed textbooks. Johann Sturm's gymnasium at Strasbourg, founded in 1538, became a model for Protestant Europe, while the Jesuits opened their first college for lay pupils at Messina in 1548.

For a great communal hunt, bands chose a leader whose orders bound everyone, and anyone who startled the herd early could be punished; his authority ended once the meat was dried. Observers recorded such hunt police in Plains buffalo drives. Mass kill sites such as Solutré in France suggest coordinated drives are far older.

A hydroelectric station drops water from a dam or diverted river through turbines that drive generators. The Adams station at Niagara Falls, opened in 1895, was a landmark: from 1896 it sent three-phase alternating current to Buffalo. Large dams later gave cheap continuous power to energy-hungry industries such as aluminium smelting, whose electrolytic process dates from 1886.

An intercontinental ballistic missile is a rocket that carries a warhead thousands of kilometres, mostly above the atmosphere, before re-entering at very high speed. The Soviet R-7 made the first successful long-range flight in August 1957 and soon afterwards launched Sputnik. Usually armed with thermonuclear warheads, ICBMs became central to Cold War deterrence and to later arms-control treaties.

Immunology studies the body's defences against infection. In Berlin in 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō showed that immunised animals produced blood antitoxins against diphtheria or tetanus toxins, and that such serum could protect others, founding serum therapy. In 1901 Karl Landsteiner used the clumping of red cells by serum to define blood groups, later central to transfusion.

A ruler cult offers worship to a living or deified monarch. Greek cities granted divine honours to Alexander's successors from around 300 BCE, and in 29 BCE Octavian, soon to be called Augustus, allowed provincials in Asia and Bithynia to build temples to Rome and himself at Pergamum and Nicomedia. Local elites competed for the cult's priesthoods.

New imperialism names the late nineteenth-century scramble by European powers, later joined by the United States and Japan, for colonies in Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Advocates presented overseas empire as an economic and strategic necessity and as a civilizing mission. At the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, European states agreed rules for claiming African territory among themselves.

An income tax charges people on what they earn each year rather than on the land, goods or windows they own. Britain's first general income tax was introduced by William Pitt the Younger in 1799 to pay for war with Revolutionary France. Repealed in 1816, it was revived by Robert Peel in 1842 and has been levied ever since.

Indigenous land rights recognize indigenous peoples' title to land they held before colonization. In Australia, the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act of 1976 allowed claims to unalienated Crown land. In 1992 the High Court's Mabo decision rejected the doctrine that the continent had belonged to no one, recognizing native title, which the Native Title Act of 1993 then regulated.

Indirect rule was colonial government through existing local rulers, who kept their courts and customs under treaty while a European resident or adviser supervised them. After 1858 British India left more than five hundred princely states under their own rulers. In Northern Nigeria from about 1900, Frederick Lugard governed through the emirs and later promoted the method widely.

Industrial arbitration sends disputes between unions and employers to conciliation boards or arbitration courts instead of strikes and lockouts. New Zealand's Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act of 1894, introduced by William Pember Reeves, created one of the first compulsory systems. Britain's Conciliation Act of 1896 took a voluntary approach, letting the government offer mediation to willing parties.

Industrial exhibitions displayed machines, manufactures and farm products in great halls, with juries awarding medals. The Great Exhibition of 1851 in London, housed in Joseph Paxton's glass and iron Crystal Palace, drew about six million visitors. Its success inspired world's fairs in Paris, Philadelphia, Chicago and elsewhere, while national and regional shows spread news of improved ploughs and reapers.

Initiation rites mark the passage from childhood to adulthood. Young people are secluded with elders, taught the group's lore about tracking, plants, animals and law, and return as adults. Such rites are recorded among many Australian and African foraging peoples. Adolescent footprints in French caves such as Tuc d'Audoubert, about 15,000 years old, are sometimes read as traces of initiation.

Variolation protected against smallpox by deliberately infecting a healthy person with material from a smallpox sore or scab, usually producing a milder illness and lasting immunity. It was practised in China, where powdered scabs were blown into the nose, and in India, the Ottoman world and West Africa before reaching Britain in 1721. Recipients could still die or infect others.

Modern states have repeatedly rebuilt their own administrations. Britain's Northcote-Trevelyan report of 1854 called for entry to the civil service by competitive examination, and the United States followed with the Pendleton Act of 1883. Later commissions merged departments, abolished obsolete offices and audited spending, treating government itself as something that could be studied and improved.

An insula was a Roman apartment block, with shops at street level and rented flats above. Livy mentions a three-storey building in Rome around 218 BCE, and by the early empire such blocks housed much of the city's population. At Ostia, Rome's port, brick-faced concrete blocks of several storeys survive from the second century CE.

Underwriters agree, for a premium, to bear part of a possible loss, writing their names under the terms of a policy. Marine insurance began in medieval Italian ports, and by the late 1680s shipowners in London met underwriters at Edward Lloyd's coffee house. In 1693 Edmond Halley published a life table from Breslau records, a basis for pricing annuities.
