A personality cult glorifies a single leader as wise, infallible and the embodiment of the nation through portraits, songs, slogans and staged devotion. Stalin's cult took shape around his fiftieth birthday in 1929, and Khrushchev denounced it in 1956. In China the cult of Mao peaked during the Cultural Revolution from 1966, when millions carried the Little Red Book.

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that boil at different temperatures, so heating separates lighter and heavier fractions. In Lviv in the early 1850s the pharmacists Ignacy Łukasiewicz and Jan Zeh distilled lamp oil (kerosene); a kerosene lamp lit a hospital operation there in 1853. Łukasiewicz opened a refinery in 1856, three years before Edwin Drake's Pennsylvania well.

A pharmacopoeia is a systematic catalogue of medicinal substances: what each is, where it comes from, how it is prepared and what it treats. The Greek physician Dioscorides compiled De materia medica in the first century CE, describing about 600 plants, and it was copied for some fifteen centuries. China's Shennong herbal classic and Indian compendia built comparable traditions.

Philosophical schools were lasting communities of teachers and pupils who debated nature, ethics and how to live. In China, the disciples of Confucius, active around 500 BCE, preserved and developed his teachings. In Athens, Plato founded the Academy about 387 BCE, and it outlived him by centuries. Aristotle's Lyceum and the Stoic and Epicurean schools followed.

Photography fixes the image formed by a lens with light-sensitive silver compounds. Louis Daguerre's process, announced in Paris in 1839, gave a single sharp image on a silvered copper plate. William Henry Fox Talbot showed his own paper process the same year; his calotype, patented in 1841, produced a negative from which many positive prints could be made.

Physiology studies how the body's parts work, not only their form. William Harvey's De motu cordis (1628) used ligature experiments and estimates of how much blood the heart pumps to show that blood circulates continuously. Ibn al-Nafis had described the blood's passage through the lungs in the thirteenth century. Marcello Malpighi described the capillaries closing Harvey's circuit in 1661.

Pigs descend from wild boar and were domesticated independently in southwestern Asia and in China, roughly by 8,500 BCE and 6,000 BCE respectively. Genetic studies show that Europe's first domestic pigs came from the Near East, and suggest further local domestications in South and Southeast Asia. Pigs need no pasture: they eat scraps and forage, and breed quickly.

Greek sanctuaries such as Olympia and Delphi drew worshippers from many rival city-states. By tradition the Olympic Games began in 776 BCE, and a sacred truce, the ekecheiria, protected athletes and visitors travelling to and from the festival. From about the eighth century BCE, the oracle of Apollo at Delphi attracted pilgrims and envoys seeking guidance before wars and colonial ventures.

A plank-built boat assembles a hull from shaped boards, sewn with cord or fastened with pegs, instead of carving it from one log, so hull size is no longer limited by a single tree. Copper and bronze tools eased the joinery. Khufu's ship at Giza, about 2,500 BCE, and the sewn-plank Ferriby boats from England's Humber show separate traditions.

In a planned town, streets, drains and building plots are laid out before construction begins. Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley, about 2600 BCE, had streets on a roughly grid-like plan, standard-sized baked bricks and covered drains along many streets. Later examples include Egyptian workers' villages and the grid towns associated with Hippodamus of Miletus in Greece.

Synthetic polymers are long chain molecules built from small repeating units. Leo Baekeland's Bakelite, made from phenol and formaldehyde and introduced around 1907-1909, was the first fully synthetic plastic and set hard when heated. In the 1930s polyethylene was made at ICI in Britain and nylon at DuPont, first sold as toothbrush bristles (1938) and stockings (1939).

Plate armour covers the body with shaped, hardened iron or steel plates articulated at the joints. European armourers moved from mail reinforced with plates to complete plate harness during the fourteenth century; by the early fifteenth, full harness was usual for wealthy men-at-arms. Quenching and tempering made plates hard but not brittle. A harness typically weighed 15 to 25 kilograms.

A plebiscite asks voters to approve or reject a ruler, a regime or a constitution directly, usually with a single yes-or-no question. Napoleon Bonaparte used such votes to endorse his consulate, his consulship for life and his imperial title between 1799 and 1804, and his nephew Louis-Napoleon did the same after his 1851 coup. Official results showed huge majorities.

An ard is a simple plough: a pointed share dragged through the soil by animals, scratching a furrow without turning it over, so fields were often cross-ploughed. The oldest known plough marks in Europe, at Sion in Switzerland, date to the early fifth millennium BCE. By the fourth millennium BCE ploughing with draught animals is attested in Europe and Mesopotamia.

Political philosophy asks what makes rule just and how constitutions compare. In Greece, Plato's Republic, written about 380 BCE, imagined an ideal city ruled by philosophers, and Aristotle's Politics compared many constitutions. In China, Mencius, active in the fourth century BCE, argued that rulers must govern for the people's welfare and that tyrants forfeit their right to rule.

Polynesian voyaging canoes joined two hulls, or one hull and an outrigger, under woven sails, carrying people, plants and animals across thousands of kilometres of ocean. Navigators steered by stars, swells and birds without compass or writing. Hawaii was reached by around 1000-1200 CE and New Zealand by about 1300, late steps in a much older settlement of Oceania.

Under a poor law, parishes levy a local rate to relieve the destitute and set able-bodied paupers to work. The Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601 consolidated earlier statutes in England, making each parish responsible for its own poor through appointed overseers. It remained the basis of English relief until the New Poor Law of 1834 imposed a stricter workhouse system.

Popular sovereignty is the principle that supreme political authority belongs to the people or the nation, exercised through elected representatives. The American Declaration of Independence of 1776 grounded government in the consent of the governed, and France's Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, in 1789, stated that sovereignty resides essentially in the nation.

Mass populism is a style of politics in which a leader claims to speak for the common people against a corrupt elite. Getúlio Vargas, who took power in Brazil in 1930, and Juan Perón, elected president of Argentina in 1946, built followings among urban workers, expanded labour rights and tied the trade unions closely to the state.

Portland cement is made by burning limestone or chalk with clay into clinker and grinding it to a powder that hardens with water. Joseph Aspdin patented the name in 1824, after Portland stone, but his product was probably underburned. Firing at much higher temperatures, as Isaac Charles Johnson did around 1845-50, produced the stronger modern material.

A portolan chart draws coastlines from compass bearings and estimated sailing distances, criss-crossed by radiating lines that help a navigator lay a course. The oldest surviving example, the Carte Pisane, dates from the late 13th century and covers the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Its makers drew on sailors' observations, not on Ptolemy's coordinate grid.

A fast wheel spins with enough momentum to keep turning between pushes, so a potter can raise a vessel from a centred lump of clay. In Mesopotamia it was adopted in the fourth millennium BCE within the Uruk world and spread unevenly. The mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls of that era, however, were probably shaped in moulds, not thrown on a wheel.

Shaping clay into vessels and firing them in an open bonfire produces porous but heat-resistant containers for boiling and storage. Pottery arose separately in several regions: sherds from Xianrendong Cave, China, date to about 20,000 years ago, and Odai Yamamoto in Japan to about 16,500 years ago. African and Near Eastern pottery traditions began later and independently.

A power loom performs weaving's repeated motions by machine: raising warp threads, throwing the shuttle across, and beating in the weft. It mechanised John Kay's flying shuttle (1733). Edmund Cartwright patented early designs from 1785, but practical looms needed later improvements by others. By about 1820 steam looms were spreading in Britain; Waltham, Massachusetts, wove by water power from 1814.

Power-sharing divides offices, seats and vetoes among a country's main communities so that none can govern alone. Lebanon's unwritten National Pact of 1943 reserved the presidency for a Maronite Christian and the premiership for a Sunni Muslim. Northern Ireland's Good Friday Agreement of 1998 required a joint executive of unionist and nationalist parties. Political scientists call such arrangements consociational.

Industrialised panel building casts whole walls and floor slabs in factories, then assembles them on site with cranes. In France, Raymond Camus's large-panel system was in use by the early 1950s. The Soviet Union adopted similar methods from the late 1950s to build the five-storey blocks called khrushchyovki, rehousing millions of families within little more than a decade.

Precision agriculture treats a field as a patchwork rather than a uniform unit. In the early 1990s, yield monitors on combines logged grain flow against satellite positions, and the maps showed yields varying within fields. Variable-rate machines, adopted from the late 1990s, adjusted seed and fertiliser by location. Uptake was uneven: early returns were inconsistent and data standards lagged.

A prefect is a state official placed at the head of a territorial division to apply central policy there. Napoleon Bonaparte's law of February 1800, dated 28 Pluviose year VIII in the revolutionary calendar, gave each French department a prefect appointed from Paris and answerable to the interior ministry. Italy and other European states later copied the model.

A presidential republic has a chief executive elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term, who cannot normally be removed by a vote of no confidence. The United States Constitution of 1787 established the model, later adopted widely in Latin America and elsewhere. Fixed terms give predictability, though conflict between president and legislature can bring deadlock or constitutional crises.

Freedom of the press means abolishing censorship before publication, so printers answer only to courts for what they have already published. Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 abolished political censorship and opened government documents to the public. England had let press licensing lapse in 1695, and the United States protected the press in its First Amendment of 1791.

Soon after printing spread in Europe, rulers and churches required printers to obtain licences and submit books for approval before publication. A 1538 proclamation by Henry VIII required licensing of new books in England, and the Catholic Church issued its Index of Prohibited Books in 1559 under Pope Paul IV. Such controls aimed to suppress heresy and sedition.

Instead of striking, a knapper presses a pointed tool of bone, antler or wood against an edge to push off thin, controlled flakes. At Blombos Cave, South Africa, at least half the Still Bay points, made from about 76,000 years ago in heat-treated silcrete, were finished this way. Solutrean knappers in France and Spain later used pressure retouch too.

In many small-scale societies leaders hold influence through skill, generosity and persuasion rather than inherited office, and followers can simply move away if dissatisfied. Ethnographers have described such headmen and big men among foragers and horticulturalists, from the Kalahari to Melanesia. Archaeologists infer similar leadership among late Ice Age hunter-gatherers, though it leaves almost no material trace.

Farm price support keeps crop prices from falling below a floor, usually by the state buying surpluses or lending against stored crops. The United States began such programmes in 1933 with the Agricultural Adjustment Act and the Commodity Credit Corporation. The European Economic Community's Common Agricultural Policy, launched in 1962, used intervention buying that later produced notorious butter mountains.

Primary health care brings basic treatment, maternal care, vaccination and advice on clean water to every community through local health workers. In China from the late 1960s, briefly trained barefoot doctors served rural communes. In 1978 the Alma-Ata Declaration, adopted at a World Health Organization and UNICEF conference in Soviet Kazakhstan, made primary care the basis of health for all.

Primogeniture passes a kingdom, title or estate whole to the eldest son instead of dividing it among all heirs. The Capetian kings of France, from 987, kept their realm intact by having the eldest son crowned in his father's lifetime, and in Normandy and England knightly fiefs were increasingly held undivided by about 1100. Younger sons sought careers elsewhere.

In tenth-century China, the minister Feng Dao sponsored the first state printing of the Confucian classics by woodblock, a project begun in 932 and completed in 953. Authorized printed editions gave schools and examination candidates standard texts at modest cost. Under the Song dynasty, the state academy continued to print and sell classics and their commentaries.

Printed newspapers were regular sheets of news, usually weekly, compiled from letters and reports arriving with the posts. Johann Carolus's Relation, printed in Strasbourg from 1605, is often called the first newspaper. In Amsterdam, a weekly Courante appeared in 1618, and Dutch papers soon carried news and commercial reports across Europe.

Around 1450 in Mainz, the metalworker Johannes Gutenberg combined a hand mould for casting uniform metal type, a lead-based type alloy, oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from presses used for wine and paper. His Bible appeared by about 1455. By 1500 presses had operated in more than two hundred European towns, sharply lowering the cost of books.

Probability became mathematics in 1654, when Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters on dividing the stakes of an interrupted game. Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, proved that observed frequencies approach the underlying probability as trials multiply. Pierre-Simon Laplace's 1812 treatise built these ideas into general methods of calculation and inference.

Professional sport arose when paid players formed teams competing in organized leagues followed by mass audiences. In the United States, baseball's National League was founded in 1876. In England, where professional players had been allowed in 1885, twelve clubs formed the Football League in 1888. Railways, cheap newspapers and shorter working weeks helped crowds follow fixtures.

The first programmable digital computers performed long calculations automatically, following instructions set by punched tape, switches or plugboard wiring rather than held in memory. They arose largely independently: Konrad Zuse's relay-based Z3 ran in Berlin in 1941; valve-based Colossus machines attacked German teleprinter ciphers at Bletchley Park from 1944; and ENIAC, completed in Philadelphia in 1945-46, computed artillery tables.

High-level programming languages let people write instructions in notation close to mathematics or English, which a compiler translates into machine code. FORTRAN, developed by John Backus's team at IBM and released in 1957, showed that compiled programs could run efficiently enough for scientific work. COBOL, LISP and ALGOL soon followed, making software easier to write and share.

Progressivism was a reform movement in the United States from about the 1890s to the 1910s. Investigative journalists, nicknamed muckrakers, exposed corrupt city machines, unsafe factories and adulterated food, and reformers turned to experts and regulation for remedies. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle helped secure the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act in 1906.

Property classes rank citizens by assessed wealth rather than birth, so a family that prospers can rise into the classes eligible for office. At Athens, Solon's reforms of about 594 BCE divided citizens into four classes by the yield of their land. Roman tradition credits King Servius Tullius with a similar census of classes, though its early form is uncertain.

Proportional representation shares seats in an assembly among parties in proportion to their votes, so minorities and new movements win seats. Belgium became the first country to adopt a list system for national elections in 1899. After the First World War, many continental European states, including Germany, the Netherlands and Italy, adopted proportional systems around 1918 to 1920.

The earliest clay tablets from Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, dated to about 3300-3000 BCE, record rations, livestock, land and labour using numerical signs and pictographic signs for goods and officials. Most are administrative accounts rather than written speech. Scribes used several different counting systems depending on what was counted, and the script only partly recorded language.

Provincial administration divides a realm into provinces, each under a governor sent by the centre to levy taxes and raise troops in the ruler's name, watched by officials and reports answering to the capital. Akkad placed governors over conquered cities around 2300 BCE; Assyria reorganized its provinces under Tiglath-Pileser III after 745 BCE; Persia's satrapies followed from about 520 BCE.

Intendants were royal commissioners sent to the provinces of France to supervise justice, policing and finance on the king's behalf. Unlike officeholders who had bought their posts, they could be recalled at will. Occasional missions became a permanent network around 1635 under Cardinal Richelieu, and after a brief suppression during the Fronde the intendants were restored under Louis XIV.

Public broadcasting means radio and later television services run by a public body, funded by licence fees or taxes and expected to serve the whole nation rather than advertisers. The British Broadcasting Corporation received its royal charter in 1927, under John Reith, and many countries founded similar broadcasters in the following decades.

Public games were regular festivals of athletic and chariot contests held before crowds drawn from many communities. The best known took place at Olympia in Greece in honour of Zeus; tradition dates the first Olympic Games to 776 BCE, and they recurred every four years for over a thousand years. A sacred truce let athletes and spectators travel safely.

Public granaries store grain in good years and sell or issue it when harvests fail. In Rome, Gaius Gracchus's grain law of 123 BCE offered citizens grain at a fixed low price from public stores. In Han China, ever-normal granaries were set up around 54 BCE to buy grain when it was cheap and sell it when dear, steadying prices.

A board of health is a public authority empowered to protect a population's health through quarantine, inspection and sanitation. Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, ordered isolation of arrivals during plague in 1377, and Venice later kept a permanent health magistracy. England's General Board of Health, created in 1848, pressed for drains and clean water. They often acted before disease causes were understood.

Endowed hospitals with wards, physicians and pharmacies took in the sick without charge. In the Islamic world the bimaristan spread from Baghdad, where one is reported under Harun al-Rashid around 800 CE. In Constantinople, the Pantokrator monastery founded by Emperor John II Komnenos had a hospital whose charter of 1136 set out its wards, doctors and staff.

Public housing is homes built and owned by local or national government and let at controlled rents. In Britain, the Addison Act of 1919 gave councils subsidies to build homes for working families after the First World War. In 1923 Vienna's socialist city council began a large building programme, producing estates such as the Karl-Marx-Hof.

Public-key cryptography uses a pair of keys: one can be published so anyone can encrypt messages or check signatures, while only its owner holds the other. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the idea in 1976, and Rivest, Shamir and Adleman described the RSA system in 1977. British government cryptographers had found similar methods earlier, kept secret until 1997.

Public libraries are funded by local taxes and open free to every resident for reading and borrowing. In Britain, the Public Libraries Act of 1850 allowed town councils to levy a rate for free libraries, and Manchester opened one in 1852. In the United States, the Boston Public Library, which opened in 1854, was a pioneering large municipal library.

Public museums open collections to visitors for study and enjoyment, with objects catalogued and displayed in order. The Ashmolean in Oxford, opened in 1683 around a donated collection of curiosities, is often called Britain's first public museum. The British Museum, established by Act of Parliament in 1753 from Sir Hans Sloane's collection, opened free to visitors in 1759.

Opera began in late sixteenth-century Italian court circles as private entertainment for princes and their guests. In 1637 the Teatro San Cassiano in Venice opened as the first public opera house, admitting anyone who bought a ticket. Commercial opera spread through Venice and then Europe, and public concert series followed in London and other cities from the later seventeenth century.

Opinion polling measures public views by questioning a sample chosen to represent the whole population. In the 1936 United States presidential election, George Gallup's sample poll correctly predicted Franklin Roosevelt's victory, while the Literary Digest's huge mail survey wrongly forecast his defeat. Polling soon spread to other countries and to questions about leaders and policies.

Some Greek cities paid a public physician from city funds to practise among their citizens. Herodotus tells how Democedes of Croton, in the later sixth century BCE, was hired first by Aegina and then by Athens at a rising yearly salary, before serving the tyrant Polycrates of Samos. Inscriptions show such public doctors in many Hellenistic cities.

A public postal service carries anyone's letters for a fee, not only government mail. Britain's Penny Post, introduced in 1840 on Rowland Hill's proposals, charged a uniform prepaid rate of one penny for a light letter regardless of distance within the country, paid by an adhesive stamp, the Penny Black. Railways made fast national delivery possible.

Competitive procurement requires public authorities to advertise contracts, publish their rules and award work to the best compliant bid, limiting favouritism and graft. Sealed tenders for public works are much older, but international rules came late: the Tokyo Round of GATT produced a Government Procurement Code in 1979, and the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement followed in 1994.

Public theatre presents drama before a large audience in a purpose-built space. In Athens, Thespis, traditionally the first actor, is said to have won a tragic contest about 534 BCE; plays were later staged at festivals of Dionysus in a hillside theatre. In India, the Natyashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on drama, dates roughly from 200 BCE to 200 CE.

Public works relief puts unemployed people to work on government projects instead of simply paying them relief. During the Great Depression, the United States created the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Public Works Administration in 1933 and the Works Progress Administration in 1935, employing millions of people to build roads, bridges, dams, schools and parks.

Puddling turned brittle pig iron into tough wrought iron without charcoal. In a coal-fired reverberatory furnace, where flame rather than fuel touched the metal, workers stirred molten iron until air burned out its carbon; the iron was then shingled and passed through grooved rolls. Henry Cort patented the rolls in 1783 and puddling in 1784; Welsh ironmasters made them practical.

Herman Hollerith, who had worked on the 1880 United States census, patented a system in 1889 that recorded each person as holes punched in a card. Electrical contacts through the holes advanced counters on a tabulating machine. Used for the 1890 census, it reportedly saved years of work. Hollerith's company later became part of IBM.

A qanat taps groundwater at the foot of hills and leads it through a gently sloping tunnel to fields and settlements downslope, without pumping. Diggers sink a line of vertical shafts for access, spoil removal and ventilation. Developed in Iran, probably during the first millennium BCE, qanats spread to North Africa, Spain and western China, and some still flow today.

A quantum computer stores information in qubits, which can hold superpositions and become entangled, so some calculations proceed in ways ordinary computers cannot efficiently imitate. Richard Feynman argued in 1981-82 that they could simulate physics. In 2019 Google's 53-qubit Sycamore processor ran a narrow sampling task claimed to be beyond classical reach, a claim IBM disputed. Early machines remain noisy.

Quantum mechanics describes matter and light at the atomic scale, where energy comes in discrete amounts. Max Planck introduced energy quanta in 1900, and Niels Bohr quantised atomic orbits in 1913. In 1925 Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Pascual Jordan formulated matrix mechanics, and in 1926 Erwin Schrödinger published wave mechanics; the two proved mathematically equivalent.

Plunging red-hot carburized steel into water or another liquid traps carbon in a very hard but brittle crystal structure, now called martensite. A curved iron knife from an eleventh-century BCE tomb at Idalion, Cyprus, was analysed by the metallurgist Erik Tholander as quench-hardened steel, one of the earliest reported cases, though known here only from secondary accounts.

Quinine is the main active alkaloid of cinchona bark, a South American remedy used against fevers in Europe from the seventeenth century. In 1820 the French chemists Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou isolated it in Paris. On William Baikie's Niger expedition of 1854, regular preventive doses kept the European crew alive, showing that malaria could be held in check.

Radar detects distant objects by transmitting radio pulses and timing their echoes. It rests on the electromagnetic waves Heinrich Hertz demonstrated in the late 1880s. In the 1930s Britain, Germany, the United States and others developed it largely in parallel; Britain's Chain Home stations operated by the late 1930s. The cavity magnetron, from 1940, made compact microwave sets possible.

Radiation detectors make invisible ionising radiation measurable. Early workers counted alpha particles as flashes on zinc sulphide screens. Hans Geiger built an electrical counter in Rutherford's laboratory from 1908, developed with Walther Müller in 1928 into a tube sensitive to many kinds of radiation. Wilson's cloud chamber (1911) showed particle tracks; film badges and, from 1948, sodium-iodide scintillators extended measurement.

Radiation protection limits harm from ionising radiation by controlling time, distance, shielding and containment, and by measuring doses against agreed limits. Injuries to early X-ray workers and to radium dial painters who shaped brushes with their lips showed the danger. An international committee formed in Stockholm in 1928, later the ICRP; Chicago's wartime Metallurgical Laboratory named 'health physics' in 1942.

Heinrich Hertz demonstrated electromagnetic waves in 1886-1888. From 1895 Guglielmo Marconi built on Hertz's oscillator and Branly's coherer to send Morse code without wires, and in December 1901 he reported receiving a signal across the Atlantic in Newfoundland, a claim later questioned. Alexander Popov, Oliver Lodge and others did parallel work, and who invented radio remains disputed.

Voice radio needs continuous waves whose strength is varied, or modulated, by sound. Reginald Fessenden promoted amplitude modulation and reportedly broadcast speech and music from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, on Christmas Eve 1906. Pittsburgh's Westinghouse station KDKA made what is often called the first scheduled broadcast on 2 November 1920, though several stations claim to have been first.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atoms. In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged wrapped photographic plates without sunlight. Marie and Pierre Curie, measuring tiny electric currents, identified polonium and radium in pitchblende in 1898. Rutherford and Frederick Soddy explained the rays as atoms transforming into other elements; handlers soon found radiation burns skin.

Radioisotopes can be made by bombarding stable atoms with particles. Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot made the first artificial radioactive isotope in 1934, and Ernest Lawrence's cyclotrons soon produced hundreds more. Reactors made isotopes plentiful: Oak Ridge sent its first, carbon-14, to a St Louis cancer hospital in August 1946. Cobalt-60 now sterilises medical devices, and iridium-192 serves industrial radiography.

Radiometric prospecting seeks uranium and thorium by detecting the gamma radiation around rocks rich in them. In the American uranium boom after the 1948 government price guarantee, Geological Survey teams drove roads with Geiger counters; airborne surveys were established by 1958. Modern spectrometers map potassium, uranium and thorium separately. About one exploration project in a thousand finds an economic deposit.

Radiotherapy uses radiation to destroy tumours while sparing healthy tissue. Soon after radium was seen to burn skin around 1901, doctors applied it to skin lesions, then placed sealed sources in body cavities or implanted needles. Centres such as the Paris radium institute developed the practice. From 1951 cobalt-60 units in London, Ontario, and Saskatoon delivered penetrating external beams.

A sea-crossing raft binds logs, bamboo or reed bundles into a platform buoyant enough to carry people over open water. No Pleistocene craft survives; such vessels are inferred from where people arrived. Settling Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea, required sea crossings by at least 50,000 years ago; the craft's form is unknown.

A railway network joins locomotives, iron rails, surveyed gradients, stations and timetables into a public system. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, was the first intercity line worked by steam locomotives and carrying passengers and freight to a timetable. Expanding networks cut inland freight costs, linked national markets and spread standardised railway time.

In early Mesopotamian states, temples and palaces issued standard rations of barley, oil and wool to workers and dependants, including widows and orphans. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, common in the Uruk period of the late fourth millennium BCE, are often read as ration measures. The Third Dynasty of Ur, about 2100 to 2000 BCE, left thousands of tablets listing rations.

Reason of state is the doctrine that a ruler's first duty is the survival and power of the state itself, placed above religious loyalties and dynastic claims. Giovanni Botero gave it a name in his treatise of 1589. Cardinal Richelieu applied it in the 1630s, when Catholic France backed Protestant powers against the Habsburgs during the Thirty Years' War.

In a referendum, voters decide a law or constitutional change directly at the ballot box rather than leaving it to representatives. Switzerland's revised federal constitution of 1874 introduced the optional referendum, letting a set number of citizens demand a popular vote on laws passed by parliament. The popular initiative followed in 1891, and both remain central to Swiss politics.

Mechanical refrigeration uses work to pump heat out of an insulated space, typically by compressing and evaporating a working fluid. In 1876 Carl von Linde, prompted by brewers, built a reliable ammonia compression machine; one served the Dreher brewery in Trieste for decades. In the same years refrigerated ships such as Ferdinand Carré's Paraguay began carrying frozen meat across oceans.

Refugee law gives people fleeing persecution travel papers and protection from being sent back to danger. After the Russian Revolution, the League of Nations high commissioner Fridtjof Nansen introduced identity certificates in 1922, later called Nansen passports, for stateless refugees. The UN Refugee Convention of 1951 defined a refugee and established the principle of non-refoulement.

Insignia of rank are objects that display authority to people who may never have met its holder. A burial at Varna in Bulgaria, about 4500 BCE, held a gold-sheathed sceptre or axe handle among many gold ornaments. The Nahal Mishmar hoard, hidden in a Judean Desert cave around 3500 BCE, contains hundreds of copper objects, many of them maceheads.

Regional self-government gives elected assemblies and governments control of services such as schools, health and roads within a region. Italy's constitution of 1947 provided for regions, although most ordinary regions gained elected councils only in 1970. Spain's 1978 constitution created autonomous communities, and in 1999 the United Kingdom opened a Scottish Parliament and a Welsh Assembly.

Reinforced concrete embeds iron or steel bars in concrete: the concrete resists crushing, the metal carries tension, and both expand similarly with heat. Joseph Monier, a Paris gardener, patented reinforced planters in 1867 and later wider uses; Joseph-Louis Lambot and William Wilkinson had experimented earlier. François Hennebique's 1892 system joined beams and columns into monolithic frames for buildings and bridges.

A relational database stores information as tables of rows and columns and retrieves it by stating what is wanted rather than how to find it. Edgar F. Codd of IBM set out the relational model in a 1970 paper. Research systems in the 1970s and commercial products around 1980 followed, and the SQL query language became the common standard.

Albert Einstein's special relativity (1905) held that light's speed is the same for all observers, so measured time and length depend on motion, and implied that mass and energy are equivalent. His general relativity (1915) described gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Satellite navigation clocks must be corrected for both effects, by about 38 microseconds a day.

In the twentieth century, mass movements sought to shape state and society by religious values, combining preaching, welfare work and politics. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh was founded in India in 1925 and the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt in 1928. After the Second World War, Christian Democratic parties became leading forces in Italy and West Germany.

Religious reform movements challenge an established clergy in the name of scripture or purer practice. In 1517 Martin Luther circulated his Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg against the sale of indulgences. Printing spread his writings rapidly, lay readers studied the Bible in their own languages, and new Protestant churches formed in Germany, Switzerland, Scandinavia and beyond.

Religious toleration lets communities of more than one faith worship openly and keep their own institutions without civil penalty for belonging to a minority. Ashoka's edicts in third-century BCE India urged respect between sects; the Edict of Milan in 313 CE allowed Christians to worship in the Roman empire; and France's Edict of Nantes, in 1598, granted Protestants limited rights.

A representative assembly summons spokesmen of the realm's estates or communities, typically nobles, clergy and towns, to consent to taxes and new laws and to petition for redress of grievances. At León in 1188, elected town representatives joined the royal council of Alfonso IX, and in 1265 Simon de Montfort's English parliament summoned borough burgesses alongside knights of the shires.

Reprocessing dissolves spent reactor fuel in nitric acid and separates uranium and plutonium from fission products by solvent extraction, the PUREX method. Wartime separation chemistry worked out at Oak Ridge's X-10 was used at Hanford to extract weapons plutonium. Civil plants such as France's La Hague, operating since 1976, recycle plutonium into mixed-oxide fuel. The United States runs none.

The research university combines teaching with original research, paying professors to advance knowledge and train new scholars. The University of Berlin, founded in 1810 under the influence of Wilhelm von Humboldt, became the model, joining lectures with seminars and laboratories. American universities such as Johns Hopkins, founded in 1876, adopted the model and its doctoral training.

Reserved seats set aside a share of places in legislatures or councils for groups that have been excluded, so that their members gain office and influence. India's constitution of 1950 reserved seats in parliament and state assemblies for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Amendments in force from 1993 reserved one third of village council seats and headships for women.

Dams of earth and stone built across valleys stored seasonal runoff for the dry months. At Jawa in the Jordanian desert, dams and reservoirs date to around 3000 BCE or earlier. In Egypt, the Sadd el-Kafara dam was built about 2600 BCE and apparently failed before completion. At Dholavira in the Indus civilisation, large stone-cut reservoirs stored water.

A resident embassy is a permanent mission at a foreign ruler's court whose ambassador reports home continuously. Venice, Milan and Mantua exchanged resident envoys from around 1400; such missions became normal in Italy late in the fifteenth century and spread northward after 1500. Earlier diplomacy relied mainly on temporary envoys. Standing missions gave steady information but invited suspicion of spying.

Responsible government meant that a colony's cabinet answered to its elected assembly rather than to an appointed governor, while the empire kept control of foreign affairs. Nova Scotia became the first British colony to gain it, in early 1848, followed by the Province of Canada later that year. In 1867 Confederation united several provinces into the self-governing Dominion of Canada.

Reusable launch vehicles recover expensive hardware instead of discarding it. The US Space Shuttle (1981 to 2011) reused its orbiter and solid boosters but needed costly refurbishment between missions. In December 2015 SpaceX landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 orbital rocket upright after launch, using engine relights, grid fins and satellite navigation; reflights followed in 2017.

Revival movements call believers to personal conversion and active good works. In late seventeenth-century Germany, Pietism promoted small devotional circles, and at Halle August Hermann Francke founded an orphanage and schools from the 1690s. In the British American colonies, the Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s brought mass open-air preaching, and evangelicals later founded charity schools and Bible societies.

A revolutionary republic is founded by overthrowing a monarchy in the name of the people, and often governs through emergency bodies while it fights for survival. The French First Republic, proclaimed in September 1792, raised mass citizen armies and ruled through the Committee of Public Safety during the Terror of 1793-1794. Later revolutions frequently borrowed its symbols and institutions.

Rhetoric schools trained young men to speak persuasively in courts and assemblies, the main route to public life in Athens and Rome. Isocrates opened a paid school at Athens around 390 BCE. At Rome, Latin rhetoric teachers were active by 92 BCE, when the censors issued an edict against them. Under the empire, rhetoric became the core of higher education.

Early-ripening rice can be harvested after a shorter season, sometimes allowing two crops a year, and tolerates drought. After a drought on the lower Yangtze and Huai rivers in 1012, the Song emperor Zhenzong had seed of such rice, called Champa rice after its Southeast Asian source, sent from Fujian and distributed to farmers in the affected region.

At Kuahuqiao on the lower Yangtze, about 7,700 years ago, villagers burned scrub on a coastal swamp, kept fields wet and probably controlled flooding with low banks, an early form of paddy farming. The site was later drowned by the sea. Fully domesticated, non-shattering rice emerged in the region over the following thousand years or so.

Rifled breech-loading guns fired elongated shells that spun in flight, reaching farther and more accurately than round shot. William Armstrong's built-up gun, with coils shrunk over a rifled inner tube, entered British service in 1859, though Britain reverted to muzzle-loaders in the mid-1860s. Prussia adopted its first Krupp breech-loader, forged from solid steel, in 1856; Krupp persevered with the principle.

Rifling cuts spiral grooves inside a gun barrel so the projectile spins, flying straighter and farther. Rifled barrels were known in Europe by the fifteenth century, though who first made them is unclear. Because a tight ball had to be forced into the grooves, rifles loaded slowly; broad military use followed the Minié bullet, adopted about 1852.

A river basin authority manages a whole watershed as one system, combining dams, navigation locks, flood control, power generation and land improvement. The Tennessee Valley Authority, created by the United States Congress in 1933, became the best-known model and was later copied in India's Damodar Valley Corporation and elsewhere around the world.

River commissions let the states along a major river agree on common navigation rules, tolls and engineering works. The Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine was established after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and is often called the oldest international organisation still working. The European Commission of the Danube, created in 1856, improved the river's mouth for shipping.

Royal road-houses were staffed stations about a day's travel apart on main roads, supplying water, food and rest to official travellers. Shulgi, king of the Third Dynasty of Ur around 2090 BCE, claimed in a hymn to have built houses with gardens along the highways. Administrative tablets from Ur III way-stations record rations issued to messengers and other travellers.

An engineered paved road is surveyed, drained and built in layers of stone, gravel and lime-bound fill to carry traffic in all weather. Rome's Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, became a model for roads linking provinces to the capital. The Inca separately built a network of stone-paved and stepped mountain roads, extended greatly in the 15th century CE.

Road traffic law governs who may drive, how vehicles are registered and how they must behave on the road. As motor traffic grew, countries introduced licences, speed limits and standard signs. The International Convention relative to Motor Traffic, signed in Paris in 1926, set common rules for cross-border driving, and the Vienna Convention on Road Traffic of 1968 updated them.

A liquid-fuel rocket feeds fuel and an oxidiser into a combustion chamber, producing thrust without drawing on outside air. Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket on 16 March 1926. Germany's A-4, later called the V-2, first flew successfully in 1942 and was used as a ballistic missile against cities from 1944.

Some farming began with plants grown from cuttings and tubers. At Kuk Swamp in the New Guinea highlands, taro was used in the early Holocene and bananas were cultivated by about 6,900 years ago, an independent origin of agriculture. In the Andes, potatoes were domesticated near Lake Titicaca; the oldest archaeological tubers are about 7,000 years old.

A rotary quern grinds grain between two round stones, the upper one turned by a handle, replacing the back-and-forth rubbing of earlier querns. The oldest known examples come from northeastern Iberia in the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. They spread through southern France and, adopted by local peoples, into central Europe and Britain; Roman expansion later carried them further.

Royal archives kept a palace's letters, treaties, inventories and accounts so they could be consulted later. At Ebla in northern Syria, excavators in the 1970s found thousands of clay tablets from about 2400 BCE in palace archive rooms. Some had evidently been stored on shelves, and many were administrative records of textiles, metals and food, written in cuneiform.

Envoys carried sealed letters and gifts between rulers, travelling under protection and received by agreed protocol. Archives at Ebla, of about the 24th century BCE, include diplomatic correspondence, and the Amarna letters, cuneiform tablets of the reigns of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten found in Egypt, record gifts and marriage talks between the pharaoh and kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria.

Royal expeditions were state ventures sent to distant lands for luxury goods, with results recorded in official texts. Egyptian kings sent ships down the Red Sea to Punt for incense, ebony and gold; one is recorded under Sahure of the Fifth Dynasty, about 2450 BCE. Queen Hatshepsut's expedition around 1470 BCE is shown in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari.

Royal judges are officials appointed to hear disputes, take sworn testimony and pronounce verdicts in the king's name. Under the Third Dynasty of Ur, about 2100 to 2000 BCE, scribes recorded completed lawsuits on tablets called ditilla, a term meaning a finished case. The Code of Hammurabi, about 1754 BCE, punished a judge who altered a sealed judgment.

A royal post is a relay system of riders, stations and fresh horses carrying a ruler's orders and officials' reports across a large state. Assyria operated relay stations along royal roads by the eighth century BCE. The Persian Achaemenid empire developed the most famous version, praised by Herodotus, along the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa.

Rural electrification extended power lines to farms and villages that private utilities found unprofitable to serve. Soviet Russia's GOELRO plan of 1920 set out a national electrification programme. In the United States, the Rural Electrification Administration, created in 1935, lent money to farmers' cooperatives, which built lines across the countryside, and the share of farms with electricity rose sharply.

Sacred kingship treats the ruler as divine or divinely chosen, and makes the king the chief mediator between gods and people through ritual, so obedience becomes a religious duty. From the First Dynasty onward, Egyptian kings ruled under a 'Horus name' that identified them with the god Horus; comparable ideas arose independently elsewhere, for example among the Inca.

Early saddles were cushions of leather and felt stitched together, like those preserved in frozen Pazyryk burials in the Altai Mountains, of about the fifth to third centuries BCE. They spread the rider's weight and eased long journeys. Later saddles were built on a rigid frame, the tree, which kept pressure off the horse's spine and could carry stirrups.

A safe-conduct is a ruler's guarantee of protection for named foreigners, their goods and servants while they travel in his lands. In early Islamic law, the aman offered such protection to non-Muslim envoys and merchants. In medieval Europe, rulers issued written letters of safe-conduct, and an English act of 1414 made breaking such a truce or safe-conduct a grave crime.

A square sail hung from a mast lets wind drive a boat downwind and along coasts. The oldest evidence is a painted disc from As-Sabiyah (site H3) in Kuwait, about 5,500-5,300 BCE, read as a two-masted boat and found with remains of seagoing reed-bundle craft. Nile images of square-sailed boats follow by about 3,500 BCE.

Salt preserves meat and fish and is a dietary necessity, yet occurs only in particular places. At Poiana Slatinei in Romania, early farmers exploited a brine spring around 6050 to 5500 BCE, the oldest known saltworks in Europe. From the mid-fifth millennium BCE, clay containers called briquetage were used to dry brine into salt cakes in central and eastern Europe.

Saltpetre rarely occurs pure: it forms as crusts and in nitre-rich soils mixed with other salts. Refiners leached such earth with water, often adding lime and wood ash, then boiled the liquor and crystallised potassium nitrate, repeating to purify it. Where and when systematic refining began is uncertain; detailed European recipes survive in fifteenth-century gunners' manuals.

A sample survey estimates totals for a whole population by measuring a randomly chosen part of it. Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis used large random samples to estimate Bengal's jute harvest from the late 1930s, and the United States began a monthly sample survey of employment in 1940, the ancestor of today's Current Population Survey.

Sanitary engineering moved water and waste through piped networks. By 1829 James Simpson's slow-sand filter was cleaning Thames water for London's Chelsea Waterworks. After Hamburg's 1842 fire, William Lindley planned sewers for the rebuilt city. London's main drainage, designed by Joseph Bazalgette and built from 1859, used brick sewers and steam pumps, while many blamed disease on foul air.

An artificial satellite is an object placed in orbit, moving sideways fast enough to keep falling around the Earth. The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957; its radio signal was tracked worldwide. Explorer 1, launched by the United States in 1958, carried transistorised instruments whose readings helped reveal the Van Allen radiation belts.

School meals give pupils a free or cheap midday meal, partly to improve health and attendance. In Britain, the Education (Provision of Meals) Act of 1906 allowed local authorities to feed needy children, after many recruits for the Boer War had been found poorly nourished. The United States passed its National School Lunch Act in 1946.

Science policy is the state's planning and funding of research according to national priorities. In 1945 Vannevar Bush's report Science, the Endless Frontier argued that the United States government should support basic research in peacetime. The National Science Foundation, created in 1950, followed, distributing grants through peer review. Many countries set up research councils.

Scientific plant breeding applied Mendel's laws to crops. In 1905 Cambridge's Rowland Biffen showed that wheat's yellow-rust resistance was inherited in Mendelian fashion. In 1908 George Shull, and independently Edward East, described hybrid vigour in crosses of inbred maize. Hybrid seed, sold from 1926 and rebought yearly, covered 6 percent of Iowa's corn in 1935 and nearly all by 1942.

Scientific societies were associations where members met to report observations, test claims by experiment and publish findings. The Accademia dei Lincei, founded in Rome in 1603, later counted Galileo as a member. The Royal Society of London was founded in 1660 and began publishing the Philosophical Transactions in 1665, one of the earliest scientific journals.

The screw propeller turns twisted blades beneath the stern, pushing water backward more efficiently, and with less exposure to damage, than paddle wheels. In 1836 Francis Pettit Smith and John Ericsson each patented screw propellers in Britain. Trials such as HMS Rattler against a paddle sloop in 1845 helped persuade navies, and screws soon drove oceangoing steamships.

Scribal schools trained students to write cuneiform, keep accounts and copy standard texts. School exercise tablets survive from Shuruppak in Sumer from about 2500 BCE. Sumerian texts copied in the early second millennium BCE describe the edubba, or tablet house, where pupils copied word lists, proverbs and literature under a master. Graduates staffed temples, palaces and merchant houses.

Script and language reforms replace or simplify a national writing system to make reading easier to learn. In 1928, Turkey replaced the Arabic-based Ottoman script with a Latin alphabet under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. The People's Republic of China introduced simplified Chinese characters from 1956. Both reforms aimed to speed mass literacy through state schools.

A scriptural canon is a fixed collection of sacred texts that defines belief and practice and is studied by trained specialists. The hymns of the Rigveda were composed in northern South Asia, probably by about 1200 BCE, and preserved orally with remarkable precision. The Torah reached its final form later, with editing often placed in the sixth or fifth century BCE.

Many foraging peoples spent most of the year in small bands but gathered at a rich place in one season to feast, trade, arrange marriages and settle quarrels before dispersing. Ethnographers recorded such gatherings on several continents. Archaeologist Margaret Conkey argued that Altamira and other Magdalenian sites in Cantabria served as aggregation places roughly 17,000 years ago.

A seasonal round is a yearly cycle of movement in which a foraging band returns to familiar camps when each resource is at its best: fish runs, nut harvests, migrating herds or ripening grasses. At Ohalo II, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, brush huts about 23,000 years old show repeated occupation of the same place.

The secret ballot lets voters mark official printed ballots in private, so landlords, employers and party agents cannot see or buy their votes. The colony of Victoria in Australia adopted it in 1856, and it spread abroad as the Australian ballot. Britain enacted it in the Ballot Act of 1872, and most American states adopted it around 1890.

A secular state recognises no official church and treats all faiths equally in law. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1791, barred Congress from establishing a religion, although some states kept official churches for decades. In France, the 1905 law separating churches and state ended public payment of clergy. Many later constitutions adopted similar principles.

Every farming people must hold back part of the harvest as seed, even when hungry, and peasant custom in many regions treated seed corn as untouchable. Keeping and replanting seed is what allowed cereals to be domesticated. Purpose-built grain stores at Levantine sites such as Dhra' and Jerf el-Ahmar, in the tenth millennium BCE, show deliberate storage.

A seed drill drops seed through tubes into furrows at even depth and spacing, saving seed and leaving rows that can be weeded. In Han China, Zhao Guo, an agricultural official under Emperor Wu (reigned 141 to 87 BCE), is credited with promoting an animal-drawn drill that sowed three rows at once. Europe's first known seed-drill patent dates from 1566.

In 1701 the English farmer Jethro Tull built a horse-drawn seed drill that sowed seed in neat rows at an even depth instead of scattering it by hand. He later developed a horse-drawn hoe to cultivate between the rows. Seed drills had long been used in China, and Europe had seen an earlier patent in 1566.

In a segmentary lineage society, descent groups nest inside larger ones: close segments may feud, but unite against more distant ones and against outsiders. There is no permanent chief, and elders or mediators settle disputes. Classic descriptions include Evans-Pritchard's study of the Nuer of South Sudan, published in 1940, and the Bohannans' work on the Tiv of Nigeria.

From the mid-eighteenth century Robert Bakewell of Dishley in Leicestershire bred livestock systematically, choosing parents for desired traits and mating close relatives to fix them. His New Leicester sheep and improved Longhorn cattle fattened quickly and became famous. Inbreeding also had costs, including lower fertility, and historians debate how original his methods were.

A semi-presidential republic divides executive power between a directly elected president and a prime minister answerable to parliament. Germany's Weimar constitution of 1919 created an early version, with a popularly elected president holding emergency powers. The French Fifth Republic, founded in 1958 under Charles de Gaulle, became the model, adding direct presidential election in 1962.

Semiconductor physics explains why materials like silicon and germanium conduct electricity better than insulators but worse than metals. In 1931 Alan Wilson used quantum mechanics to describe their energy bands; Walter Schottky and Nevill Mott explained rectifying metal contacts in 1938-39, clarifying radio crystal detectors. In 1940 Russell Ohl at Bell Labs found a silicon junction generating voltage under light.

Separation of powers assigns lawmaking, execution and judging to distinct bodies so that none holds all authority. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748), drawing on an idealised reading of England, gave the idea its classic statement, and the United States Constitution of 1787 built it into checks and balances. Critics note that strict separation can produce deadlock between branches.

Under service tenure a ruler grants land, or the income from land, to people who owe military or other service in return, so an army can be supported without a cash payroll. Hammurabi's laws, of about 1750 BCE, regulate such holdings, known as ilku. Comparable arrangements include medieval European fiefs, the iqta of the caliphates and the Ottoman timar.

Settler land grants transferred surveyed public land to families who would farm it. The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres to settlers who lived on and cultivated the land for five years, paying only small fees. Millions of acres passed to homesteaders, though railways and speculators gained much land, often taken from Native American nations.

An eyed needle draws thread through holes in hide or cloth, joining pieces into close-fitting garments and bags; earlier awls only punched lacing holes. A bone needle from Denisova Cave, Siberia, is often dated to roughly 50,000 years ago, and eyed needles were widespread in Eurasia by roughly 25,000 years ago. Tailored clothing eased life in the cold.

Many foraging peoples recognise a few individuals as mediators with the spirit world who heal, divine and lead rites, though such specialists are hard to see archaeologically. Figurines from Hohle Fels in Germany, at least 35,000 years old, hint at ritual life, and a woman buried at Hilazon Tachtit in Israel about 12,000 years ago is often interpreted as a shaman.

Sharecropping is a contract in which a landowner supplies land and often seed or oxen, while a tenant family supplies labour, and the harvest is divided in agreed shares. Islamic jurists from around the eighth and ninth centuries discussed such contracts, called muzara'a and musaqat. In medieval Tuscany, the similar mezzadria system spread widely from about the thirteenth century.

Wild sheep and goats of the Zagros and Taurus uplands were the first livestock of Southwest Asia, managed from probably between 10,000 and 8,000 BCE. At Ganj Dareh in Iran, goat bones show herders slaughtering young males while keeping females to breed, a hallmark of herding rather than hunting. Goats were also managed early at Nevalı Çori.

Bronze can be hammered into thin sheet and shaped into vessels and armour by raising, working the metal from outside over a small domed anvil, with repeated annealing to relieve work-hardening. In central Europe sheet-bronze vessels and armour appear with the Urnfield period; a hoard of bronzeworking tools from Hradok, Slovakia, dates to about 1225-1175 BCE.

A framed hut uses posts, poles or large bones as a skeleton, covered with hides, brush or turf, giving shelter that can be reoccupied across seasons. Hut traces at Dolní Věstonice in Moravia date to about 26,000 years ago; on the Ukrainian plain, the Mezhyrich dwellings of interlocked mammoth bones are later, about 18,000 years old.

A ship of the line was a large sailing warship with two or three gun decks, strong enough to take a place in the line of battle, in which fleets sailed in single file to fire broadsides. English and Dutch navies formalised the line in the 1650s and 1660s. Such ships carried from about sixty to over a hundred guns.

A sickle is a haft set with sharp blades for cutting stalks. Glossy flint blades at Ohalo II in Israel, about 23,000 years old, are the earliest known cereal-harvesting inserts. Among the Levant's Natufians, about 15,500 to 11,600 years ago, flint-bladed sickles hafted in wood, bone or antler became common, their edges polished by plant stems.

Siege and road engineers are specialist troops who build ramps, bridges, tunnels and tracks for an army. Palace reliefs of the Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II, from the ninth century BCE, show sappers undermining walls, siege engines pushed up to the defences and soldiers crossing rivers on inflated skins. These skills served road-building in peace.

Neo-Assyrian armies of the ninth to seventh centuries BCE attacked city walls with battering rams housed in wheeled, roofed frames, some built as towers with archers on top, pushed up earth ramps to the wall. Palace reliefs of Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in Judah, 701 BCE, depict the method, and archaeologists have excavated the Assyrian siege ramp there.

Signal beacons are chains of fires or smoke on hilltops and towers, passing a prearranged message from post to post faster than any runner. Letters from Mari on the Euphrates, written to King Zimri-Lim in the eighteenth century BCE, mention fire signals. In China, tradition places frontier beacon towers by about 800 BCE, and later ones lined the Great Wall.

Sericulture raises domesticated silkworms on mulberry leaves and unwinds the continuous filament of their cocoons, softened in hot water, into thread. In China, silk fabric survives from at least the third millennium BCE, with earlier traces debated. Under the Han dynasty silk was made on a large scale and carried west along Asian trade routes; the craft itself spread slowly.

A steel-frame skyscraper carries floors and outer walls on a metal skeleton of columns and beams instead of thick masonry, so height no longer requires ever-thicker base walls. Chicago's Home Insurance Building, designed by William Le Baron Jenney and completed in 1885, is often called the first, though this is debated. Cheap steel, fireproofing and passenger elevators made such towers usable.

A sledge drags a load on smooth runners instead of rolling it, spreading weight across snow, mud, marsh or grass where a wheel would sink. Wooden runners preserved in waterlogged Mesolithic sites in Finland and in Russia's Vychegda basin date to the 7th and 6th millennia BCE. Long after wheels appeared, sledges remained practical on snow and soft ground.

A slide-rest lathe holds the cutting tool in a carriage moved by screws instead of by hand, so cuts are straight and repeatable. Henry Maudslay's London lathes of about 1800 combined a rigid metal frame, slide rest and lead screw with change gears to cut accurate threads. Thread standards followed, notably Joseph Whitworth's of 1841 and William Sellers's of 1864.

A sling is a pouch on two cords: whirled and released, it hurls a stone or a clay or lead bullet with great force. Made of fibre or leather, slings seldom survive; early use is inferred from shaped projectiles. Herders used slings to guard flocks, and Assyrian reliefs of the siege of Lachish, 701 BCE, show slingers beside archers.

A smart grid adds digital metering, communication and automatic control to the electricity network. Operators can then see conditions almost as they happen, and customers' demand can respond to prices or shortages. Networked meters and sensors spread in many countries during the 2000s, helping to balance variable wind and solar output and many small producers.

A smartphone joins a mobile telephone, a general-purpose pocket computer and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, using cellular data to reach the internet wherever coverage exists. Handheld devices combining phones and personal organisers appeared in the 1990s, such as IBM's Simon (1994). Touchscreen models from 2007 onward, including Apple's iPhone and Android phones, spread the form worldwide within about a decade.

Social Christianity was the churches' response to industrial poverty. In London from 1848, Christian socialists such as F. D. Maurice and Charles Kingsley backed workers' cooperatives. American Protestants of the Social Gospel movement, from the 1880s, campaigned for labour reform and relief in the cities. Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum Novarum, in 1891, defended just wages and workers' associations.

Social contract theory holds that political authority is not natural or divinely given but rests on an agreement among people, or on their consent. Thomas Hobbes argued in Leviathan, published in 1651, that people surrender liberty to a sovereign for security. John Locke's Two Treatises of Government, about 1689, made consent the condition of legitimate rule and justified resisting tyranny.

Social democracy seeks socialist goals through elections and parliament rather than revolution, pressing for social insurance, labour law and public services. German socialists united on the Gotha Programme of 1875 and adopted the Erfurt Programme in 1891. Eduard Bernstein's revisionism, set out around 1899, argued that capitalism could be reformed step by step rather than overthrown.

Social insurance requires workers and employers to pay into public funds that cover sickness, accident and old age. Germany under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck pioneered it with sickness insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and invalidity pensions in 1889. Other countries, including Britain with its National Insurance Act of 1911, soon followed.

Social media platforms let anyone publish text, photos and video to followers and join large online networks. Earlier sites such as Friendster and MySpace prepared the way. Facebook was launched in 2004 and Twitter in 2006, and both grew to hundreds of millions of users. Such platforms reshaped news, advertising and political campaigning worldwide.

Social surveys turned distress into evidence. Charles Booth mapped poverty street by street in London from 1886, and Seebohm Rowntree measured it in York in 1899. Their findings shaped old-age pensions and national insurance in Britain, while later programmes were piloted, evaluated and revised, so that relief came to rest on measured results rather than charity alone.

Socialism arose in early industrial Europe as a demand that productive property be held in common and that class exploitation end. Robert Owen founded cooperative communities such as New Harmony in Indiana in the 1820s. In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Communist Manifesto, calling on workers of all countries to unite and overthrow capitalist rule.

Soda (sodium carbonate), needed for glass, soap and textiles, long came from plant ashes. Nicolas Leblanc patented a French process in 1791 that made it from common salt: treating salt with sulphuric acid, then roasting the product with limestone and coal. It bound soda making to the acid industry; its acid fumes later prompted Britain's Alkali Act of 1863.

Sodalities are societies that recruit members across lineages and villages, such as warrior, dance or ritual societies. Members keep a lodge, hold rites and may police camps, and a member is welcomed by his society wherever it meets. Ethnographers recorded kiva societies among Pueblo peoples and soldier societies on the Plains. Some archaeologists read Göbekli Tepe as their meeting place.

Soil conservation protects farmland from erosion by wind and water through contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops and shelter belts of trees. After the Dust Bowl storms on the American Great Plains in the 1930s, the United States created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935, led by Hugh Hammond Bennett, which sent advisers to work with farmers.

A photovoltaic cell turns sunlight directly into electric current at a junction between two kinds of semiconductor. Russell Ohl observed the effect in a silicon p-n junction in 1940. In 1954 Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson at Bell Laboratories made a practical silicon cell of about six per cent efficiency; satellites were early users from 1958.

South of the Sahara, farmers domesticated cereals suited to heat and erratic rain. Chaff of wild and domesticated sorghum in pottery from eastern Sudan dates to the fourth millennium BCE, and domesticated pearl millet appears in southeastern Mali in the third millennium BCE. Both crops later crossed to India; pearl millet arrived within about a thousand years.

Selection by lot fills offices by drawing names among eligible citizens, so no faction can buy or monopolize them and any qualified citizen may serve. In democratic Athens the archons were chosen by lot from 487 BCE, and most magistrates and the large citizen juries were also allotted, by the fourth century with stone allotment machines.

An interplanetary probe is an uncrewed spacecraft sent beyond Earth's orbit to study other worlds at close range. The American Mariner 2 flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, the first spacecraft to encounter another planet successfully. Passing about 35,000 kilometres away, it found a dense atmosphere and surface temperatures of at least 425 C.

Space-based solar power is a proposed system in which large satellites collect sunlight in high orbit, above clouds and in near-continuous daylight, and beam the energy to ground receivers as microwaves or laser light. Peter Glaser described such a design in 1968. Small power-beaming tests have flown, but launch and assembly costs have so far prevented any working power station.

A space station is an orbiting habitat where crews live for weeks or months, working in near-weightlessness. The Soviet Union launched Salyut 1 in 1971, and the American Skylab followed in 1973. Mir was assembled in orbit from 1986. The International Space Station, built by several partner agencies, began assembly in 1998 and has hosted crews continuously since November 2000.

A telescope above the atmosphere escapes its blurring and can observe ultraviolet and infrared light that barely reaches the ground. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, returned blurred images because its main mirror suffered spherical aberration. In December 1993 astronauts on five spacewalks installed corrective optics and a new camera; later instruments carried their own corrections.

A special economic zone is a designated area where tariffs, taxes and regulations are lighter than in the rest of the country, to attract investment and exporters. Ireland opened a duty-free zone at Shannon Airport in 1959. China designated Shenzhen and three other coastal zones in 1980, and Shenzhen grew from a modest border county into a major industrial city.

Spectacles mount two convex glass lenses in a frame before the eyes, helping people whose near vision fades with age. In a Florence sermon of 1305 or 1306 the Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making them was under twenty years old, placing the invention in Italy in the 1280s; the original maker is unidentified.

A spectroscope spreads light into its colours so that fine lines can be measured. Around 1814 Joseph von Fraunhofer charted hundreds of dark lines in sunlight without explaining them. In 1859-60 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed that each element emits and absorbs its own lines, found caesium and rubidium, and identified iron, sodium and other elements in the Sun.

The spinning jenny let one worker spin several threads at once. A hand-turned wheel drove a row of spindles while a sliding clamp drew out the cotton, imitating a spinner's hand. James Hargreaves of Lancashire built it around 1764 and patented it in 1770. Early machines carried eight spindles; jenny yarn was soft, suited mainly to weft.

The spinning mule, completed by Samuel Crompton near Bolton around 1779, joined the jenny's moving carriage to the water frame's drafting rollers, hence its hybrid name. Rollers drew the cotton out; the carriage then ran back, stretching and twisting it further. The thread was fine and strong enough for muslins, long imported mainly from India. Crompton never patented it.

Spinning twists short fibres into continuous, strong thread. A drop spindle is a stick weighted with a whorl of stone, clay or bone that keeps it turning while the spinner draws out flax, wool or cotton. Perforated whorls are common at Neolithic sites in southwest Asia and Europe by roughly 6,000 BCE. Spinning often took more labour than weaving.

The spinning wheel turns the spindle with a hand-driven wheel and band, spinning much faster than a hand spindle, although early wheels made the spinner alternate twisting and winding. It probably originated in India, China or the Islamic world late in the first millennium CE and reached Europe by the thirteenth century. A later flyer allowed continuous spinning.

The coach was a passenger carriage whose body hung from leather straps, and later from steel springs, to soften the ride. The word is often traced to Kocs, a Hungarian village known for light carriages in the fifteenth century. Scheduled stagecoach services, changing horses at regular stages, appeared in seventeenth-century England, carrying passengers, mail and light goods.

A stamp seal is a carved object pressed into soft clay to leave a recognisable mark. Stamp seals were used in the Near East by the seventh millennium BCE, and at Halaf-period sites of the sixth millennium clay sealings closed jars, baskets and storeroom doors. A broken sealing revealed tampering, so seals controlled stores and marked ownership without writing.

A balance supports fair exchange only if weights agree. Indus cities from about 2500 BCE used chert cubes on one standard, a common unit near 13.7 grams, scaling by doubling and then by tens. Mesopotamia counted shekels, minas and talents in sixties, with local variation. After unifying China in 221 BCE, the Qin state imposed uniform weights by edict.

A standing army is a permanent professional force, paid and supplied by the state in peace and war, which replaces or supplements seasonal levies, making soldiering a full-time occupation. An inscription of Sargon of Akkad, about 2300 BCE, claims 5,400 men ate daily before him; Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III, after 745 BCE, made provinces supply troops able to campaign year-round.

A state academy is a ruler-funded institution where scholars study and future officials are trained. In Alexandria, the Ptolemies founded the Mouseion with its great library about 290 BCE, supporting scholars at royal expense. In China, Emperor Wu of Han established the Imperial Academy in 124 BCE to teach the Confucian classics to students who could then enter government service.

State-sponsored exploration meant rulers funding and directing long voyages, then claiming or recording what they found. Between 1405 and 1433 Ming China sent seven great fleets under Zheng He across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa. Portugal's voyages along the African coast began after the capture of Ceuta in 1415 and were long associated with Prince Henry.

A state gazette is an official bulletin through which a government publishes news, decrees and appointments. In 59 BCE, Julius Caesar as consul ordered the publication of the Roman Senate's proceedings, and the Acta Diurna, posted publicly in Rome, reported official business and notable events. Imperial China later circulated court gazettes, known as dibao, among officials.

A state monopoly reserves the making or selling of a staple to the government, turning an everyday necessity into revenue. Under Emperor Wu of Han, salt and iron production was taken over by state agencies from about 117 BCE to pay for wars against the Xiongnu. A court debate of 81 BCE, the Discourses on Salt and Iron, contested it.

A state navy is a permanent war fleet that the state builds, crews and pays for. Phoenician cities supplied fleets to kings by about 700 BCE. In 483 BCE Athens used a rich silver strike at Laurion to build a fleet of triremes on Themistocles' proposal, and it fought at Salamis three years later.

State propaganda offices shape news, posters, films and broadcasts to mobilize public opinion behind a government. The United States created the Committee on Public Information in 1917 to promote its war effort, and Germany's Reich Ministry for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda under Joseph Goebbels, founded in 1933, controlled the press, radio and film.

A state religion is a faith established by law, with its clergy supported and its rivals placed at a disadvantage. Armenia is traditionally held to have adopted Christianity as its official religion around 301 CE. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica, issued by Theodosius I with his co-emperors, made Nicene Christianity the required faith of the Roman Empire.

State resettlement moved whole conquered communities to distant provinces, to farm empty land, supply labour and break old loyalties. The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III, who reigned from 745 BCE, made mass deportation a regular policy. After capturing Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BCE, the Babylonians deported much of Judah's elite to Babylonia, an episode remembered as the Babylonian exile.

Royal storehouses held a ruler's revenue in kind, such as grain, wine, livestock and silver, and released it only against sealed written orders. The Persepolis Fortification tablets, thousands of clay records from about 509 to 493 BCE under Darius I, document such stores and the rations issued to workers, travellers and officials around the Achaemenid heartland.

Statecraft doctrine is practical advice on running a state: managing officials, collecting revenue, gathering intelligence and waging war. In India, the Arthashastra, traditionally linked to Kautilya at the Maurya court, is thought to have been compiled over several centuries from about 300 BCE. In China, the Han Feizi, from the mid-third century BCE, set out Legalist doctrines of rule.

After independence, India faced demands to redraw provinces inherited from British rule along lines of language. Andhra State was formed for Telugu speakers in 1953, after the death of Potti Sriramulu during a hunger strike. A commission followed, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew boundaries so that most states were organized around a major language.

Stealth, or low observability, reduces how easily radar, infrared and other sensors detect an aircraft, using shapes that deflect radar waves away from the transmitter and radar-absorbent materials.
