The American F-117, first flown in 1981, used flat faceted surfaces because computers of the time could calculate their radar returns; its unstable shape required computerised fly-by-wire control.

Thomas Newcomen's engine of 1712 used the pressure of the air, not of steam, to do work. Steam filled a cylinder, a jet of cold water condensed it, and the partial vacuum let the atmosphere push a piston down, rocking a beam that worked mine pumps. Its first cylinders were brass; cast-iron cylinders came from Coalbrookdale in the 1720s.

High-pressure engines used steam well above atmospheric pressure to drive the piston directly, without a condenser or heavy beam. Richard Trevithick in Cornwall and Oliver Evans in the United States built such engines around 1800-1804. Compact and powerful, they could move themselves: Trevithick's locomotive ran at Penydarren, Wales, in 1804. Their boilers needed wrought iron, made in quantity by puddling.

Steam power transformed printing in the nineteenth century. Friedrich Koenig's steam-driven cylinder press printed The Times of London in 1814, far faster than hand presses. In the 1840s, Richard Hoe of New York developed a rotary press that printed thousands of sheets an hour. Cheap mass-circulation newspapers followed, carrying news, prices and political debate to wide readerships.

Early steam engines pumped water with an up-and-down beam. Between 1781 and 1784 Boulton and Watt made their engine turn a shaft through the sun-and-planet gear and made it double-acting, with steam pushing the piston both ways. Rotary engines could drive textile and other machinery directly, so factories no longer had to stand beside fast rivers.

James Watt saw that the atmospheric engine wasted fuel by cooling and reheating its cylinder at every stroke. His remedy, patented in 1769, was a separate vessel where steam condensed while the cylinder stayed hot. Engines built by Boulton and Watt from the 1770s used much less coal for the same work, so steam power paid far from coalfields.

A steam turbine draws work from expanding steam with rows of blades on a spinning shaft instead of a piston. In 1884 Charles Parsons built a multi-stage turbine where steam expanded in many small steps; Gustaf de Laval developed an impulse design in Sweden. Turbines suited high-speed generators, and Parsons's Turbinia showed their speed at sea in 1897.

A steamboat drives paddle wheels with a steam engine, freeing travel from wind and current. Several inventors built experimental vessels in the 1780s and 1790s; Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat began regular service on the Hudson between New York and Albany in 1807. Steamers soon worked upstream on large rivers and, later in the century, crossed oceans.

Bloomery iron is soft; holding it in contact with hot charcoal lets carbon diffuse into the surface, turning it into steel that takes a harder edge. Some early iron blades from the eastern Mediterranean, including a knife from Idalion, Cyprus, of the twelfth or eleventh century BCE, were deliberately carburized, though few objects that old have been analysed.

A steppe empire is a confederation of nomadic clans united under a single ruler, with the army organized in decimal units of tens, hundreds and thousands and lands assigned to the ruler's kin. Modu Chanyu forged the Xiongnu empire around 209 BCE. Temüjin, proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206, built the Mongol Empire on similar lines.

A sternpost rudder is a single blade hinged on the centreline at a ship's stern, replacing large steering oars over the side. A pottery ship model from a Han tomb at Guangzhou, of about the 1st century CE, shows an early axial rudder. In northern Europe hinged rudders appear around 1180. The rudder let larger hulls be steered precisely.

Stirrups give a rider footholds, steadying the seat for archery and close combat. Single mounting stirrups appear in China by the fourth century CE; the earliest dated pair, from the tomb of Feng Sufu in northeast China, who died in 415 CE, is wood sheathed in metal. Paired stirrups reached Europe by about the seventh century, probably with the Avars.

A stock exchange is a regulated market where shares in companies, and often government debt, are bought and sold. Antwerp opened a purpose-built bourse in 1531, used mainly for commodities and bills of exchange. When the Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602, its shares began trading in Amsterdam, often regarded as the first continuous market in company stock.

Stock friendship is a pastoral practice in which herders place animals with partners in other districts and keep the partners' animals in return. Spreading a herd this way insures against drought, disease and raiding, and builds lasting alliances. Ethnographers have described it among East African peoples such as the Turkana, Jie and Maasai; its prehistoric origins are inferred, not documented.

Dry-stone construction builds walls from unmortared stones held in place by their weight, shape and careful placement. Large-scale stone building is attested at Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey from about 9,500 BCE. At Skara Brae in Orkney, about 3,000 BCE, houses, beds and dressers were built of stacked flagstone. Terraces and field walls use the same craft.

Ashlar fortification applies dressed-stone building to defence: thick walls of heavy blocks that resist battering rams, towers projecting so defenders can shoot along the wall face, and gates built as defended passages. Late Bronze Age examples include the walls and gates of Hattusa, the Hittite capital, and the Lion Gate at Mycenae, both about the thirteenth century BCE.

Strategic stockpiles are reserves of fuel, metals and other essentials that a state holds to release when imports or supplies fail. The United States began stockpiling critical materials under a law of 1939, and after the Arab oil embargo of 1973 it created the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in 1975, storing crude oil in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast.

Stratigraphy reads rock layers as history. In 1669 Nicolaus Steno argued that sediments settle in horizontal layers, the lowest oldest. William Smith found that English strata follow a regular order recognisable by their fossils; his 1815 map covered a whole country. Such maps let geologists predict hidden coal or ironstone, and Britain founded a geological survey in 1835.

Iron became a structural material in Britain once coke smelting made cast iron plentiful. The Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale, cast by Abraham Darby III, was erected in 1779 and opened in 1781. Shrewsbury's Ditherington Flax Mill (1797) had an internal frame of iron columns and beams to resist fire. London's Crystal Palace of 1851 assembled prefabricated iron and glass.

Submarines travel beneath the surface by flooding and emptying ballast tanks to change buoyancy. Practical boats around 1900, such as John Holland's design for the US Navy, ran petrol engines on the surface and battery-powered electric motors underwater. In the First World War, German U-boat campaigns against merchant shipping showed the submarine's strategic weight and helped prompt Allied convoys.

Submarine cables carry telegraph signals under the sea inside insulation of gutta-percha, a latex from Southeast Asian trees. A working cable crossed the English Channel in 1851. The 1858 transatlantic cable failed within weeks, but the steamship Great Eastern laid a lasting one in 1866. By the early 1870s cables linked Britain with India and Australia.

A succession rule fixes who inherits power, by birth order or election within a defined group, so a ruler's death need not reopen the struggle for power. The Hittite Proclamation of Telipinu, about 1500 BCE, set an order of royal heirs after dynastic murders; Zhou China favoured the senior line of elder sons; Mongol khans were chosen by a kurultai.

Succession oaths bind powerful subjects in advance to accept a chosen heir. In 672 BCE the Assyrian king Esarhaddon made officials and vassal rulers swear loyalty to his son Ashurbanipal, under long lists of divine curses. Copies of these treaties were found at Nimrud and at Tell Tayinat in Turkey, and Ashurbanipal took the throne as planned in 669 BCE.

Sugarcane was first domesticated in New Guinea, but boiling its juice until sugar crystallised into storable granules is credited to India, where the technique developed about two thousand years ago and was refined in the early centuries CE. From the seventh century the expanding Islamic world carried cane and sugar-making westward to Egypt, North Africa, Spain and Italy.

Sulfonamides were among the first synthetic drugs to treat bacterial infections inside the body. At Bayer in Germany, Gerhard Domagk found in 1932 that the dye Prontosil was far more effective than earlier dyes; results appeared in 1935. Researchers in Paris then showed that the active part was sulfanilamide. In 1936 Leonard Colebrook sharply reduced childbed-fever deaths with sulfonamides.

Sulphuric acid became the basic reagent of chemical industry. Earlier makers burned sulphur with saltpetre over water in fragile glass vessels. In 1746 John Roebuck, in Birmingham, replaced them with chambers of riveted lead sheet, a cheap metal the acid barely attacks, cutting costs sharply. The acid then fed soda making and, from the 1840s, superphosphate fertiliser.

Superalloys are nickel-based alloys that keep their strength when red-hot and under stress. Patents from 1929 showed that titanium and aluminium could form tiny strengthening particles in nickel-chromium. After a British government request in 1939, Mond Nickel tested over a thousand experimental alloys; Nimonic 80, introduced in 1941, became the standard turbine-blade alloy of British gas turbines.

In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes's Leiden laboratory found that mercury cooled with liquid helium to about 4 kelvin loses all electrical resistance. Early superconductors failed in modest magnetic fields; from 1961-62, niobium-tin and niobium-titanium wires carried large currents in strong fields and were wound into magnets. Niobium-titanium filaments finer than a hair now carry the Large Hadron Collider's magnet currents.

A supranational union pools parts of its members' sovereignty in common institutions with their own law, court and market. Six western European states founded the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 under a shared High Authority. The Maastricht Treaty created the European Union in 1993, building a single market with free movement of goods and people.

A surgical instrument set is a standardised kit of specialised tools: scalpels, probes, forceps, hooks, specula and bone levers, usually of bronze or iron. Roman sets survive from Pompeii, buried in 79 CE, and from a second-century doctor's grave at Bingen, Germany. Indian texts in the Sushruta tradition also list instruments. Roman legionary forts had dedicated hospitals.

Measuring fields and recording their sides and areas let early administrations assess land and settle claims. Tablets from Shuruppak in Mesopotamia, about 2600 BCE, already tabulate areas computed from lengths, and Egyptian papyri of the second millennium BCE work out the areas of fields. Keeping such results beyond one surveyor's memory depended on a written system of numbers.

Sustained-yield forestry divides woodland into measured plots, cuts them in rotation and replants, so that no more timber is taken each year than grows back. Colbert's French forest ordinance of 1669 regulated royal forests partly to secure naval timber. In Saxony in 1713, the mining official Hans Carl von Carlowitz wrote Sylvicultura oeconomica, often credited with the idea of sustainability.

Sworn treaties are written agreements between rulers, sealed by oaths before the gods, with lists of divine witnesses and curses on whoever breaks them. They fixed peace, borders, alliance and the return of fugitives. A well-preserved example is the treaty between Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Hattusili III, of the mid-thirteenth century BCE.

Synoptic meteorology combines simultaneous weather observations from many places into a single map. After a storm wrecked French and British ships near Balaklava during the Crimean War in 1854, Urbain Le Verrier organised a telegraphed network of observing stations in France. In Britain, Robert FitzRoy began issuing public storm warnings in 1861, using telegraphed reports from coastal stations.

In 1856 William Perkin, a teenage student trying to synthesise the antimalarial quinine, instead obtained a purple dye from aniline, a coal-tar product. He patented mauveine and opened a factory in 1857. Chemists then searched for other coal-tar colours, beginning with magenta; by 1914 German firms produced about 90 percent of the world's dyes.

Systematic theology uses philosophical reasoning to organise religious doctrine into a coherent whole. Augustine of Hippo, writing around 400 CE, joined Christian belief with Platonist philosophy. In medieval universities, scholastic masters taught doctrine through questions and formal disputation, and Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae, written between about 1265 and 1274, drew heavily on Aristotle.

Notches cut into bone store a count outside memory. Notched bones from Border Cave, southern Africa, over 40,000 years old, are read as notational, and the Ishango bone from the Congo, about 20,000 years old, bears grouped notches. Whether they record numbers, lunar months or something else is debated; one study found Ishango poorly suited to exact calculation.

A tank is an armoured, tracked vehicle carrying its own guns. British designers drew on the crawler track of agricultural tractors such as Benjamin Holt's, first tested in 1904, to cross trenches. Tanks first went into action at Flers-Courcelette on the Somme in September 1916, some carrying six-pounder guns, others only machine guns. Early tanks were slow and unreliable.

Tax farming hands the collection of a tax to private contractors, who bid for the right, pay the state an agreed sum and keep whatever more they collect. Classical Athens let tax contracts through officials called poletai; Roman censors auctioned contracts to companies of publicani; and France's General Farm, created in 1681, collected indirect taxes until the Revolution abolished it.

Early taxation took the form of tribute in kind: a counted share of grain, livestock or craft goods owed to a ruler or temple. In Uruk-period Mesopotamia, from about 3300 BCE, officials recorded receipts and rations on clay tablets and sealed stored goods; in early dynastic Egypt, wealth was counted and harvests assessed, partly in light of the Nile flood.

Biological classification sorts living things into nested groups and gives each a stable name. Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae (1735) ranked organisms in kingdoms, classes, orders, genera and species. His Species Plantarum (1753) used two-word names consistently for nearly 6,000 plants and is still the formal starting point for scientific plant names.

State technical academies trained engineers and mining officials in mathematics, chemistry, mechanics and geology. The mining academy at Freiberg in Saxony, founded in 1765, where Abraham Gottlob Werner taught mineralogy, drew students from across Europe. Revolutionary France founded the École polytechnique in 1794 to train engineers for state service, and similar schools followed in many countries.

The electric telegraph sends coded pulses of current along wires. In 1837 William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle telegraph in Britain, while Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail developed a recording system in the United States, where a Washington-Baltimore line opened in 1844. Messages could now routinely outrun couriers, reshaping railways, markets, journalism and government.

Telegraph news agencies gathered news and market prices by wire and sold them to many newspapers at once. Bernhard Wolff founded a telegraphic bureau in Berlin in 1849, and Paul Julius Reuter, who had used carrier pigeons to bridge a gap in the telegraph lines, opened his London office in 1851. Agence Havas in Paris was older still.

The telephone converts speech into a varying electric current and back into sound. Alexander Graham Bell received a United States patent in 1876, amid a rival filing by Elisha Gray and earlier work by Antonio Meucci and others. Carbon transmitters soon made speech louder and clearer, and within a few years cities had exchanges where operators connected calls by hand.

The first telescopes came from Dutch spectacle makers. In October 1608 the States General in The Hague considered a patent for Hans Lipperhey's instrument but refused it as too easy to copy, and others claimed the idea. Galileo built stronger instruments from 1609 and in March 1610, in Sidereus Nuncius, reported bodies circling Jupiter.

Television transmits moving images by scanning a scene line by line and turning brightness into a signal. John Logie Baird demonstrated mechanical television in London in 1926, while Philo Farnsworth, Vladimir Zworykin and others developed electronic camera tubes. The BBC began a regular high-definition service from Alexandra Palace in 1936, and mass ownership grew after 1945.

Quenched steel is hard but brittle; reheating it to a moderate temperature relieves internal stress, giving up some hardness for much greater toughness. When smiths first tempered deliberately is hard to establish. Roman writers praised ferrum Noricum, steel from the eastern Alps, from the late first century BCE, though its quality is attributed largely to manganese-rich, low-phosphorus ore.

In Sumerian cities, temples were great households that owned fields, herds and workshops, employed labourers and stored and redistributed grain. Clay tablets from the Eanna precinct at Uruk, from about 3200 BCE, are among the earliest writing anywhere, and most of them record such goods and rations. The temples' economic weight varied between cities and periods.

Tenancy protection gives sharecroppers and tenants security against eviction and a fair, fixed rent or share. Ireland's Land Act of 1881 granted fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale, an early example. In West Bengal, Operation Barga, launched in 1978, registered sharecroppers so they could not be evicted while they paid the legal share of the crop.

Term limits restrict how many times, or for how long, a person may hold an office, forcing regular change at the top. Mexico's constitution of 1917 barred presidential re-election after the long rule of Porfirio Diaz. In the United States, George Washington's two-term precedent became law in 1951 with the Twenty-second Amendment, after Franklin Roosevelt won four elections.

Terraces cut hillsides into level steps held by walls, slowing runoff, trapping soil and creating fields on slopes too steep to plough. They were built independently in many mountain regions. In highland Yemen terrace farming dates to at least the third millennium BCE; in the Andes terraces were intensively used centuries before the Inka, and about a million hectares survive.

Territorial kingship unites many communities under one hereditary king, who governs through a royal household and appointed officials, commands the army and acts as supreme judge, with authority resting on divine sanction or dynastic right. Early examples arose separately in Egypt, unified by about 3100 BCE, Akkad under Sargon about 2300 BCE, and Shang China from about 1600 BCE.

In a theocracy, supreme political authority belongs to religious office-holders, or to a ruler whose title is religious, and religious law serves as the law of the state. Examples include Thebes under the high priests of Amun from the eleventh century BCE, the Papal States from 756 CE, and Tibet under the Fifth Dalai Lama (1617-1682) and his successors.

Thermodynamics is the science of heat, work and energy. Sadi Carnot's 1824 study of heat engines showed that their efficiency has an upper limit. After James Joule and others showed in the 1840s that heat and work are interchangeable forms of energy, Rudolf Clausius (1850) and William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin (1851), stated its laws; Clausius named entropy in 1865.

A thermonuclear weapon uses a fission explosion to compress and heat hydrogen isotopes until they fuse, releasing far more energy than fission alone. The United States tested the first full-scale device, Ivy Mike, on 1 November 1952; the Soviet Union tested its own in November 1955. Such weapons became central to Cold War deterrence and later arms-control negotiations.

Think tanks are independent institutes that employ researchers to analyse public policy and propose reforms. The Institute for Government Research, founded in Washington in 1916, later merged into the Brookings Institution. RAND began as an air force research project in 1946 and became an independent nonprofit corporation in 1948, applying systems analysis to defence and later social policy.

In three-field rotation, a village's land was divided so that one field carried winter wheat or rye, a second spring crops such as oats, barley, peas or beans, and the third lay fallow. Only a third rested each year instead of half. Estate surveys from Carolingian Francia around 800 CE show the system, which spread across northern Europe.

Timber-frame building sets heavy posts in the ground or on sills and links them with beams, so the frame rather than the walls carries the roof. Linear Pottery farmers in central Europe, from about 5,500 BCE, raised longhouses often over 20 metres long, with rows of internal posts and wattle-and-daub walls. Polished stone adzes shaped the timber.

Alloying copper with up to about ten percent tin makes tin bronze. Tin bronzes appear in Mesopotamia and Anatolia in the early third millennium BCE, although neither region had significant tin sources; a bronze foil from Plocnik, Serbia, about 4650 BCE, is claimed as earliest. Bronze-making there therefore depended on tin brought from elsewhere.

Tinplate is thin iron sheet coated with tin so it resists rust, making light, cheap containers and kitchenware. It was produced in Bohemia and the Upper Palatinate by the late Middle Ages from hammered sheet dipped in molten tin. In about 1720 ironworks at Pontypool in Wales began making it from rolled sheet, and tinplate later supplied the tin can.

Shaped clay counters appear at Near Eastern farming sites from about 8000 BCE. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued that each shape stood for a fixed quantity of a particular commodity, letting people keep accounts beyond memory. Her further thesis, that tokens led directly to writing, is influential but debated, though accounting needs are widely seen as one root of writing.

Torsion artillery stored energy in tightly twisted bundles of sinew or hair rope that drove two throwing arms. Greek engineers developed it in the fourth century BCE, probably under Philip II of Macedon, from earlier bow-powered catapults. Later writers such as Philon of Byzantium recorded formulas sizing the spring to the weight of the shot: engineering by calculation.

Total mobilization directs the whole economy and manpower of a state to war. When general mobilization was ordered across Europe in 1914, millions of reservists were called up within days. As the war dragged on, governments conscripted labour, controlled raw materials, fixed prices and converted factories to munitions, a pattern repeated on a larger scale in the Second World War.

Coal gas is made by heating coal in closed retorts and piping the gas to burners. William Murdoch lit his house at Redruth in Cornwall with it in 1792. The Gas Light and Coke Company, chartered in London in 1812, laid mains under the streets, and within decades gaslight illuminated city streets, mills and homes across Europe and North America.

The bastion fort, or trace italienne, answered siege cannon with low, thick, earth-backed walls faced in masonry, and angular bastions projecting from them. Bastions let defenders' guns sweep every face of the wall, leaving no dead ground at the foot of the curtain. Italian engineers developed the system around 1500, and it spread across Europe and to European overseas outposts.

A trackway is a deliberately built route: logs, planks, brushwood or laid stones that keep feet and loads above mud. The Sweet Track across England's Somerset Levels, a raised plank walkway, was built from timber felled around 3,800 BCE, a date fixed by tree rings. Such causeways linked dry ground across wetlands and were an early investment in routes.

The traction trebuchet is a pivoting beam with a sling on its long arm; a crew hauling ropes on the short arm swings it to hurl a stone. The Mohist Mojing, compiled in China around the fourth century BCE, describes such engines. Byzantine sources record them by the late sixth or early seventh century CE, possibly introduced through the Avars.

Exchange between distant communities is ancient, but organized trade with records and agents becomes clearer in the fourth millennium BCE, when Uruk-style settlements appeared far up the Euphrates. Around 1900 BCE, Assyrian merchants sent tin and textiles by donkey caravan to Kanesh in Anatolia, leaving tens of thousands of tablets documenting partnerships, prices and debts.

Trade treaties are agreements between rulers that protect merchants, set tolls and decide where disputes are heard. A treaty between Ebla and Abarsal in Syria, from about the twenty-fourth century BCE, is among the oldest known. Around 1900 BCE, Assyrian merchants trading in Anatolia operated under sworn agreements with the local rulers of Kanesh and other towns.

Trademark law lets makers register a distinctive name or sign for their goods and makes copying it an offence, so distant buyers can trust a brand. France passed a general trademark law in 1857. Britain's Trade Marks Registration Act of 1875 opened a register, and the Bass brewery's red triangle is often cited as its first entry.

Shared-river treaties divide the water of rivers that cross borders so that irrigation on each side has an assured supply. The 1929 Nile Waters Agreement between Egypt and Britain, acting for Sudan, allocated most of the river's flow to Egypt. The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, brokered by the World Bank, divided the Indus rivers between India and Pakistan.

Transhumance is the seasonal movement of herds between summer pastures in the mountains and winter grazing in the lowlands, along customary routes. It lets each range recover while the animals are elsewhere. Isotope studies of animal teeth suggest such movement in the Zagros and Alpine regions by about 5000 BCE, and it continues today in the Alps, Pyrenees and Balkans.

A transistor uses a semiconductor crystal to amplify or switch a current, doing a vacuum tube's work with far less power and heat. At Bell Telephone Laboratories, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built a point-contact transistor in December 1947, and William Shockley designed the junction transistor in 1948, building on the p-n junction Russell Ohl had found in 1940.

Transitional justice covers the trials, truth commissions, reparations and purges with which societies confront abuses after dictatorship or civil war. Argentina's National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created in 1983, documented thousands of disappearances under military rule. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, set up in 1995, offered amnesty to those who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes.

Patrons paid scholars to translate works of science and philosophy from other languages and to copy the results widely. In Abbasid Baghdad during the ninth century, caliphs and wealthy families sponsored translations of Greek texts into Arabic, an effort associated with the House of Wisdom and with Hunayn ibn Ishaq. In twelfth-century Toledo, scholars rendered Arabic works into Latin.

The counterweight trebuchet replaced the hauling crew of the earlier lever engine with a heavy weighted box on the short arm, giving more power and consistent shots. It appears in the eastern Mediterranean, in Byzantine and Islamic contexts, during the twelfth century. Engineers from the Islamic world built such machines for the Mongol siege of Xiangyang in 1273.

Trepanation is the deliberate removal of a piece of the skull vault by scraping, grooving or drilling, first with stone tools. Healed bone edges show that many patients survived. A burial at Ensisheim, Alsace, dated about 5100-4900 BCE, is among the earliest widely accepted cases, and the practice arose independently elsewhere, notably in the pre-Columbian Andes.

A tribal confederacy joins autonomous tribes or chiefdoms in a sworn league. Each member keeps its own leaders and customs, while a shared council handles war, peace and disputes between members, sometimes under a common war leader. The Xiongnu of the Mongolian steppe formed one around 209 BCE; the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy is another, though its founding date is debated.

In a tributary system, lesser rulers send envoys and gifts to a central court and receive titles, presents and trading access in return. After a defeat around 200 BCE, the Han dynasty of China made heqin agreements with the Xiongnu, sending princesses and goods. Later Han rulers received tribute missions from many neighbours, a pattern that long persisted in East Asia.

Trigonometry relates angles to lengths. Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya of 499 CE tabulated the half-chord, the ancestor of the sine, at steps of 3 degrees 45 minutes. Astronomers in the Islamic world extended the method: in the late tenth century Abu al-Wafa used the tangent, compiled finer tables and proved the sine rule for spherical triangles, used in astronomical computation.

A trip hammer is a heavy beam lifted by cams on a turning water-wheel shaft and then dropped under its own weight. Chinese writers of the Han period, around the turn of the first century CE, describe water-powered hammers husking grain; later they crushed ore and pounded fibres. Medieval Europe used similar cam-driven hammers for forging iron and fulling cloth.

Turnpike trusts were bodies set up by Act of Parliament to collect tolls from road users and spend them on repairing and improving a stretch of highway. England's first turnpike act, in 1663, covered part of the Great North Road. From about 1706, trusts run by local trustees spread rapidly, and by the 1830s they managed most main roads.

Type founding casts many identical metal letters. Each letter is cut in relief on a hard punch, struck into a softer copper matrix, and the matrix fitted into an adjustable hand mould for pouring molten alloy. Johannes Gutenberg developed this system in Strasbourg and Mainz around the 1440s. Earlier movable type in China and Korea was made by other methods.

In archaic Greece a tyrant was a ruler who seized power in a city outside the traditional aristocratic order, often with popular support or hired soldiers. Cypselus took Corinth around 657 BCE, and Peisistratus established lasting rule at Athens around 546 BCE. Tyrants often ruled through patronage, festivals and public works such as temples, fountains and harbours.

Unemployment insurance pays a weekly benefit to insured workers who lose their jobs while they look for new work. Part II of Britain's National Insurance Act of 1911 created one of the first compulsory national schemes, at first covering trades such as building and shipbuilding. The United States Social Security Act of 1935 established federal and state unemployment insurance.

Universal conscription makes military service a legal obligation for men of set ages, enforced through registration and regular call-up. Revolutionary France decreed a levée en masse in 1793, and the Jourdan Law of 1798 established regular conscription by age class. It produced much larger armies but also evasion, desertion and heavy burdens on families and farm labour.

Universal secondary education keeps children in school into their teens, in free state secondary schools. In England, the Fisher Act of 1918 raised the leaving age to fourteen, and the Butler Education Act of 1944 made state secondary schooling free for all, with the leaving age raised to fifteen in 1947. Many countries made similar reforms after 1945.

Universal service policies require telephone carriers to connect households and remote areas at affordable, regulated rates, often using profits from busy urban lines to subsidize rural ones. In the United States, the Communications Act of 1934 set the goal of service for all the people, and the Federal Communications Commission it created oversaw rates.

Enrichment raises the share of fissile uranium-235 above its natural 0.7 per cent. Ore concentrate is first converted to uranium hexafluoride. Wartime Oak Ridge used electromagnetic separators wound with borrowed Treasury silver and the vast K-25 gaseous-diffusion plant; centrifuges later cut the electricity needed about fiftyfold. Reactor fuel needs 3-5%, weapons far more, so the step is internationally safeguarded.

Radioactive ore processing began with radium: in 1898 the Curies traced it through Joachimsthal pitchblende residues, and a Joachimsthal works held a radium monopoly in 1909-1913. Modern uranium mills crush ore, leach it with sulphuric acid and precipitate yellowcake, recovering 90-95% of the uranium. Over half of today's uranium is dissolved underground in place; mill tailings stay radioactive.

Vaccination replaced smallpox material with cowpox, a related cattle disease, giving protection without variolation's risk of severe smallpox. Edward Jenner tested it in England in 1796, drawing on the rural belief that milkmaids who caught cowpox escaped smallpox; the farmer Benjamin Jesty had tried it in 1774. Vaccination spread worldwide within decades. Smallpox eradication was certified in 1980.

Laboratory vaccines are made by deliberately weakening or killing pathogens grown under controlled conditions. Louis Pasteur produced attenuated vaccines against chicken cholera and anthrax between 1879 and 1881, and gave a rabies vaccine to a person in 1885. Growing viruses in cell culture later enabled Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine, licensed in 1955.

A vacuum tube controls electrons flowing from a heated electrode through an evacuated bulb. John Ambrose Fleming's diode of 1904 let current pass one way only, which made it a radio detector. In 1906 Lee de Forest sought a patent for what became his three-electrode Audion, whose grid let a weak signal control a stronger current.

A value-added tax is collected in stages: each business charges tax on its sales and deducts the tax already paid on its purchases, so only the value it adds is taxed. The French official Maurice Lauré designed the first practical version, introduced in 1954. Denmark and Brazil adopted broad versions in 1967, and the tax has since spread worldwide.

A vanguard party is a disciplined organization of professional revolutionaries that claims to lead the working class rather than follow it. Vladimir Lenin set out the idea in What Is to Be Done?, written in 1902. In October 1917 his Bolshevik party seized power in Petrograd and went on to govern Russia as the single ruling party.

Vaults and domes extend the arch into three dimensions: a barrel vault is a continuous arch, a dome an arch rotated about its centre. Roman builders cast them in concrete of lime and volcanic ash, as in the Pantheon's dome of about 125 CE. Hagia Sophia's brick dome followed in 537 CE; medieval masons built ribbed vaults of dressed stone.

Vernacular literature is writing in the spoken language of ordinary people rather than a learned language such as Latin or classical Chinese. In Japan, Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji in Japanese around 1008 CE, using the kana script. In Italy, Dante composed his Divine Comedy in Tuscan in the early fourteenth century, shaping literary Italian.

Veteran colonies settled discharged soldiers on surveyed plots of land, creating loyal communities that could defend and farm new territory. In Ptolemaic Egypt, soldier-settlers called cleruchs received allotments, many in the newly reclaimed Fayum during the third century BCE. In the late Roman Republic, generals from Marius onward secured land for their veterans, founding many colonies of former legionaries.

Veterans' benefits help former soldiers return to civilian life through schooling, training and help buying homes. The United States Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, paid college tuition and guaranteed home loans for millions of returning soldiers. Britain's Further Education and Training Scheme of 1945 paid for ex-service men and women to study.

Livestock disease campaigns use vaccination, surveillance and movement controls to suppress cattle plagues. The Office International des Épizooties was founded in Paris in 1924, after rinderpest reached Belgium, to share information between countries. The Global Rinderpest Eradication Programme, launched in 1994, coordinated vaccination and surveillance, and in 2011 rinderpest was declared the second disease ever eradicated, after smallpox.

Victory stelae are carved stone slabs set up by rulers to proclaim military triumphs and warn rebels. The stele of Naram-Sin of Akkad, about 2250 BCE, shows the king climbing a mountain over defeated enemies. Egypt's Senusret III placed boundary stelae at Semna, in Nubia, around 1850 BCE, forbidding Nubians to pass northward except to trade.

Early farming spread partly through village fission, in which a group of households left a crowded village with seed and livestock to found a new one nearby. Farming villages appeared in Greece by about 7000 BCE. Around 5500 BCE the Linearbandkeramik culture, named for its banded pottery, spread rapidly across central Europe, founding longhouse villages along fertile loess valleys.

In many medieval villages the assembly of tenants set the dates of ploughing, harvest and gleaning, limited how many beasts each household could graze on the common, and fined offenders. English manorial court rolls record such by-laws from the later thirteenth century. In the Swiss forest cantons, open-air assemblies of free men, the Landsgemeinde, governed shared pastures and common affairs.

Early farming villages protected their stored harvests with ditches, walls, palisades and watchmen. At Jericho a stone wall and a massive round tower were built about 8000 BCE, though their purpose is debated. In central Europe many villages were ringed by ditches and palisades around 5000 BCE, a period that also left mass graves of massacred villagers, as at Talheim.

In many farming villages one household head is recognized as headman: he speaks for the village to outsiders, calls households to common work and helps settle disputes, but leads mainly by persuasion. Ethnographers recorded headmen on every inhabited continent. In Ubaid villages of Mesopotamia, about 5500 to 4000 BCE, larger central houses are often read as homes of leading families.

In ancient Mesopotamian kingdoms, villages and city wards had heads who answered to the palace for taxes, labour and crimes, and spoke for their communities. Old Babylonian texts of about 1900 to 1600 BCE mention the rabianum, or mayor. The Code of Hammurabi makes the town and its mayor repay a robbery victim if the robber is not caught.

Public vocational training prepares young people for skilled trades to national standards. The United States Smith-Hughes Act of 1917 provided federal funds for agricultural, trade and home economics education in high schools. West Germany's Vocational Training Act of 1969 put the long-standing dual system, which combines workplace apprenticeship with part-time schooling, on a national legal footing.

A war band is an armed party raised from kin and allies for a raid or feud, led by a man chosen for skill and followed only for that venture. The cemetery at Jebel Sahaba in Sudanese Nubia, at least 13,000 years old, holds many skeletons with embedded stone points, among the earliest evidence of repeated violence between groups.

Rationing shares scarce food by fixed allowances per person, so that shortages fall evenly rather than on the poorest. Germany and Britain both rationed food during the First World War. In January 1940 Britain began rationing bacon, butter and sugar through ration books issued to every household, and some foods stayed rationed until 1954.

In the low-lying Netherlands, landholders formed water boards to build and maintain dikes, sluices and drainage, each paying a levy according to the land protected. The Hoogheemraadschap van Rijnland, chartered by the Count of Holland in 1255, is among the oldest. Dutch water boards remain elected public authorities today, with their own taxes.

A water clock measures time by a steady flow of water, not by the sky, so it works at night. The oldest surviving one, an outflow vessel from Karnak made under Amenhotep III around 1390-1350 BCE, has twelve columns of marks, one per month, to allow for changing night lengths. An earlier official, Amenemhet, claimed its invention in his tomb.

Rome created a permanent board of water commissioners, the cura aquarum, in 11 BCE to maintain the city's aqueducts, license private connections and punish illegal tapping. Frontinus, appointed curator in 97 CE, wrote a treatise on the aqueducts describing their sources, capacities and the frauds he uncovered. His work remains a key account of Roman water administration.

The water frame spun strong cotton thread by drawing fibre between pairs of rollers turning at rising speeds, then twisting it onto a bobbin with a flyer. Richard Arkwright patented it in 1769, adapting roller drafting tried by Lewis Paul and John Wyatt in 1738. Its firm yarn suited warp. Arkwright began building a water-powered mill at Cromford in 1771.

A water mill uses a flowing stream to turn a wheel driving millstones, replacing human or animal labour in grinding grain. Greek evidence suggests water-driven wheels by about the third century BCE, though it is debated; a Perachora wheel probably lifted water instead. Roman engineers spread water mills, and Han China developed water power independently by the first century CE.

Where farming depended on canals, law had to settle who could draw water and who must maintain the banks. The Code of Hammurabi of Babylon, about 1754 BCE, made a farmer who neglected his dike liable for the damage when it broke and flooded neighbours' fields. Comparable rules appear in many irrigation societies, from ancient Egypt to medieval Spain.

The water screw is a helix of planks or tubing fixed inside an inclined cylinder; turning it lifts water from the lower end to the upper. Ancient writers credited Archimedes of Syracuse, of the third century BCE, though earlier origins have been proposed. It irrigated Egyptian fields and drained Roman mines, and its principle survives in modern pumps and conveyors.

A water turbine passes water under pressure through curved blades in a closed casing, extracting more energy than an open wheel, especially from high falls. Benoît Fourneyron's turbine of 1827 in France, James Francis's inward-flow design in the United States (1849), and Lester Pelton's impulse wheel in California (about 1880) made high heads usable. Turbines later drove hydroelectric generators.

In arid lands, those who built an irrigation channel often owned its flow, divided into timed turns that could be inherited or sold. The Greek historian Polybius reports that Persian Achaemenid kings granted the use of new underground channels, or qanats, to their builders for five generations. Timed water shares of this kind survive in Iranian and Omani villages today.

Watertight bulkheads divide a hull into sealed compartments with solid cross-partitions, so a breach floods one section rather than the whole ship. Chinese shipbuilders used them in junks by about the middle of the first millennium CE. The Quanzhou wreck, sunk around 1275, had thirteen compartments. European ships widely adopted the principle only in the 19th century.

Wayfinding lore is knowledge of routes, landmarks, water sources and the rising points of stars, memorized in songs and stories so travellers can journey far and return. Raw materials carried hundreds of kilometres by about 40,000 years ago suggest such knowledge was old. Aboriginal Australian songlines, which encode tracks across country in sung sequences, are a well-documented living example.

Numerical weather prediction forecasts the atmosphere by solving equations for motion, heat and moisture on a grid, starting from conditions reported by stations and radio balloons. Lewis Fry Richardson hand-computed a forecast during the First World War; published in 1922, it failed badly. In 1950 a Princeton team including Jule Charney produced the first successful computer forecasts, on ENIAC.

A weekly rest day releases workers from labour at regular intervals. In the Hebrew Bible, the commandment in Deuteronomy, a book whose core is often dated to the seventh century BCE, extends sabbath rest to servants, resident foreigners and working animals. The seven-day cycle of rest later spread with Judaism, Christianity and Islam, each keeping its own holy day.

Universal social security covers every citizen from cradle to grave through insurance for all and a safety net beneath it. In Britain, William Beveridge's report of 1942 proposed attacking five giant evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. The National Insurance and National Assistance Acts, in force from 1948, put much of the plan into practice.

A dug well reaches groundwater through a lined shaft, allowing settlement away from rivers and water in drought. Stone-lined wells are known from Neolithic Cyprus and from Atlit-Yam, a village now under the sea off Israel, roughly 10,500 to 8,300 years ago. Linear Pottery farmers in central Europe lined wells with split oak felled around 5,200 BCE.

The state sovereignty system treats states as legally equal, each holding exclusive authority within its borders. It is often traced to the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, which ended the Thirty Years' War, though historians debate how far those treaties actually created it. The principle of non-interference in domestic affairs later became a foundation of modern international law.

A solid wheel turning with an axle lets a load roll instead of being dragged. Wheels made from one to three shaped planks appear in Europe and Mesopotamia during the 4th millennium BCE, so close in date that no single place of invention can be fixed. These heavy disc wheels suited slow wagons and carts drawn by oxen.

Spoked wheels replaced the heavy disc with a hub, radiating spokes and a jointed rim, cutting weight while keeping strength. The earliest known examples, surviving as stains in graves of the Sintashta culture east of the southern Urals, date to around 2,000 BCE. Light enough for fast horse-drawn chariots, the design spread across much of Eurasia within centuries.

The wheellock struck sparks by spinning a serrated wheel against a piece of pyrite, so a gun could be carried loaded and fired without a burning match. It was devised in Europe around 1500 to 1515, and Augsburg armourers were among the first makers of wheellock pistols. Intricate, often made by clockmakers, it was first fitted to horsemen's firearms.

A modern wind turbine turns a rotor of a few long blades to drive a generator that feeds the electricity grid. Johannes Juul's Gedser turbine of 1957 in Denmark used an induction generator kept in step with the grid, a layout later called the Danish concept. From the 1980s Danish manufacturers produced such turbines in series, with glass-fibre composite blades.

A post mill carries its whole body, sails and gearing on one upright post, so the miller can turn it to face the wind. Documents first record such mills in England and Flanders in the late twelfth century. Needing no river, they spread through manors and monasteries; later windmills with turning caps also drained low-lying land, notably in the Netherlands.

In a vertical-axis windmill, sails of cloth or reed matting turn around an upright shaft, so the wind drives the millstone directly without gearing. Such mills are associated with Sistan, on the arid borderland of Iran and Afghanistan, where strong seasonal winds blow. Geographers writing in Arabic described them by the tenth century; earlier reports are uncertain.

Roman builders set panes of glass, cast flat or made by blowing, into window openings. The oldest Roman window glass known comes from Pompeii and Herculaneum, buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE. Such panes were valued in baths and houses for keeping in warmth and securing openings more than for clear views, since the glass was rarely transparent.

Wire drawing pulls a metal rod through successively smaller holes in a hard drawplate, thinning and lengthening it into uniform wire for mail, pins and the cards used to comb wool. Hand drawplates long preceded machines; wire-drawers are recorded in Nuremberg by 1360, and water-powered drawing mills spread in late medieval Germany, raising output.

Tax withholding makes employers deduct income tax from wages before paying them and pass it directly to the treasury. Wartime needs drove its spread: the United States adopted general withholding with the Current Tax Payment Act of 1943, and Britain introduced Pay As You Earn in 1944. Collection at the source made taxing mass incomes practical.

A witnessed agreement is a sale, loan or pledge made before named witnesses who can later swear to its terms, letting strangers trust a deal. The practice almost certainly predates writing. Some of the earliest Sumerian land-sale documents, including tablets from Fara, ancient Shuruppak, of about 2600 BCE, list witnesses alongside the buyer, seller and price.

In the later nineteenth century, colleges and secondary schools opened to women and girls, and women began to take degrees and enter professions such as medicine and teaching. Girton College, founded in 1869, was an early college for women associated with Cambridge, and France's Camille Sée law of 1880 created state secondary schools for girls.

Women's suffrage gives women the vote on the same terms as men. New Zealand, then a self-governing British colony, became in 1893 the first country to grant women the vote in national elections, after petitions led by Kate Sheppard. Australia followed for federal elections in 1902, Finland in 1906, and many countries after the First World War.

Woodblock printing transfers ink from a carved relief block to paper, copying a whole page at once. It developed in East Asia by the eighth century CE; a Buddhist charm sealed in a Korean pagoda by 751 may be among the earliest prints. The Diamond Sutra scroll found at Dunhuang, dated 868, is the oldest dated printed book known.

Wool is the fine, crimped underfleece of domestic sheep. Wild sheep carry mostly coarse hair, and the first herders in southwest Asia, about 11,000 years ago, kept sheep chiefly for meat and milk. Woolly breeds became economically important later, notably in fourth-millennium-BCE Mesopotamia. Spun fleece provided cloth without setting aside farmland for a fibre crop.

Crucible steel is made by sealing iron with carbon-bearing material in clay crucibles and heating until the charge melts, giving uniform high-carbon steel. South India and Sri Lanka produced it from around the mid-first millennium BCE, and such ingots fed the famous patterned Damascus blades. At Merv, Turkmenistan, ninth-century smiths made crucible steel by a different co-fusion route.

Reciprocal work parties are gatherings in which households call on neighbours to help raise a house or bring in a harvest, repaying them with food, drink and labour in turn. They are widely recorded among farming peoples. At Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, from about 7400 BCE, houses were repeatedly rebuilt on the same spot, which may have involved neighbourly cooperation.

Workmen's compensation requires employers to pay for injuries suffered at work, regardless of who was at fault. Germany introduced compulsory accident insurance in 1884 as part of Bismarck's social legislation, funded by employers' associations. Britain's Workmen's Compensation Act of 1897 made employers in many dangerous trades liable for workplace accidents. Similar laws spread widely afterwards.

A written constitution is a single fundamental law that establishes government's organs, defines their powers and is usually harder to amend than statutes. England's Instrument of Government of 1653 is an early example, and the United States Constitution of 1787 is often described as the oldest national constitution still in force. Text alone does not guarantee rulers observe it.

X-rays are invisible, penetrating radiation that Wilhelm Röntgen discovered on 8 November 1895 while experimenting with a cathode-ray tube in Würzburg. Because bone absorbs them more strongly than soft tissue, his early images showed the bones of a hand. Within months doctors used radiographs to locate fractures and embedded bullets. Early operators, unaware of the hazard, suffered serious radiation injuries.

Elected rural councils run local schools, clinics, roads and relief for a district. In Russia the zemstvo reform of 1864, which followed the emancipation of the serfs, created district and provincial assemblies elected by landowners, townspeople and peasant communities, weighted towards the gentry. They built schools and clinics and organized grain relief. England created elected county councils in 1888.

Zoning divides a city into districts with permitted uses, such as housing, commerce or industry, and rules for the height and bulk of buildings. New York City's 1916 Zoning Resolution, prompted partly by the towering Equitable Building, required tall buildings to step back from the street and became a model for zoning across the United States.
